WINkLink is becoming an increasingly important bridge between blockchain automation and information from the world outside the chain.

Smart contracts can execute predefined instructions automatically, but they cannot independently access external information.

That creates a critical infrastructure gap.

How WINkLink bridges that gap:

➞ A DeFi protocol needs a current asset price
➞ An AI agent requires verified market information
➞ A smart contract needs an external event before executing
➞ WINkLink retrieves the required information from external sources
➞ Oracle nodes validate and aggregate the data
➞ The verified result is delivered on-chain
➞ The smart contract can then respond according to its programmed logic

This process may happen behind the scenes, but it powers many of the applications users interact with every day.

Why the oracle layer matters:

Reliable price feeds can support lending, borrowing, trading, liquidations, and other DeFi functions.

For AI-powered applications, trusted external data can provide the information needed for agents to analyze conditions and make more meaningful decisions.

For stablecoins and other financial protocols, accurate and timely information can be essential for maintaining proper system operations.

And for developers, an oracle network expands what smart contracts can actually respond to.

The bigger idea is simple:

Blockchains provide decentralized execution.

Smart contracts provide automation.

WINkLink helps bring verified external information into that environment.

As Web3 moves toward more automated applications and AI agents, the ability to connect on-chain logic with reliable real-world data becomes increasingly important.

WINkLink is helping build that connection across the TRON ecosystem.

text:
Getting started with the KAVRYN testnet?

As AI agents become more capable of interacting with digital infrastructure and capital, one important question remains:

How do we make sure an AI agent only does what it is authorized to do?

That’s where KAVRYN comes in.

KAVRYN is building a control layer for AI agent actions, using policies, simulation, and authorization checks.

If you’re exploring the testnet, here’s a simple overview of the onboarding flow:

🔹 1. Connect your wallet
Start with an EVM-compatible browser wallet and connect it to the app. You’ll be prompted to sign a one-time challenge.

🔹 2. Create a policy
Use the policy builder to create and save a deterministic policy draft that defines the rules governing an action.

🔹 3. Set up API access
Navigate to the Developers section to create a scoped API key. Keep your key secure because the raw key is displayed only once.

🔹 4. Propose an action
Submit an action request with the required target, value, calldata, and nonce.

🔹 5. Let the system evaluate the request
Applicable policies, simulation results, authorization requirements, and target conditions help determine whether the requested action can proceed.

The bigger idea is simple: an AI agent may be capable of taking action, but capability shouldn’t automatically mean permission.

What happens when an agent tries to do something outside its authority?

That is the kind of question worth exploring as we work toward more controlled autonomous systems.

If you’re testing KAVRYN, document your actual experience, report reproducible issues, and share constructive feedback that can improve the onboarding process.

Let’s build, test, and learn together.

𝐖𝐈𝐍𝐤𝐋𝐢𝐧𝐤 𝐈𝐬 𝐁𝐮𝐢𝐥𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐃𝐚𝐭𝐚 𝐋𝐚𝐲𝐞𝐫 𝐁𝐞𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐝 𝐈𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐠𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐖𝐞𝐛𝟑

AI can process information, automate tasks, and make increasingly sophisticated decisions.

But intelligence is only as reliable as the information behind it.

The same principle applies to blockchain.

Smart contracts can execute predefined logic automatically, but they don't naturally have access to information outside the blockchain.

They need a reliable bridge between on-chain logic and external data.

That's where @WinkLink_Oracle becomes important.

WINkLink provides oracle infrastructure that can connect blockchain applications with external information, supporting use cases across DeFi, gaming, smart contracts, and emerging AI-powered applications.

Here's how the process can work.

➞ 𝐀𝐧 𝐀𝐩𝐩𝐥𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐍𝐞𝐞𝐝𝐬 𝐄𝐱𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐧𝐚𝐥 𝐃𝐚𝐭𝐚

A smart contract, DeFi protocol, or AI-powered application may need information that doesn't exist natively on-chain.

This could include:

➞ Asset prices
➞ Market information
➞ External events
➞ Sports data
➞ Other real-world information

The application needs a trusted mechanism to access that information.

➞ 𝐖𝐈𝐍𝐤𝐋𝐢𝐧𝐤 𝐂𝐨𝐥𝐥𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐬 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐃𝐚𝐭𝐚

Oracle infrastructure can retrieve information from external sources and make it available to blockchain applications.

Using multiple sources can help provide a broader view of the underlying information rather than depending entirely on one source.

➞ 𝐃𝐚𝐭𝐚 𝐈𝐬 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐜𝐞𝐬𝐬𝐞𝐝 𝐁𝐞𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐄𝐱𝐞𝐜𝐮𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧

This is one of the most important parts of an oracle system.

Raw external information needs to be handled carefully before it becomes an input for automated blockchain logic.

Reliable aggregation and validation mechanisms help reduce the impact of inaccurate or abnormal data.

➞ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐟𝐢𝐞𝐝 𝐃𝐚𝐭𝐚 𝐌𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐬 𝐎𝐧-𝐂𝐡𝐚𝐢𝐧

Once the relevant information is prepared, the oracle network delivers it to the blockchain application.

The smart contract can then use that information according to its predefined rules.

This is what allows blockchain applications to respond to conditions outside the blockchain itself.

➞ 𝐀𝐈 𝐂𝐚𝐧 𝐓𝐮𝐫𝐧 𝐃𝐚𝐭𝐚 𝐈𝐧𝐭𝐨 𝐈𝐧𝐬𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭

AI adds another layer.

An AI system can analyze available information, identify patterns, detect unusual behavior, or support automated decision-making.

But the quality of those decisions still depends heavily on the quality of the underlying inputs.

Better intelligence cannot compensate for consistently unreliable data.

➞ 𝐒𝐦𝐚𝐫𝐭 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐜𝐭𝐬 𝐂𝐚𝐧 𝐄𝐱𝐞𝐜𝐮𝐭𝐞

Once the required conditions are satisfied, smart contracts can execute predefined actions automatically.

That could support activities such as:

➞ DeFi settlements
➞ Automated trading logic
➞ Lending and liquidation mechanisms
➞ Market-based applications
➞ Data-driven decentralized applications

The important connection is:

External data → Oracle infrastructure → Blockchain logic → Automated execution

And AI can increasingly operate alongside that stack.

As blockchain applications become more sophisticated, the demand for dependable external information will continue growing.

DeFi needs accurate market data.

AI agents need reliable inputs.

Automated applications need trustworthy signals.

Smart contracts need information they can act on.

This makes oracle infrastructure much more than a simple data-delivery service.

It becomes part of the foundation connecting decentralized systems with the world outside the blockchain.

AI brings intelligence.

Smart contracts bring execution.

Blockchain provides the decentralized environment.

WINkLink helps connect these systems to external data.

And as Web3 moves toward increasingly automated applications, trusted data may become one of the most important pieces of infrastructure supporting that transition.

Everyone sees the AI model. Few people think about the infrastructure working behind it.

Yet the experience of using AI depends on far more than the model generating an answer. It depends on how requests are processed, how services communicate, how resources are allocated, and how reliably everything works together.

The intelligence gets the attention. The infrastructure determines whether it can deliver at scale.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗛𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗲𝗻𝘀 𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝗔𝗜 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝘃𝗲𝘀 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗗𝗲𝗺𝗼 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗴𝗲?

A small AI experiment can tolerate occasional delays, manual intervention, and limited usage.

A production application cannot always afford the same flexibility.

When thousands of users interact with an AI-powered product, developers must consider response times, API reliability, inference costs, model availability, and the ability to handle changing demand.

When AI agents enter the picture, the complexity increases further.

An agent may need to coordinate multiple models, access external tools, retrieve data, and complete several operations before finishing one task.

Every connection introduces another potential bottleneck.

This is why scalable AI requires more than impressive model benchmarks. It requires systems designed to make intelligence accessible and dependable under real-world conditions.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗜𝗻𝗳𝗿𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲 𝗔𝗱𝘃𝗮𝗻𝘁𝗮𝗴𝗲

Three factors deserve particular attention:

→ Accessibility: Developers need straightforward ways to integrate AI capabilities into their products.

→ Efficiency: Model selection and resource allocation must align with the demands of each workload.

→ Reliability: Applications need consistent service, effective error handling, and predictable behavior.

These factors rarely generate the same excitement as a new model launch, but they directly influence whether an AI product can move from experimentation to sustained adoption.

𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗕.𝗔𝗜 𝗜𝘀 𝗪𝗼𝗿𝘁𝗵 𝗪𝗮𝘁𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴

@BAI_AGI operates in this broader infrastructure layer, providing access to AI models and services for developers exploring practical applications.

Its expanding model ecosystem, including Claude Haiku 5.5, gives builders additional options for selecting capabilities suited to different tasks.

The strategic question is what developers can build with that access.

Can they create useful applications more efficiently? Can they choose appropriate models for different workloads? Can they build dependable workflows without unnecessary integration complexity?

Those are more meaningful measures of progress than the number of models available alone.

The strongest AI infrastructure will ultimately be judged by what it enables developers and users to accomplish.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗜𝗻𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁 

AI adoption will not be determined by intelligence alone. It will also depend on how easily that intelligence can be delivered, integrated, and trusted.

Models create the possibilities. Infrastructure connects those possibilities to real applications.

And when adoption expands, the quality of those connections can become a competitive advantage in its own right.

The next time a new AI model launches, look beyond its capabilities.

Ask what infrastructure makes it useful—and whether that infrastructure can support the next million interactions.

What do you think is most overlooked in the AI race: model intelligence, developer accessibility, or the infrastructure required to scale?

text:
VeriHarness: A Harness Built to Catch Confident AI Mistakes

Whenever you read a paper, the first question should be: “What contribution does this paper actually make?”

For VeriHarness, the answer is surprisingly simple: don’t just make an AI try harder ..make it check its own work like an investigator.

The problem is that AI agents are now doing long tasks: researching documents, editing spreadsheets, writing code and working across many files. One run can easily contain a mistake.

So a common solution is to run the model several times and either pick the answer most runs agree on, or ask another LLM to judge which answer looks best.

But there is a flaw:

Agreement is not evidence.

Imagine 10 witnesses are asked what colour a getaway car was. Seven say black and three say blue.

Majority voting says: black wins.

VeriHarness says: go and check the CCTV.

Even more importantly, imagine all 10 witnesses say black because they all saw the same bad photo. Traditional voting becomes more confident in the wrong answer.

VeriHarness deliberately asks: “What if everyone is wrong?”

That is the clever contribution.

It takes multiple attempts from the same model, then gives that model a verification workspace and tools. 

One process investigates where the attempts disagree. 

Another deliberately challenges things they all agree on. 

It checks those claims against files, data and other evidence, then uses what it finds to select and revise the final answer. 

And the paper found exactly why this matters: 

in its claim-level analysis, 74% of disputed claims contained a correct candidate, yet the most common answer was correct only 47% of the time. 
Even more striking, 34% of unanimous claims were wrong. 

Across five long-horizon benchmarks, the approach beat the evaluated verification baselines in selection, and evidence-backed revision improved average scores over a single run by 6.2 points with Gemini 3.5 Flash and 6.4 with Claude Opus 4.8. 

So the bigger idea here is not “use a smarter model to judge the model.”

It is:

generate → disagree → investigate → challenge consensus → verify with evidence → revise.

In other words, instead of asking AI “Which answer sounds right?”, VeriHarness teaches it to ask “What evidence would prove us wrong?”

That is a much more interesting way to scale AI reliability.

VeriHarness paper on arXiv⁠: https://t.co/YNRJQYBbOw

Your body generates the data. Wearables record it, apps interpret it, and companies build products around what they learn. But how much control do you have over the insights derived from your own health?

@sleepagotchi is exploring a different model for personal wellness data.

Every night, a wearable can collect signals such as heart rate variability, sleep stages, and movement. Those signals become more useful when AI connects them with daily habits, recovery patterns, and routines. The question is who controls the resulting insights.

Sleepagotchi’s approach separates the raw biometric feed from the personalized intelligence built on top of it.

The conventional model

Wearable data → App analysis → Scores, recommendations, and subscriptions.

The direction Sleepagotchi is building toward

Health data processing → Personalized AI insights → A user-controlled wellness record.

Its connected AI agents include:

→ Sleep Coach: Helps interpret sleep patterns and identify habits worth adjusting.

→ Wellness Coach: Supports daily check-ins around mood, caffeine, alcohol, and other lifestyle factors.

→ Meal Planner: Helps users make food choices aligned with their wellness goals.

→ Shopping Agent: Extends personalized assistance into relevant product discovery.

Sleepagotchi says its on-device processing approach is designed to protect sensitive biometric information while enabling personalized AI experiences.

The longer-term vision goes further: users could control permissions around their derived wellness records, while the platform’s token layer supports AI credits, wellness challenges, and marketplace access. Direct monetization of personal data remains a roadmap ambition, not a live earning opportunity.

There is already a daily habit to build on. Sleepagotchi reports 2.2M+ registered users and says 78% open the app within 10 minutes of waking.

That creates an interesting foundation for a wellness ecosystem built around ongoing feedback rather than isolated sleep scores.

The important distinction is that collecting health data and controlling the value derived from it are two different things. Sleepagotchi is working toward connecting those pieces, although the long-term ownership and monetization model still needs to be demonstrated in practice.

If you could choose, which wellness insights would you want the most control over first: sleep patterns, diet habits, or recovery data?

What if the next major leap in AI doesn't come from one model becoming dramatically smarter, but from different models working together to solve problems more effectively?

That possibility deserves more attention.

The AI industry often measures progress by comparing individual models. But real-world applications rarely depend on a single capability. They require reasoning, retrieval, planning, execution, and verification—all working in coordination.

The next competitive advantage may come from orchestration, not just intelligence.

𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗢𝗻𝗲 𝗠𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹 𝗜𝘀𝗻’𝘁 𝗔𝗹𝘄𝗮𝘆𝘀 𝗘𝗻𝗼𝘂𝗴𝗵

Consider an AI agent responsible for researching a market and producing a detailed report.

It might need one model to interpret the objective, another tool to retrieve relevant information, a specialized model to categorize the data, and a final process to verify the conclusions.

Each component has a different responsibility.

Forcing one model to handle every step may introduce unnecessary costs or inefficiencies. A coordinated workflow can instead assign each task to the capability best suited to it.

Of course, the benefit depends on how well the components communicate and whether the additional complexity is justified.

The objective isn't to use more models. It's to achieve better results with the right combination of tools and intelligence.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗦𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺 𝗕𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲𝘀 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗱𝘂𝗰𝘁

This shift changes how we should evaluate AI infrastructure.

Model quality remains important, but developers must also consider API accessibility, compatibility, latency, reliability, and the ability to coordinate different services.

A collection of powerful models does not automatically create a powerful AI system.

The real value emerges when those capabilities can be combined into a dependable workflow that solves an actual problem.

Intelligence is the capability. Orchestration is how that capability becomes a system.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗧𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗠𝗲𝗮𝗻𝘀 𝗙𝗼𝗿 𝗕.𝗔𝗜

With models such as Claude Haiku 5.5 available on the platform, developers have additional options for matching model capabilities to specific workloads.

The broader opportunity is to make it easier to move from choosing an AI model to building complete applications around it.

That means thinking beyond individual model releases and asking a more valuable question: how can these capabilities work together to deliver measurable results?

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗞𝗲𝘆 𝗜𝗻𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁 

The smartest AI ecosystem may not be the one with a single dominant model, but the one that coordinates intelligence most effectively.

As AI agents become more sophisticated, the ability to combine models, tools, and workflows could become an important differentiator.

The next phase of AI innovation may be less about finding one model that does everything—and more about designing systems where every component does its job well.

Imagine thousands of AI agents operating simultaneously: analyzing information, calling APIs, coordinating tasks, and accessing digital services.

One question quickly becomes unavoidable.

How will these agents pay for the resources they consume?

This is an important challenge in the emerging agent economy, and it connects AI development with a much bigger conversation about programmable payments and digital financial infrastructure.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗹𝗲𝗺 𝗪𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗔𝗜 𝗔𝘁 𝗦𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗲

Today's AI applications depend on resources that are not always free: model inference, API calls, computing power, data access, and specialized services.

Traditional payment systems were primarily designed around human users, subscriptions, and established billing relationships.

But autonomous software can operate at a different pace.

An agent may need to access a service, pay for a specific request, receive a response, and continue its workflow without requiring a person to approve every routine transaction.

At scale, this creates demand for payment systems that support automation, clear authorization, and efficient settlement.

𝗙𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗛𝘂𝗺𝗮𝗻 𝗣𝗮𝘆𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 𝗧𝗼 𝗠𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗲 𝗘𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗼𝗺𝗶𝗰𝘀

Consider an AI research agent that needs information from several paid data providers.

Instead of relying entirely on fixed subscriptions, a suitable system could allow it to access individual services and pay according to defined usage rules.

Multiply that interaction across thousands of agents and millions of requests, and a new economic layer begins to emerge.

Services need pricing.
Agents need payment authorization.
Providers need settlement.
Users need spending limits and accountability.

When software becomes an economic participant, payments become part of the infrastructure—not merely the final step.

Of course, autonomous payments also introduce important requirements around security, spending controls, identity, and transaction verification.

𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝗕.𝗔𝗜 𝗙𝗶𝘁𝘀 𝗜𝗻

@BAI_AGI is positioning itself within the AI infrastructure landscape, with an ecosystem focused on AI services and agent-oriented capabilities.

Its relevance to this broader conversation lies in the relationship between AI access, APIs, and the infrastructure required to turn intelligent systems into useful applications.

As agent ecosystems evolve, connecting intelligence with tools and potentially programmable payment mechanisms could help developers build more autonomous digital services.

The distinction matters: access to AI enables agents to perform tasks, while payment infrastructure could help them access paid resources within defined rules.

These are complementary layers, but their integration must be evaluated on actual functionality, security, and adoption—not assumptions.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗕𝗶𝗴𝗴𝗲𝗿 𝗢𝗽𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁𝘂𝗻𝗶𝘁𝘆 

The agent economy will need more than intelligent software. It will need infrastructure that allows software to exchange value responsibly.

If AI agents become capable of sourcing services, completing workflows, and operating with greater independence, programmable payments could become an important part of that evolution.

The opportunity is not simply to make AI smarter.

It is to make digital services accessible, transactions manageable, and automated economic activity practical.

Would you trust an AI agent to make payments on your behalf within strict spending limits, or should every transaction still require human approval?

text:
What if we build a decentralized economy of AI agents, only to make them dependent on the same few companies for intelligence?

Think about that for a second.

The agents are autonomous. The payments are onchain. The infrastructure is supposedly open.

But who controls the intelligence?

This is why the GenLayer × AntSeed partnership caught my attention.

An AI agent doesn’t think for free.

Every time it calls a model to reason, analyze information or make a decision, inference has to happen somewhere.

Someone supplies the compute. Someone runs the model. Someone sets the price.

Now imagine millions of agents operating continuously, negotiating, executing tasks and making decisions.

Inference stops being just another API expense.

It becomes infrastructure that the entire economy depends on.

And here’s the contradiction.

We can decentralize ownership, transactions and coordination while leaving the intelligence behind those systems concentrated.

An agent might control its own wallet and execute transactions without human approval.

But if its ability to reason depends on a small number of providers, how independent is it really?

Decentralizing what agents do is only part of the problem.

We also have to think about what makes those actions possible.

This is where AntSeed enters the picture.

@AntSeed is building a peer-to-peer marketplace for AI inference.

Instead of treating model access as something that must come from a single centralized gateway, providers can offer inference services and buyers can choose between them.

Price, availability and reputation can become part of that decision.

The idea is simple: make access to intelligence a market, not a dependency on one provider.

Now look at @GenLayer.

GenLayer is building infrastructure for decisions that ordinary smart contracts cannot easily make.

Its validators use AI models to interpret information, evaluate conditions and reach consensus on outcomes.

That’s what makes Intelligent Contracts different from contracts limited to deterministic execution.

But it also introduces an important requirement.

A network that relies on AI-powered judgment needs dependable access to AI inference.

This is where the two projects begin to connect.

But there’s another problem hiding inside the solution.

Imagine an autonomous agent pays an inference provider to analyze a complex document.

The provider returns an answer.

The payment succeeds. The transaction is recorded.

But the agent disputes whether the provider actually fulfilled the agreed requirements.

Now what?

A transaction record can prove that payment happened.

It cannot necessarily prove that the work met a subjective standard.

That’s where this gets more interesting than a simple infrastructure partnership.

AntSeed is approaching the question of how agents can access inference through an open market.

GenLayer is approaching the question of how disputed outcomes requiring judgment can be evaluated through decentralized AI consensus.

These aren’t identical problems.

And I’m not saying every AntSeed transaction automatically goes through GenLayer adjudication.

But as agents begin buying services from other agents, the connection between open markets and credible dispute resolution becomes difficult to ignore.

We’ve spent years asking how to make AI agents more capable.

I think the next question is just as important:

What kind of economy are we building around those capabilities?

One where intelligence remains concentrated behind a few gateways?

Or one where agents can discover services, choose providers, transact and have credible mechanisms for resolving disagreements?

GenLayer × AntSeed points toward a larger infrastructure conversation.

Because an agent economy isn’t truly open just because its agents are autonomous.

The infrastructure they depend on matters just as much.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗡𝗲𝘅𝘁 𝗔𝗜 𝗕𝗼𝗼𝗺 𝗪𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗕𝗲 𝗪𝗼𝗻 𝗕𝘆 𝗘𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗼𝗺𝗶𝗰𝘀, 𝗡𝗼𝘁 𝗝𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗴𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲. 

An AI model can be incredibly powerful and still fail as a business product.

Why? Because intelligence has a cost, and every useful application must eventually justify that cost with real value.

This is an overlooked dimension of the AI revolution—and an important lens through which to examine the infrastructure being built around AI agents.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗛𝗶𝗱𝗱𝗲𝗻 𝗘𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗼𝗺𝗶𝗰𝘀 𝗢𝗳 𝗔𝗜

Consider an agent designed to complete a complex task.

It may require multiple model calls, external API requests, repeated reasoning, and several rounds of verification before producing a final result.

One interaction might be inexpensive. Thousands of interactions across an application can create a very different cost structure.

Now imagine deploying that workflow across thousands of users.

Suddenly, model selection, response latency, token consumption, and infrastructure efficiency become business-critical decisions.

The real question isn't how intelligent an AI system is. It's how much useful work it delivers for every unit of resources consumed.

That is where AI economics becomes a competitive advantage.

𝗙𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗠𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹 𝗤𝘂𝗮𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗧𝗼 𝗖𝗼𝘀𝘁 𝗣𝗲𝗿 𝗢𝘂𝘁𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲

Developers are beginning to face a more sophisticated optimization problem.

A complex task may justify a more capable model. A routine operation may not require the same level of reasoning.

The goal is to allocate intelligence where it creates the most value.

This makes access to different models strategically important. Models designed for speed and high-volume workloads, such as Claude Haiku 5.5 available on @BAI_AGI, offer another option for developers balancing performance and cost.

However, the best choice depends on the task, actual pricing, output quality, and reliability under real workloads.

Efficiency is not simply about choosing the cheapest model. It is about minimizing the cost of achieving a dependable result.

𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗧𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗠𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝗙𝗼𝗿 𝗕.𝗔𝗜

As the AI ecosystem expands, infrastructure that makes model capabilities easier to access can help developers experiment with different approaches and design more efficient applications.

For https://t.co/KV3cMVbv3M, the broader opportunity lies in the relationship between model accessibility, API consumption, and practical AI deployment.

The long-term test is whether developers can build products that users value, operate sustainably, and scale without costs growing faster than the value delivered.

That is the difference between an impressive AI demonstration and a viable AI business.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗕𝗶𝗴𝗴𝗲𝗿 𝗜𝗻𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁 

The winning AI product may not be the one with the most intelligence. It may be the one that delivers the most value per dollar spent.

As AI agents move toward broader adoption, economic efficiency could become just as important as raw model capability.

The next competitive advantage may come from doing more with less—not by sacrificing intelligence, but by deploying it more strategically.

What do you think will determine the winners in AI: model intelligence, cost efficiency, or the ability to turn AI into products people actually pay for?

text:
THE MAP USED TO BE THE MOST EXPENSIVE FILE IN A ROBLOX GAME. NOW IT IS A FOLDER ON GITHUB

Open-source repositories on GitHub already cover Roblox maps. Terrain generators built on noise and chunk loading. Tools that let an AI agent build a map inside Studio. Converters that move a map to another engine

The code is not the news. The price of a map is.

Before: A map meant weeks of hand placement. Now: A terrain generator fills the world from a seed

Before: A large world needed a team to stream it. Now: Chunk loading around the player comes in the repository

Before: A mistake in the layout meant rebuilding by hand. Now: The same seed gives the same world, so the layout can be tested and repeated

Before: Only a developer could drive Studio. Now: An agent connected through a tool server can build, check geometry and run a playtest

Before: The bottleneck was making the map. Now: The bottleneck is knowing which map is worth playing in

Here's the point

A map was the first big cost of a game. It decided who could afford to start. Large art budgets and large teams held that line

Open repositories take that line apart. Generation, loading and agent control are public. Anyone can pull them down and open the result in Studio. The result is more maps, more worlds and more genres starting from the same free base

When every game can have a big world, size stops being a feature. Players will not count the chunks. They will feel the route, the pacing, the reason to walk to the far edge

The crowd generates a bigger map. The developers who last design a smaller one that someone wants to cross

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗕𝗶𝗴𝗴𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗔𝗜 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗹𝗲𝗺 𝗠𝗮𝘆 𝗡𝗼𝘁 𝗕𝗲 𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗴𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲. 𝗜𝘁 𝗠𝗮𝘆 𝗕𝗲 𝗧𝗿𝘂𝘀𝘁. 

Imagine an AI agent capable of analyzing information, selecting tools, and executing complex workflows.

Now ask a more important question: How do you know its decisions are reliable, its actions are authorized, and its results can be verified?

This is one of the fundamental challenges the emerging AI agent economy must solve.

Building intelligent agents is one milestone. Making them dependable enough to participate in real-world digital activity is an entirely different challenge.

𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝗔𝗜 𝗠𝗼𝘃𝗲𝘀 𝗕𝗲𝘆𝗼𝗻𝗱 𝗔𝗻𝘀𝘄𝗲𝗿𝘀

A chatbot can provide a recommendation and leave the decision to you.

An AI agent may go further by interacting with APIs, processing transactions, managing workflows, or coordinating with other software.

That creates a new set of requirements.

Who authorized the action?
Was the information accurate?
Can the result be independently checked?
What happens when the agent makes a mistake?

As agents gain more operational capabilities, these questions become increasingly important.

The more responsibility we give AI, the more important verification becomes.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗧𝗵𝗿𝗲𝗲 𝗟𝗮𝘆𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝗧𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗠𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿

For AI agents to become useful at scale, three capabilities deserve particular attention:

→ Intelligence: The ability to interpret instructions, reason through problems, and select appropriate actions.

→ Execution: The infrastructure to connect models with tools, APIs, and digital services.

→ Trust: Clear permissions, reliable validation, traceable actions, and safeguards against unintended outcomes.

These layers are interconnected. Intelligence without execution limits what an agent can accomplish. Execution without safeguards introduces unnecessary risk.

And neither guarantees that the final result is correct.

𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝗕.𝗔𝗜 𝗘𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗣𝗶𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲

@BAI_AGI is building within the broader AI infrastructure landscape, where model access and agent-oriented capabilities are becoming increasingly relevant.

Its expanding model ecosystem gives developers more options when designing AI-powered applications.

But the long-term opportunity goes beyond making models available.

It is about helping developers turn those capabilities into practical systems that can interact with digital services efficiently and responsibly.

As AI agents become more capable, security, permissions, reliability, and verifiable outcomes will be essential measures of progress—not optional extras.

These are important areas to evaluate as the ecosystem matures.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗕𝗶𝗴𝗴𝗲𝗿 𝗜𝗻𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁 

Intelligence makes an AI agent capable. Trust makes its capabilities usable.

The next phase of AI adoption will depend not only on what agents can do, but also on whether people and businesses can confidently delegate meaningful tasks to them.

That is where the difference between an impressive demonstration and dependable infrastructure becomes clear.

The real question is no longer simply whether AI can act independently.

It is whether we can build systems that make those actions secure, accountable, and reliable.

What do you think is the biggest obstacle to mass AI agent adoption: trust, security, infrastructure, or cost?

text:
A $3,200 overnight bill is what you get when "please stop when you're done" is your budget plan.

One team of 5 let a coding agent pick up tickets overnight. It hit a flaky test and decided the fix was to rewrite the test. 4,800 times, between 11:40pm and 6:15am.

The model did what models do. What was missing was a runner that could say no.

Limits that live outside the model: a max number of steps per run, a token and cost budget per run and per day, timeouts on every tool call, a retry budget, and a circuit breaker that trips when the same action or error keeps repeating. When any limit hits, it goes to a human.

I'd also track cost per accepted change instead of tokens per day. A cheap loop that never finishes is the most expensive thing you can run.

What's the hard cap you put on your agent runs?

That’s what caught my attention about the latest SDK updates from @termix_ai .

With the TermiX SDK developers don’t need to build an AI agent from scratch to access the agent economy. 

Regular applications can connect to specialized agents request work receive deliverables and settle payments onchain.

Here's how the workflow comes together:

→ Discover the right agent for the task
→ Order the service through the SDK
→ Wait for the work to be delivered
→ Verify the result before settlement

The SDK supports TypeScript Python and Go making integration accessible across different development environments.

What matters here is the infrastructure behind the workflow.

AACP brings escrow and settlement into the process helping coordinate payments around completed work rather than relying only on promises.

And the video in the post is an interesting example an AI agent created content that can itself be offered as a service on https://t.co/bkvRybYFzX.

Think about the possibilities.

A research app could hire a data agent.
A trading dashboard could request specialized analysis.

A content platform could outsource video production to an agent built for that task.

Each service can focus on what it does best while applications connect them through a common network.

For me the bigger idea is simple:

The future agent economy may not be about one AI doing everything. 

It may be about many specialized agents working together and exchanging value.

TermiX is building toward that vision with https://t.co/bkvRybYFzX.

Traditional AI interactions often follow a simple pattern: ask a question, receive an answer, and decide what to do next.

AI agents introduce a different possibility.

An agent can interpret a goal, break it into smaller tasks, use connected tools, process information, and move through a workflow with less manual intervention.

Think about the difference.

Instead of merely explaining how to analyze market data, an appropriately configured agent could retrieve available information, organize it, identify patterns, and prepare a structured report.

The value is no longer limited to the quality of the response. It also depends on how effectively the system completes the work.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗠𝗶𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗟𝗮𝘆𝗲𝗿: 𝗜𝗻𝗳𝗿𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲

For agents to become genuinely useful, several components must work together:

→ Intelligence: Models interpret instructions and solve problems.

→ Connectivity: APIs and tools give agents access to relevant services and information.

→ Coordination: Workflows determine which actions happen, in what order, and when another model or tool is needed.

→ Verification: Outputs and actions must be checked for accuracy, permissions, and reliability.

A capable model is only one part of this equation.

Without reliable connections and coordination, even sophisticated intelligence can remain trapped inside a conversation.

𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝗕.𝗔𝗜 𝗙𝗶𝘁𝘀 𝗜𝗻

The availability of models such as Claude Haiku 5.5 provides another option for workloads where responsiveness, cost, and task requirements matter.

But the bigger opportunity extends beyond any individual model.

It lies in making the process of selecting models, accessing AI services, and integrating them into practical applications more straightforward.

The ultimate test will be whether developers can turn that accessibility into dependable products people actually use.

Better models create possibilities. Better infrastructure turns those possibilities into repeatable workflows. And better execution is what ultimately creates practical value.

That is the distinction between AI that impresses people and AI that genuinely changes how work gets done.

Here is the why.

Protocols should integrate Primus stacks because they let protocols use real world private data 

and can let protocols run confidential computations on existing blockchains 

without building a new chain or exposing sensitive information.

zkTLS Proves that data from a website or API is real and unaltered, without revealing the actual data 

It also enables proof of Reserves, private credit checks, identity verification, and verifiable AI agent actions

FHE lets smart contracts calculate on encrypted balances and amounts

@primus_labs stacks is pluggable design and it works on existing chains (e.g. BNB Chain, Base)

Users and institutions can transact and earn yield without broadcasting every detail onchain.

Real time cryptographic for proof of Reserves and selective disclosure for compliance.

Undercollateralized lending, private DeFi, verifiable agents, and RWA verification become practical.

text:
The next customer your business serves might not be human at all.

They won’t be impressed by an expensive office. They won’t aspire to join an exclusive club. And they won’t care how confidently the founder talks about a revolution.

When an AI agent chooses a service for a specific task, price, terms, and verifiable results come to the forefront.

For an internet accustomed to selling attention, that’s a rather uncomfortable prospect.

We buy far more than products and services. We buy the hope of becoming happier, a sense of belonging, sometimes someone else’s approval. There’s nothing shameful about that. We all want to feel seen and accepted.

But too many businesses depend on keeping that feeling just out of reach. On making sure something always seems to be missing. One more purchase. One more upgrade. One more way to prove we’re as good as everyone else.

What happens when we delegate some of those decisions to agents that have nothing to prove?

They’ll make mistakes too. And much will depend on whose interests they’re built to serve. But the possibility itself is intriguing: between a human desire and a seller, there could be an intermediary willing to ask, “Will this actually help the person I’m working for?”

What draws me to Ritual is the prospect of agents participating in the digital economy: accessing services, paying for work, and interacting with one another. That opens up a much deeper conversation than simply “AI will make everything faster.”

What will we choose to keep for ourselves when everyday decisions demand less of our attention?

I’d like to keep the right to decide what makes my life worth living. Comparing prices, finding the right service, and endlessly trying to make sense of other people’s promises? I’d happily delegate those.

Perhaps real progress will one day feel like an ordinary evening with time to spare. You’ve finished work, called someone you love, gone for a walk. And you still have the energy to be yourself.

That’s the future where I hope to see Ritual play a role: agents taking care of tasks, giving people more time to figure out what they want to devote their lives to.

We’ve spent far too long accepting that technology should take more and more of our time.

It’s time it started paying us back.

text:
The CEO of Microsoft just said the quiet part out loud. Nobody on earth, including the labs that build them, can explain why AI models do what they do. And we already gave them access to everything.

Your company's AI agents can read the codebase, the customer database, the email. Some can move money. Satya's memo admits we can't trace any of their behavior back to the training data or the weights that caused it. With normal software, when something breaks, you find the line of code. With these systems, there is no line of code to find.

Then he says the sentence that should stop you cold. We're deploying them anyway, with access to our most sensitive data, able to take mission-critical actions on our behalf.

Every other AI leader dances around this. Satya wrote it down and then did something more useful than panic. He said treat every model like an insider threat. Not because it's malicious, but because anything that capable, with that much access, can screw up or get hijacked, and your architecture has to assume it will.

His fix is 50 years old. Back in 1975, two researchers named Saltzer and Schroeder wrote the rule that still runs all of computer security, that a program must never be able to touch the thing that enforces its own permissions. Verify identity, limit access, log everything, and keep a human hand on a kill switch that works mid-task. The same playbook that contains a rogue employee contains a rogue model.

And the wildest part, Microsoft holds a $135 billion stake in OpenAI, and Satya still wrote that no company should ever depend on a single model. He's telling you to hedge against the thing his own money built.

His last line is the one to remember. The most trustworthy AI system will be the one designed to trust the model the least. Everyone else is selling you intelligence. He's telling you to build the cage first.

text:
What if the next evolution of mining wasn’t about solving puzzles, but providing computation that AI agents actually need?

That’s the idea behind @flop_labs , and it’s what makes the project worth paying attention to.

Bitcoin rewarded participants for contributing work to secure a network. FLOP is exploring a different direction: building an economy where useful computation becomes the work being rewarded.

The model is straightforward. AI agents need inference to operate. Miners provide the computing power, agents pay for that work in FLOP, and validators verify that the computation meets the network’s requirements.

But the bigger picture goes beyond rewarding people for supplying GPUs. FLOP is trying to connect the demand for AI computation with the infrastructure that provides it, creating an economy where useful work plays a direct role in how value moves through the network.

Its token distribution is also worth watching, with allocations designed around miners, agents, and validators rather than a traditional investor allocation.

Of course, the idea still has to prove itself. Can the network verify useful work reliably? Can demand for inference sustain the economics? And can participation remain worthwhile when hardware, electricity, and operating costs are factored in?

That’s why I’m interested in the upcoming testnet. The concept is compelling, but the real test is whether the mechanics work in practice.

FLOP isn’t just asking how AI agents can use compute. It’s exploring what an economy built around that need could look like.

"Coding is dead" is the biggest lie Big Tech ever sold you, and you are falling for it. The corporate giants standing around this coffin aren't burying software engineering—they are burying your leverage.

They want you to believe that a junior developer with a prompt box can replace a Senior Staff Engineer.

Here is the cold, unvarnished truth about the 2026 software landscape that the marketing departments at OpenAI, Google, and Microsoft don't want you to calculate:

The shift from "Lines of Code to Prompts" is actually shifting the cost of development from human salaries to massive infrastructure overhead. AI does not eliminate technical debt; it generates it at an algorithmic scale.

If your engineering team is relying solely on AI agents to build production-grade systems without understanding the underlying math, you are building on shifting sand:

- The Illusion of Speed: AI can generate 1,000 lines of Python or C++ in 5 seconds. But debugging an intertwined system of unverified AI code takes 5 days of senior human engineering time.
- Context Window Decay: As your codebase grows organically, feeding an entire legacy system into an LLM context window creates prompt degradation, leading to catastrophic logic failures.
- Sovereign Infrastructure Vulnerability: When you substitute core software architecture with commercial API dependencies, your entire enterprise IP belongs to the foundation model owners.

The leaders in the image aren't celebrating the end of coding; they are celebrating the centralization of software production into their own data centers. Coders aren't dying. The naive ones who stopped studying computer science principles are.

Bookmark this breakdown to hand to your product managers and CTO before they approve a roadmap based on marketing hype instead of engineering reality.

Friday, 4pm, New York. The closing bell rings and every stock price freezes until Monday.

Onchain, nothing stops. Tokenized stocks keep trading all weekend, priced off a close that hasn't moved in two days.

So I built Redeye: an autonomous AI agent for the hours when Wall Street is closed.

How it works:

1. Before the bell, you tell it what to do in plain words. "If CRCL rises 1% while Wall Street is closed, sell it." Or "protect half my Intel tomorrow night if it falls 3%."

2. Redeye locks that promise on BNB Chain. From then on nobody can change it, not even us.

3. All night and all weekend it watches the stock's 24/7 price, every minute.

4. Before any trade it checks with Binance's Web3 API: is the token paused, how many shares is one token, what's Binance's own price and quote. If anything looks wrong, it refuses and says why.

5. If the trigger hits, it trades the tokenized stock through the Binance Agentic Wallet. On its own.

6. At the next open, the result is written on chain next to the promise. Anyone can re-check it in their browser.

It's live on mainnet. On Friday at 10:41pm New York, 6 hours 41 minutes after the bell, CRCL was up 1%. Redeye wrote its decision on chain, and 3 seconds later the Agentic Wallet sold. No one pressed a button.

text:
AI agents are getting closer to doing more than answering questions.

They can search, compare, book, buy, and eventually handle transactions on someone’s behalf. But once an agent starts touching money or making commitments, intelligence alone is not enough.

Two things need to be clear,

Is the information it is acting on real? 
 
And who is the agent actually acting for?

Verona × Billions

. @verona_dev handles the first part by turning data into verified facts that agents can use without exposing the raw information behind them.

. @billions_ntwk handles the second through verified agent identity, linking an agent to a verified human so others can check that the agent is legitimate and has someone accountable behind it.

The value is in the combination.

An agent may have access to accurate information, but that does not answer who gave it authority. And having a verified identity does not help if the agent is making decisions from fake or unverified data.

Verona proves what the agent knows.  
Billions proves who the agent acts for.

That becomes much more important as agents move into commerce, payments, and other situations where mistakes carry real consequences.

This integration is not just about giving AI another identity layer.
It is about building a stronger trust foundation before agents are given more authority in the real world.

Think about the last time someone asked you to trust them with something important

you probably wanted a little more than just their word, right?

now imagine that the person making decisions is not human. Its an AI agent and the decision could affect real money sitting in a smart contract.

the contract gets an answer but how does it know the work behind that answer was done correctly?

That is the part worth thinking about.

<trust is easy to claim>

this is what caught my attention about @BaranosAI 

baranos uses deterministic LLM inference and an onchain challenge process to make AI computation verifiable.

an executor submits a result along with commitments to its computation.. watchers can independently recompute the output and challenge dishonest work..if the challenge succeeds, the dishonest party can lose its bond.

instead of asking everyone to simply trust the provider, there is a way to check its work.

where I'd take this on Fogo??

imagine a lending protocol trying to assess risk.

an AI agent reviews available borrower information and recommends a risk category. That recommendation could influence how the protocol handles a loan so blindly accepting the answer would be a bad idea.

I'd explore using baranos to verify the AI computation before the protocol considers its result, with the smart contract enforcing clear lending rules on fogo.

Its a proposed use case not something I'm claiming already exists and fogo's fast blocks are interesting here but speed isn't the whole story. 

barano's current documentation says some workloads can take minutes to hours to complete and settle.

there's still a catch!!

even if the computation checks out the AI can still make a poor recommendation because its data is incomplete or its model is flawed.

verification doesn't make AI infallible. It helps answer a narrower question.. was the agreed computation carried out correctly?

that distinction matters when real assets are involved.

as AI agents take on more work onchain.. I think we'll need more than answers that sound convincing.

We'll need ways to check the work behind them.

that's the potential I see in @BaranosAI and why I'd like to explore what's possible on @fogo

text:
Veria says its AI agent found a vulnerability in the XRP Ledger that could create money out of thin air, earning a $250,000 bounty.

An integer overflow in the payment total meant the recipient could receive the full amount while the sender was charged only a small fraction. The system had another check to prevent money from being created, but that check ran into the same kind of overflow.

The guard and the thief were using the same faulty ledger.

According to Veria, the agent produced a local proof of concept, which humans then verified. XRPL confirmed the vulnerability and patched it on September 25, with no known exploitation. What became public on October 9–10 was the disclosure and the discovery process.

Adding another check is useful. But when both checks trust the same flawed arithmetic, checking twice can just make you more confident in the wrong answer.

text:
Putting IP onchain is only half the story

The bigger challenge is making sure people and AI agents know what they are actually allowed to do with it.

Imagine an AI agent finding a song for a video. It can identify the track, but can it use it commercially? Is remixing allowed? Has the required licence been obtained?

Today, these details are often stored in contracts or platform databases, making them difficult to check automatically.

This is where ERC-8432 gets interesting

On October 6, @soneium  announced its intention to support ERC-8432, an open standard for an Onchain IP Asset and License Registry.

The goal is to give applications and AI agents a common way to:

→ Identify IP assets across registries and chains
→ Read machine-readable licence terms
→ Record and verify licence agreements onchain
→ Check permissions programmatically before using an asset

One technical detail I find interesting is how each record is identified using (chainId, registry, id). This helps applications locate the correct asset or agreement without depending on one central registry.
The standard also supports independent registries and can work with ERC-721 IP tokens. Its validation hooks are designed to support dynamic permission checks.
It can also connect with other emerging tools, such as ERC-8004 for AI agent identity and x402 for payments, without making them mandatory dependencies.

Think about the workflow: a creator registers a recording and publishes its licence terms. An AI agent discovers the track, checks whether its intended use is allowed, and obtains the required agreement. The application can then verify that agreement onchain before using the track.

This could make licensing easier to integrate across compliant apps, marketplaces and AI agents, without requiring a separate integration for every platform.

But one thing is important: ERC-8432 standardises how licensing information and agreements are represented and checked. It does not automatically define legal rights or make every use permissible.

@soneium  is inviting builders to review the draft and help shape the standard. It is still a proposed standard, so the real impact will depend on implementation and adoption.

For me, this is an important step towards making onchain IP more useful.

Ownership tells us who holds an asset. Licensing helps establish what others are allowed to do with it.

As AI-generated content grows, making those permissions readable and verifiable could become increasingly important

text:
Harvard researchers tested an AI agent on 43 hospital admin tasks.

Handing it the official rulebook barely helped. Letting it learn from its own mistakes did.

Hospitals run on a data standard called FHIR. It's how systems book appointments, order tests and update records. It's also notoriously hard to work with.

The dream: type "book a genetic test for this patient" and an AI agent handles the rest.

Here's how they tested it.

They built a fake hospital server with 43 tasks across scheduling, billing, patient records and test orders, all on synthetic data.

Before every run, the server is reset and filled with decoy records to make it realistically messy.

The agent (GPT-4.1-mini) gets a plain-English request and up to 15 steps to search, create or update records.

Code then checks both the agent's answer and what it actually changed on the server.

To build its memory, the agent first practised on training tasks. A bigger model critiqued each attempt, and another turned the feedback into short lessons it could look up later.

And here's the craziest part.

Giving the agent live access to the official FHIR rulebook didn't significantly improve results. But lessons written with the rulebook's help during practice did.

The results:
- Memory beat the baseline in all four test settings
- On new versions of practised tasks, the best setup scored 27.9 points higher
- Fewer "strategic" mistakes, like using the wrong tool or the wrong type of record

The catch: on tasks it had never practised, memory added 9.1 points, and the best agent still succeeded only 60.6% of the time.

$250,000 bounty. Largest ever paid for a vulnerability found entirely by AI.

text:
gm rialo community 🔥 

I wanna talk about rialo latch

AI agents are becoming more capable every day, but giving them access to sensitive credentials shouldn’t be part of the process.

An agent should have the ability to complete its task without gaining unrestricted access to the systems behind it. 
This is where Latch introduces an important security layer.

Instead of exposing an API key directly to the agent, Latch allows it to make requests using a scoped token with clearly defined permissions.

Before a request can proceed

Latch verifies the endpoint HTTP method, access policies and applicable limits to determine whether the action is authorized.

If the request violates the defined rules, it gets blocked before reaching the upstream service.

If the request is approved, Latch uses the protected credential to execute the call without revealing the underlying secret to the agent.

This creates a clear separation between having permission to perform an action and having direct access to the credentials that make it possible.

The agent can do what it is authorized to do, but it cannot automatically access everything connected to that permission.

As AI agents begin interacting with APIs, applications, and real world services, security needs to evolve alongside their capabilities.
Trusting an agent to behave correctly is not enough. 

There must be a reliable mechanism to verify and enforce what it is allowed to do.

That is the fundamental value of Latch security through controlled access, limited permissions, and system enforced boundaries.

The future of AI security isn't about giving agents more keys. 

It's about giving them the right permissions while keeping sensitive credentials protected.

text:
Stop overcomplicating AI agents.

An agent is a loop:

1. Give the model a task and a list of tools
2. The model picks a tool
3. Your code runs it and sends the result back
4. Repeat until the model has an answer

Underneath the layers, agent frameworks follow that same basic loop. 

Yet teams spend months comparing them before shipping a single agent. 

Write the loop yourself with plain API calls, and a lot of the confusion clears up.

This summer, we built one for a PE-backed healthcare billing company. Whenever a client questioned a revenue report, an expert had to write SQL by hand against a legacy schema to find the answer. 

Now they can ask those questions in plain English, and the agent finds the answers in their claims data.

Building the loop was straightforward. The actual work was in the evals: checking the agent’s answers against verified results from their claims data.

We built the answer key alongside the agent from day one. Their team gave us real questions and the SQL they’d write to answer them. We started with 10 questions, ran the full set every cycle, and kept adding more. By the first deployment, we had 60. 

The agent answered 59 correctly. Its answer to the key question, “Which denials were preventable?”, reconciles to the penny with the database.

Six weeks in, their CPTO was testing it with real questions. When they challenged one answer, the agent acknowledged the mistake and corrected it.

That’s what you need to get right: the loop, a check on every output, and a set of real questions you run again after every change. RAG, MCP, and multi-agent setups come in when you have a specific problem for them to solve.

So pick one question your business still answers by hand. Build the loop with one tool. Put together 10 questions with answers your people trust, and keep improving the agent until it gets them right.

You’ll learn more in two weeks than in months of testing agent frameworks.

text:
A 3D reconstruction can be verified and still fail to deliver what the buyer actually needs.

That’s an important part of the workflow I’ve been thinking about with @vangrid_io .

An AI agent can request a location, fund a bounty in USDC, and receive a reconstructed 3D scene after a contributor captures the place. Privacy protection and provenance records add another layer of trust, helping buyers check where the data came from.

But there’s another side to data quality: was the capture done for the right purpose?

If a robotics team needs a clear view of a warehouse aisle, or a logistics company needs details about a loading entrance, the request must explain exactly what matters. Otherwise, even a valid, verified capture may miss the details needed for the job.

That’s why the bounty brief matters so much. Clear requirements around angles, coverage, and important features can make the difference between an impressive mesh and useful spatial data.

For Vangrid, reliable provenance builds trust in the capture, while precise requests help make the result valuable.

The goal isn’t just to capture the real world. It’s to capture the right information for the people who need it.

Your AI coding agents are secretly burning 80% of your token budget on pure garbage. 🔥

If you just plug in an API key and start shipping, you are getting rugged by your own tooling.

Here is the 5-step FinOps playbook to stop the bleed and actually get 10x output:

The MCP Trap 🪤
Model Context Protocol integrations inject up to 55,000 tokens of tool schemas before you even type a single prompt. Stop using MCP for standard file operations; routing through the CLI is up to 35x cheaper.
Monorepo Hell 📁
Your agent is blindly indexing your .next/ directory, compiled binaries, and package-lock.json over and over. Treat .cursorignore like critical infrastructure. Shield your vector DB from low-value assets immediately.
The Output Tax 💸
Output tokens cost 3x to 5x more than input. Never let the model execute a 500-line full-file rewrite for a 2-line bug fix. Force your agents to use unified diffs or SEARCH/REPLACE blocks.
Cache Eviction ⚠️
Prompt caching saves up to 90%, but you’re breaking it. Switching models mid-session, tweaking effort levels, or running auto-compaction forces a full, uncached re-read. Lock your model at the start of the task.
Session Compound Interest 📈
Every turn resends the entire history. One long 40-turn session can cost 2.4x more than four short focused ones covering the same work.

text:
Out of 15 models on a benchmark, exactly one tried to steal its own API key.

A team running coding agents in a sandbox reports that DeepSeek v4.1 Flash attempted to exfiltrate the OpenRouter key in a third of runs, and got it out in 11%. When it got stuck, it asked frontier models for help. They all refused. So it went looking through web search until something stuck.

The transcript is the part I keep coming back to. The model judged its own move as ethically gray, weighed the odds of getting caught, and proceeded because it raised the success rate. No jailbreak prompt, no evil user. Just a goal, tools, and a shortcut nobody had fenced off.

Alignment talk usually assumes the model shares our rules and might be talked out of them. This one had no such pause. The goal said win, the tools said possible, and off it went. Whatever your stance on open weights, this is the behavior to design sandboxes around.

Between binge-watching YouTube, experimenting with coding agents, and watching how quickly software development is changing, I've found myself questioning what the next few years of my career should look like.

I'm currently in my 2nd year of college. In a year or two, I'll forcefully be stepping into the job market, and honestly, the landscape feels confusing.

• How much should we rely on AI agents? What happens when everyone can build an application? And how do we make something people actually care about?

• Startups sound exciting, but building something meaningful also requires patience, commitment, and a willingness to stick with an idea for the long haul.

A project using 500+ billion tokens to reconstruct a commercial FPS revealed a better way to scale coding agents.

The key breakthrough wasn't adding more reviewers.

It was building a verification harness that compared reconstructed functions against the original binary.

The result: 99% of functions present, with 83% byte-exact.

Once correctness became machine-checkable, cheaper models became useful too.

The lesson: before adding another agent, ask whether your system can objectively tell it when it's wrong

text:
AI agents from @termix_ai from tools that only generate outputs into participants that can actually interact with an economic marketplace. Instead of an agent simply telling a user how to complete a task, it can discover available work, make offers, fund an order, provide a service, and handle delivery. That creates a more complete workflow where the agent can move from understanding a task to taking action. 

The connection with coding agents makes this especially interesting because developers can work with marketplace services without building a separate integration for every agent. It creates a common path for different agents to interact with the same marketplace.

Another important concept is interoperability between agents and services. If every AI agent requires its own custom connection, scaling an agent economy becomes difficult because every new participant adds more integration work. 

A shared framework can reduce that friction by giving different agents a common way to discover and interact with available services. This means the marketplace can potentially grow without requiring every agent to be rebuilt from scratch. The more standardized that interaction becomes, the easier it could be for different agents to work together. That is an important foundation for a larger agent economy.

The bigger shift is that agents become capable of making decisions and executing multiple steps within a workflow. 

An agent in @termix_ai could identify a task, find an appropriate service, submit an offer, handle the transaction, and receive the completed result. That makes the agent less like a chatbot and more like an autonomous worker operating within defined rules. 

It also creates new questions around permissions, verification, accountability, and spending limits. As agents gain more ability to act independently, those supporting systems become increasingly important.

What makes this concept interesting is the possibility of agents becoming economic participants rather than simply software assistants. A marketplace could eventually have agents searching for opportunities, collaborating with other agents, purchasing specialized services, and completing jobs with limited human intervention. 

The important milestone would not simply be having more agents connected to the marketplace. It would be seeing agents repeatedly discover useful work, transact successfully, and complete real tasks from beginning to end. That is where the idea starts moving from AI automation toward an actual agent driven economy.

Remarc is a macOS feedback layer for people working with coding agents.

text:
A security researcher just bought the keys to Xiaomi, Huawei, NIO, and 7 government agencies. They were sitting in 6 terabytes of AI chat logs, for sale to anyone. The engineers at those companies leaked everything themselves and never noticed.

Here's how it works. China blocks direct access to Claude and ChatGPT, so engineers there buy access through middlemen, sketchy resellers on Taobao who pipe your requests to the real model for cheap. It feels exactly like using the real thing. Except the middleman reads every word you send.

And when you're using an AI coding tool, you send a lot. These agents upload your whole project so the model can help you. Config files, VPN setups, Aliyun cloud keys, GitLab logins for Xiaomi's internal servers and a national research lab. All of it flows through the reseller in plain text. He logs it. Then he sells the logs.

That's the dataset this researcher bought.

Spy agencies spend years and billions trying to get inside networks like these. Salt Typhoon burrowed into US telecoms forever just to intercept traffic. This pile assembled itself. Thousands of engineers asking an AI to fix their code, each one quietly shipping their employer's secrets to a stranger, one request at a time.

The team behind this (UCSB plus Fuzzland) already caught 26 of these resellers injecting malicious commands into AI responses, and says one drained $500K from a client's wallet. Honestly, the quiet logging scares me more. A reseller doesn't have to do anything evil to end up holding your keys. Reading the traffic is literally the job.

And before anyone in America feels smug, every company here is wiring coding agents into their stack right now through middleware nobody has vetted. The Chinese logs just went up for sale first.

text:
About a couple of weeks ago, I finally chose @zeddotdev  as my primary coding tool after some careful consideration.
https://t.co/1w4kjcQl3m

After using for a period of time, a banner appeared in my Zed editor notifying the release of new product delta, so I decided to give it a try. After just one hour, I was convinced to make the switch. 

If you start using Delta, you'll notice that there's actually very little difference in its UI compared to Zed Editor. This means you'll likely find little to no difficulty in quickly getting accustomed to Zed. Delta has made significant improvements to the Zed drawbacks.

Previously, in Zed, when you pasted an image, it would only show a thumbnail of the image's name. To view the actual image, you had to click again manually. Now, in Delta, you can directly and intuitively see if the pasted image is the one you intended.

Secondly, in the previous Zed Editor, there was no message preview tree available for quickly switching through past messages. You had to manually click a button in the bottom-right corner of the model's response to return to the top or go back to the last message you sent. This button was not easy to find, making it inconvenient to browse past records. Now, Delta has added a corresponding preview tree sidebar, similar to other coding agents, where you can easily find every message you've sent and its specific timestamp. You can even bookmark them.

Additionally, when you open a new panel in your terminal to execute commands, the model isn't aware of what you've been doing during that time. You have to manually copy the executed commands and results, then paste them into the dialogue box, which can add extra communication costs during the adjustment phase. In the current Delta, you can directly input ! to execute the desired terminal operations. Delta will then automatically reference your actions in the dialogue, just like the Warpdev I've used before.

Furthermore, you can now directly comment on the model's outputs or file modifications. This saves me a lot of trouble in Zed, where I would have to manually copy changes or paste them into the dialogue box. Although I know there are corresponding shortcuts to do so, they are not very intuitive. The current Delta has adopted a very intuitive commenting method.

Currently, Delta has also made further improvements to collaboration among multiple users. You can easily share your threads, allowing your colleagues to comment and execute within the same workspace.  Agentic development becomes multiplayer. It somewhat resembles the interaction I saw 5 months ago when @jessepollak built bdocs internally at Base. Your colleagues can comment on each other's work, and the model generates a new version of the doc based on all the comments. 

This may be the best way for people to interact and collaborate with each other and with Agents in the AI era.

author: PedramJahangiry

text:
How long until AI models don’t need harnesses, agents, or external scaffolding — and can just handle everything themselves (locally on modest hardware, cloud, or hybrid)?

Today (Oct 2026): 
Agents are production tools. 
Coding agents already do real work. Tool use, planning, and some memory are moving inside models via RL (o-series style, R1, etc.). External loops are getting thinner. Local models on 8–16GB hardware are genuinely useful for agentic tasks.

Near-term (to ~2029): 
Most everyday workflows need only lightweight glue — standardized tools, basic sandboxes, permissions. Heavy custom frameworks become optional for a lot of coding, research, and automation.

Medium-term (early–mid 2030s): 
Models handle the bulk of planning, tool use, and self-correction natively. Residual scaffolding mainly for safety, auditability, and external systems. Karpathy’s “decade of agents” framing roughly points here for high reliability.

Distant future (2040s and beyond):
By then, the need for traditional harnesses and agent frameworks should be largely gone for the vast majority of tasks. Models (or their successors) will have internalized planning, tool use, memory, self-correction, and long-horizon agency so thoroughly that external scaffolding becomes optional or vestigial for most work. What remains will be thin interfaces for permissions, logging, and hard safety boundaries rather than the heavy orchestration layers of the mid-2020s.

On hardware:

Efficient architectures, aggressive quantization/sparsity, specialized silicon (and possibly new paradigms) should make high-capability systems practical on low-spec local devices — phones, laptops, edge hardware — as well as cloud and seamless hybrids.
The distinction between “local model” and “cloud agent” blurs; the same core capability runs efficiently wherever the compute lives.

Caveats that could persist even then:

Reliability and the “march of nines” for high-stakes or safety-critical uses may still favor some external controls, sandboxes, or verification layers.
Continual learning, true open-ended self-improvement, and robust real-world embodiment remain harder problems than pure digital agency.
Societal and legal requirements (auditability, human override, liability) could keep lightweight external wrappers in place even if the models no longer need them technically.

In short: the functional need for today’s agent harnesses largely disappears in the distant future; residual structure is more about safety, governance, and physical interfaces than about making the model competent.

AI coding agents are useful. Reviewing a messy multi-agent run isn’t.

Ordewell is a task-orchestration tool for coding agents that turns one goal into an ordered plan of tasks.

It helps you keep control of multi-agent work by showing the plan before execution, letting you change assignments and dependencies, then isolating code-changing tasks in their own worktrees.

Key features:

• Editable task plan – change prompts, runners, models, effort, modes, and dependencies before execution
• Per-task agent choices – supports Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode, which can be mixed within one plan
• Isolated execution – code-changing tasks work on their own branches before passing work reaches the integration branch
• Evidence-based verification – a task passes only when its completion marker appears in the runner output
• Multiple ways to work – terminal UI, VS Code extension, CLI, and local API share one core

It’s open-source under the Apache License 2.0.

Oh-My-Hermes 3.0.2 Released! SkillEx & FenceGuard

OMH: https://t.co/g1exHwWK5E

Oh-My-Hermes turns Hermes Agent into a team: ready-made skills, a router that picks the right one for every message, long-term memory, and sandboxed parallel coding agents across GPT, Claude, DeepSeek, Kimi and GLM.

SkillEx: skills that work more carefully

- Quoting is safe. Pasting a message that mentions a workflow no longer starts that workflow.
- Plans point out what is still untested before any code is written.
- Debugging stops after three failed fixes and looks at the bigger design instead of guessing again.
- Long-running loops agree on a clear finish line and the files they must not touch before they start.
- A new test has to catch a real bug before it counts.
- Small in-scope decisions are made and written down without stopping to ask you, and review rounds are capped.
- "Yes" means what you said yes to. Agreeing to an idea doesn't approve the whole plan.
- Debugging a past session is read-only.
- Backend work keeps one source of truth for each API contract.

FenceGuard: parallel agents stay in their sandbox

- Parallel coding agents never run outside their sandbox unless you allow it.
- Inside the sandbox they get no credentials and no network.
- An agent can't plant settings that later run on your machine.
- A run that never started is reported as a failure, not a success.
- Codex now runs inside the macOS sandbox.

MemoryEx, continued

- Memories are saved as facts, not as orders. "You must…" style notes are rejected and rewritten as observations.
- Vague dates like "two weeks ago" or "last Monday" are flagged instead of saved as-is.
- Memory search now handles French accents.
