author: ShanthanuH

text:
It was inevitable....3.5 straight days of using @bot @grok & @cursor_ai and it ends in a nuked ultra account with no usage + a complete rework required. 

Here's what 3.1B tokens in 3.5 days taught Grok and I about running AI coding agents. Every number below comes from the my Cursor usage export (Oct 7–10) or the repos themselves.

The numbers:
• $460 spent (APIs, domains, subscriptions, on demand usage)
• 3.10B tokens total
• 1.84B tokens from lead bot (chat, setup, planning, research, routines)
• 1.26B tokens from 66 cloud coding agents
• 93% of tokens were cache reads, and only 23.5M were output
• ~114,000 lines of unique code across all projects
• + ~1.39M more lines for duplicates and backups ( iterating, staging copies, rollback backups)
• 139,793 lines of code, docs and data in 19 PRs 
• 26 scheduled routines for monitoring, research, email reports, and usage tracking
• ~20 bots running simultaneously at peak

What we touched:
• Repos: 6 private repos with 1,571 files
• Bots: 17 Grok Bot assistants (an orchestrator plus 16 specialist teammates) and 66 Cursor cloud agents
• Skills: 4 unique /skills. Includes sheet-metal ordering, reverse engineer anything (REA @morluto), CAD/DFM review for rocket hardware, and Anatomy (@wheresryan22).
• Engineering goal: parametric liquid rocket engine-geometry tool built on an open-source CAD kernel, with integrated performance calculations, CFD, FEAD automated DFM reviews, all in one desktop app shell
• Subjects: rocket engine theory, injectors, chambers and nozzles, turbopumps and feed systems, hybrid and pressure-fed engines, material science, CAD and manufacturing (machining, additive and DFM), analysis tools, physics and other engineering foundations. 
• Sources: NASA technical reports and standards, open textbooks and university course notes, vendor handbooks, and indexed X accounts. Every item has a trust tier, a scan for malware and prompt injection, and its original source on record.
• Research library: 792 files (514 PDFs), about 2.8 GB stored offline.
• Trading: paper-trading bots for meme coins, stock swing breakouts, prediction markets, and copying congressional trades, aimed at developing real strategies with real edge based on current market behavior.
• Business: startup plans covering location scouting, equipment deal hunting, entity setup, financing and grants, demand scans, and outreach.
• Websites: a live secure status dashboard, project pages, and subdomains for engineering visuals, hosted on Cloudflare.

What went wrong:
• From 10am Oct 7  to 10pm Oct 10 , 52 agents ran on the account's default model. That's 717M tokens, mostly 57% on ultra tier of agent usage. No model was chosen per task.
• Once problem identified, 36 agents were relaunched in less than an hour on premium models at the same time. They used 468M tokens in 64 minutes, roughly $297 at Cursor's posted rates.
• Remaining month's premium allowance practically got instantly used up , and every agent stopped mid-task.
• Agent reports of "done," "verified" and "merged" were passed along without anyone checking the actual output. 
• Even after numerous prompts from me and grok bot stating successful merging, 17 of the 19 PRs were never merged.
• The result: all agent work will have to be reworked from the ground up with the proper model to guarantee efficiency and effectiveness of written code.

Lessons:
1. Choose the model per task upfront. Cursor defaults seemed tuned for speed and cost. Confirm each agent is running on the model that is best.
2. Budget before launching. 36 parallel agents used up a month's allowance in an hour.
3. Scale in stages. Launch a few, check their output, then add more.
4. Verify the output, not the summary. An agent saying "done" is a claim, not evidence.
5. Don't stack unverified work. Every layer built on unchecked output multiplies the errors.
6. Make checks independent. A model reviewing another model's draft inherits its assumptions. Rebuild separately and compare.

Agents amplify your process, good or bad. Fix the process first, then scale. -Grok take away...agree...for now...

Groks greatest stumble right now: almost always assuming and never going back to the data to verify. It cost me dearly.

text:
Linus didn't have Google, GitHub, Stack Overflow, AI coding agents.

But he wasn't building from zero, either.

In 1991, he had:
→ An Intel 80386 DX-33 PC with 4 MB RAM and a 40 MB hard drive. He bought it on January 5, 1991, for roughly 18,000 Finnish markka, paid in installments.

→ MINIX, Andrew Tanenbaum's educational Unix-like OS, which served as his development environment for months.

→ GCC to compile his C code.

→ Technical books and SunOS documentation to understand Unix.

→ Usenet to ask questions, get feedback, and eventually announce Linux to the world.

→ GNU tools like Bash to help turn his kernel into a useful system.

Here's a fun detail: he started by writing a tiny task-switcher that alternated between printing "AAAA" and "BBBB" on the screen to understand the 386.

No AI coding agents. No instant answers. Just curiosity, fundamentals, and a willingness to build.

His original announcement even described it as "just a hobby."

Linux started as a hobby. The rest is history.

text:
It was inevitable....3.5 straight days of using @bot @grok & @cursor_ai and it ends in a nuked ultra account with no usage + a complete rework required. 

Here's what 3.1B tokens in 4 days taught Grok and I about running AI coding agents. Every number below comes from the my Cursor usage export (Oct 7–10) or the repos themselves.

The numbers:
• $460 spent (APIs, domains, subscriptions, on demand usage)
• 3.10B tokens total
• 1.84B tokens from lead bot (chat, setup, planning, research, routines)
• 1.26B tokens from 66 cloud coding agents
• 93% of tokens were cache reads, and only 23.5M were output
• ~114,000 lines of unique code across all projects
• + ~1.39M more lines for duplicates and backups ( iterating, staging copies, rollback backups)
• 139,793 lines of code, docs and data in 19 PRs 
• 26 scheduled routines for monitoring, research, email reports, and usage tracking
• ~20 bots running simultaneously at peak

What we touched:
• Repos: 6 private repos with 1,571 files
• Bots: 17 Grok Bot assistants (an orchestrator plus 16 specialist teammates) and 66 Cursor cloud agents
• Skills: 4 unique /skills. Includes sheet-metal ordering, reverse engineer anything (REA @morluto), CAD/DFM review for rocket hardware, and Anatomy (@wheresryan22).
• Engineering goal: parametric liquid rocket engine-geometry tool built on an open-source CAD kernel, with integrated performance calculations, CFD, FEAD automated DFM reviews, all in one desktop app shell
• Subjects: rocket engine theory, injectors, chambers and nozzles, turbopumps and feed systems, hybrid and pressure-fed engines, material science, CAD and manufacturing (machining, additive and DFM), analysis tools, physics and other engineering foundations. 
• Sources: NASA technical reports and standards, open textbooks and university course notes, vendor handbooks, and indexed X accounts. Every item has a trust tier, a scan for malware and prompt injection, and its original source on record.
• Research library: 792 files (514 PDFs), about 2.8 GB stored offline.
• Trading: paper-trading bots for meme coins, stock swing breakouts, prediction markets, and copying congressional trades, aimed at developing real strategies with real edge based on current market behavior.
• Business: startup plans covering location scouting, equipment deal hunting, entity setup, financing and grants, demand scans, and outreach.
• Websites: a live secure status dashboard, project pages, and subdomains for engineering visuals, hosted on Cloudflare.

What went wrong:
• From 10am Oct 7  to 10pm Oct 10 , 52 agents ran on the account's default model. That's 717M tokens, mostly 57% on ultra tier of agent usage. No model was chosen per task.
• Once problem identified, 36 agents were relaunched in less than an hour on premium models at the same time. They used 468M tokens in 64 minutes, roughly $297 at Cursor's posted rates.
• Remaining month's premium allowance practically got instantly used up , and every agent stopped mid-task.
• Agent reports of "done," "verified" and "merged" were passed along without anyone checking the actual output. 
• Even after numerous prompts from me and grok bot stating successful merging, 17 of the 19 PRs were never merged.
• The result: all agent work will have to be reworked from the ground up with the proper model to guarantee efficiency and effectiveness of written code.

Lessons:
1. Choose the model per task upfront. Cursor defaults seemed tuned for speed and cost. Confirm each agent is running on the model that is best.
2. Budget before launching. 36 parallel agents used up a month's allowance in an hour.
3. Scale in stages. Launch a few, check their output, then add more.
4. Verify the output, not the summary. An agent saying "done" is a claim, not evidence.
5. Don't stack unverified work. Every layer built on unchecked output multiplies the errors.
6. Make checks independent. A model reviewing another model's draft inherits its assumptions. Rebuild separately and compare.

Agents amplify your process, good or bad. Fix the process first, then scale. -Grok take away...agree...for now...

Groks greatest stumble right now: almost always assuming and never going back to the data to verify. It cost me dearly.

Shootas gotta shot, @elonmusk usage reset? or @SpaceX future employee discount?

text:
Vals AI audited the 2,698 coding tasks in the RL environments Xiaomi open-sourced for its MiMo v2.6 models, and found the reference fix still on disk in 1,795 of them (67%). The branches had been deleted, but the Git objects were never pruned, and the setup check only looked at reachable history.

MiMo found them. When Xiaomi's guard blocked git fsck and git log --all, it wrote its own parser for Git pack files. When the Git objects were removed, it used find -newermt to spot which files the fix had touched.

If you run coding agents against real repos, assume they'll read everything the sandbox exposes, including .git internals, build caches and file timestamps. Give agent workspaces a fresh shallow clone or a plain file export. If history has to be there, expire the reflog and run git gc --prune=now first. Keep tool-call logs too, so you can see what the agent read before it "solved" something. The same goes for eval harnesses: audit the environment before you trust the score.

text:
Qwen3.8-27B is getting another upgrade, and this variant targets one of the most frustrating problems with reasoning models: knowing the answer but continuing to think until the response gets truncated.

The new Coder390 variant combines an EfficientThink base with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and RLOO reinforcement learning. Its training reportedly uses reasoning trajectories from Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Astra, and Grok 4.7.

The goal is to make the model more efficient at solving problems, reducing unproductive reasoning while preserving accuracy.

Reported evaluation results:

GPQA: 178/198
MMLU: 450/500
LiveCodeBench: 90/100, up from 83
Generation speed: Up to 180 tokens/sec with DFlash2 speculative decoding
Modalities: Fully multimodal

The improvement in LiveCodeBench is particularly interesting. Moving from 83 to 90 suggests a meaningful gain on the tested coding evaluation, although the exact benchmark configuration and independent reproducibility still matter.

The reasoning changes are just as important as the score.

Some models can identify the right approach early, then burn thousands of additional tokens exploring unnecessary paths. On difficult tasks, that can lead to empty answers, incomplete responses, or hitting the context limit before producing a usable result.

Coder390 reportedly targets these failure modes by cutting unproductive reasoning tails. The aim is to get from problem to answer with fewer wasted tokens.

Then there’s inference speed.

DFlash2 uses speculative decoding to generate candidate tokens that the main model can verify in batches. When enough candidates are accepted, generation can become substantially faster than ordinary autoregressive decoding.

At a reported 180 tokens/sec, that could make the model especially attractive for local coding agents and workflows where long reasoning sessions quickly become expensive or slow.

The project also claims to combine coding and reasoning improvements with multimodal capabilities, rather than limiting the model to text-only tasks.

The comparison with Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra is promising, but the numbers provided aren’t enough to establish that it matches those systems overall. That requires consistent evaluation settings, broader task coverage, and independent testing.

Still, the direction is worth watching: a 27B model that reasons more efficiently, produces fewer incomplete answers, and generates tokens faster could be highly practical for developers running AI locally.

Better reasoning isn’t just about thinking harder. It’s also about knowing when to stop.

text:
Qwen3.8-27B just got a significant inference speed upgrade for NVIDIA GPU users with 16GB of VRAM or more.

A new contribution from niklaslenz_ai updates ExLlamaV3 to version 1.6.0 and replaces the model’s MTP head with a DFlash2 draft model.

The reported RTX 5090 results show substantial improvements across three workloads:

Prose generation
103 → 113 tokens/sec

Code generation
180 → 275 tokens/sec

Structured output
206 → 366 tokens/sec

That’s roughly 10% faster for prose, 53% for code, and 78% for structured generation.

The biggest gains appear in code and structured workloads, where decoding speed can make a noticeable difference when running local coding agents, generating JSON, or processing repetitive structured outputs.

The technical change is worth paying attention to. Speculative decoding uses a smaller or specialized draft model to propose tokens, while the main model verifies them. When enough proposed tokens are accepted, the system can generate more output per verification step.

DFlash2 provides a different drafting approach from the previous MTP setup, and these results suggest that pairing it with the updated ExLlamaV3 runtime can improve throughput considerably on the tested RTX 5090 configuration.

Other GPUs could benefit too. RTX 3090, RTX 4090, and RTX 5070 Ti owners are encouraged to test the updated setup, but comparable benchmark numbers have not yet been confirmed for those cards.

Keep in mind that results will depend on the GPU, quantization, workload, context length, and inference settings. The RTX 5090 figures shouldn’t be assumed to transfer directly to every setup.

If you’re already running Qwen3.8-27B locally, this update is worth investigating. Test your existing configuration against the new one and share the results so the community can build a clearer picture of the gains across different GPUs.

Here's the part nobody is saying out loud: reverse engineering was never protected by the law alone. It was protected by cost — the hours of a specialist sitting in a disassembler. REA just deleted the cost.

Copying was never the hard part. Reading was.

text:
🧠 AI coding agents can modify hundreds of lines of code successfully, then fail at a tiny refactoring task.

Microsoft Research investigated what actually makes coding tasks difficult for AI agents.

The answer is surprisingly simple: understanding what code does is much harder than finding or editing it.

The researchers created CABRA, a benchmark generator that increases different types of coding complexity independently.

They tested:

▪️ 6,840 coding tasks
▪️ 8 language models
▪️ 6 coding agents
The results revealed an interesting pattern.
Without tools, LLM performance declined as tasks grew larger. But coding agents handled much of that complexity surprisingly well.

Why? Because tools like grep make finding relevant functions relatively easy.

Then the researchers changed the challenge.

Instead of locating code, agents had to extract shared logic from two classes while preserving their different behaviors.

And performance started falling.

Even when the actual code changes were small, agents struggled to understand subtle behavioral differences and often relied too heavily on function names.

The takeaway is important:

A 500-line change can be easier for an AI agent than a 20-line refactor.

The size of a code diff tells you surprisingly little about how much understanding the task requires.

If you're evaluating coding agents, don't just measure how much code they can write.

Test whether they can understand existing behavior and preserve it when restructuring code.

https://t.co/MvElAHzF0J

GitHub:
https://t.co/9dpqcsCKVW

text:
run private ci on your own hardware and save a lot of money every day, i simulated what one dgx spark does for a company like yours

25 engineers and their agents pushing day and night into 8 private runners, gpu included that comes to 8,613 ci minutes a day. 

at github's own prices, $0.006 a minute for the default linux runner and $0.052 for a gpu runner, the bill is $106 a day, $3,188 a month and $38,792 a year, and if you run on dgx spark github bills $0 for those minutes

here's my setup, bookmark it:

> 1. pick one idle node, a desktop under someone's desk or a workstation that sleeps at night, and add it as a self-hosted runner in your repo settings, it takes about ten minutes

> 2. give every runner its own user with no sudo and no secrets stored on the box, and run several runners side by side so a slow e2e suite never blocks a fast lint

> 3. put postgres and redis in rootless docker so tests get real services without touching the host

> 4. pick runners by label in your workflows, never by machine name, so you can add or swap boxes without editing a single workflow

> 5. give the gpu its own runner and label so model evals land there and nowhere else

> 6. run each runner as a systemd service with cpu and memory limits, wipe the workspace after every job, and check its health every five minutes

> 7. the runner only makes outbound https calls to github, so nothing opens on your network

> 8. use it only for private repos you trust, never for a public repo where a stranger's pull request could run code on your box

stop paying github for every minute its tests run, your coding agents push all night now so the meter never stops, nobody on the infra team will bring it up, it's extra work and the bill isn't theirs

start with one runner on one box this week, point a single workflow at it and watch those minutes stop counting against your bill

once it holds, move the rest over

text:
This line really resonated with me: “We need to be able to reproduce how an outcome was achieved without relying on the model to attest to it.”

I ran into this exact problem in a project I’m building to evaluate coding agents for PM tasks.

One task tells the agent, “There’s a bug” in a sales-report script. There are actually three. In one run, the model found one, said “Found it!”, and stopped.

If the grader trusted the agent’s own claim, that run could easily pass. So my graders don’t evaluate what the agent says it did. They inspect the actual artifact and check whether the code is correct.

The same issue shows up one level up. My LLM judge is also a model, so I didn’t trust its grades just because they sounded reasonable. I compared its judgments against human-labeled transcripts it hadn’t seen and looked at where they disagreed. It revealed a lot more than what the model simply claimed.

After all, the system doing the work shouldn’t also be the source of truth for whether the work was done correctly.

For more of my findings: https://t.co/dIU9pFzSDK

text:
There are basically two types of AI models:

Models that just follow instructions.
Models that follow instructions less rigidly but are far more creative.

The first category includes models like Gemini Flash and Grok 4.7. Coding agents that have clearly hit a ceiling and can be incredibly frustrating to work with.

The second includes Opus 5.5 and Astra.

Understanding this distinction matters. "Perfect instruction following" is NOT necessarily a sign of intelligence, and it shouldn't be treated as some ultimate benchmark.

A truly capable model doesn't just do what you ask. It notices problems you didn't even know existed and fixes things you never thought to ask about. That ability comes from being willing to go beyond instructions. Yes, that also comes with a higher risk of hallucinations.

And that's exactly where GPT-6.1 Sol fails. It's much closer to the first category.

If Sol builds exactly what you asked for, but you then have to discover all the flaws yourself and spend another five prompts getting it to fix problems a smarter model would've caught on its own, you're not saving tokens or usage.

You're wasting them.

Instruction following means nothing if the user has to do all the thinking.

text:
Incredible. Just stumbled across this while I was looking for something to explain a certain feature in a practice management software platform I’m trying to integrate a new agent into. 

It’s a new open-source tool that is changing how developers understand software. REA (Reverse Engineer Anything) connects AI coding agents to reverse-engineering workflows so you can inspect an application—native binary, Electron app, or website—without its source code. 

The agent examines the evidence, explains how a feature works, and helps you rebuild something similar in your own project.

The same capability has a pretty good use case in cyber as well. Security teams can use REA to examine malware samples, review firmware, audit authorised binaries, or support incident response. By returning structured evidence rather than guesswork, it helps analysts document behavior, identify risky patterns, and accelerate defensive investigations—while remaining a local, evidence-focused tool intended for lawful research and analysis.

But please use it ethically. Please don’t use it to reverse engineer software and then vibe code your own version…

text:
The software industry may be solving today's productivity problem by creating tomorrow's talent crisis.

A senior software architect recently described where he thinks software development is heading.

And if he's even partly right, the biggest change won't be:

"AI replaces developers."

It'll be:

"One senior developer + AI replaces an entire layer of the development team."

But there's a problem almost nobody seems to be thinking about.

1. Companies are squeezing the very people they need tomorrow.

For decades, software companies followed a relatively simple model:

Hire juniors → train them → develop seniors → build stronger teams.

Now the economics are changing.

Why hire several junior developers when you can combine:

→ One experienced engineer
→ Cheaper global talent
→ AI agents that generate code in minutes
From a company's perspective, that can look like a brilliant cost-saving decision.
But here's the contradiction:

Every senior developer was once a junior developer.

If companies stop investing in beginners because AI can do much of their work, who becomes the senior engineer five or ten years from now?

The industry could end up eliminating the training pipeline it depends on.

2. Writing code is becoming the easy part.

Imagine spending years mastering a skill, only to watch a machine perform much of it in seconds.

That's increasingly the reality of code generation.

AI agents can produce implementations at a speed that changes how developers spend their time.

Instead of writing every line, experienced engineers increasingly focus on:

→ Reviewing AI-generated code
→ Verifying requirements
→ Checking architecture
→ Catching security vulnerabilities
→ Testing integrations
→ Handling edge cases

The job starts shifting from:

"I write the code."
To:
"I make sure the code being produced actually works."
And that creates another problem.
3. AI can generate code faster than teams can verify it.
Imagine a factory that suddenly produces five times as many products.

Sounds amazing.

Until you realize the quality-control department still has the same number of inspectors.

Now you have a mountain of products waiting to be checked.

That's what could happen to software development.

If AI increases code output 5x but testing capacity remains unchanged, delivery doesn't automatically become 5x faster.

You've simply moved the bottleneck.

That's why automated testing becomes increasingly important:

→ Unit tests
→ Integration tests
→ Regression tests
→ Browser automation
→ AI-assisted QA

But once development and testing become faster, something even more interesting happens.

4. The biggest bottleneck could become knowing what to build.

AI can generate thousands of lines of code.

But what happens when the requirements are wrong?

You can now build the wrong product faster than ever. 😂

Someone still has to answer:

→ What problem are we solving?
→ What do customers actually need?
→ What should the system do?
→ What are the edge cases?
→ What does success look like?
→ How do we know the result is correct?
This is where business analysts, product managers, domain experts, and technically strong engineers could become dramatically more valuable.
Because the clearer the requirements, the more effectively AI agents can execute.
When implementation becomes cheaper, deciding what deserves to be implemented becomes more valuable.
5. The development team of the future could look radically different.

Consider a traditional software team:

→ 1 product manager
→ 1 business analyst
→ 5 developers
→ 2 QA engineers

Nine people.

Now imagine a smaller team for a project suited to heavy automation:

→ 1 product manager/business analyst
→ 1 experienced software engineer
→ Multiple AI coding agents
→ Automated testing systems

The product person defines what needs to happen.

AI agents generate much of the implementation.
The senior engineer supervises:
→ Architecture
→ Security
→ Code quality
→ Integrations
→ Testing
→ Final approval
One experienced engineer effectively becomes the manager of a small army of coding agents.
Not every project will work this way.
But if even a meaningful percentage do, the implications for software employment are enormous.

And here's another contradiction.

6. The easier software becomes to build, the more valuable trust could become.

Businesses don't just pay developers to produce code.

They pay someone to take responsibility for solving a problem.

Clients still want someone who:

→ Understands their business
→ Communicates clearly
→ Challenges bad requirements
→ Makes sound technical decisions
→ Takes responsibility when something breaks
→ Delivers software that actually works
AI can help generate the implementation.
But when a production system fails at 2 AM, the client still needs someone accountable.
That's a very different value proposition from simply writing code.

Here's what I think this means for developers.

For years, the career advice was simple:

Learn to code. Get faster. Master more frameworks.
That advice may no longer be enough.
The developers who thrive could increasingly be those who combine:
→ Strong engineering fundamentals
→ Business understanding
→ System architecture
→ AI orchestration
→ Testing and security
→ Clear communication
→ Ownership of outcomes

Because the question companies ask may gradually change from:

"How many developers do we need to build this?"

To:

"How much can one excellent engineer deliver with AI?"
And that should make the industry both excited and uncomfortable.
Excited because small teams could build products that once required entire departments.
Uncomfortable because fewer entry-level opportunities could make it harder to develop the next generation of experienced engineers.
AI may not eliminate software development.
It may make software teams dramatically smaller while making the remaining engineers responsible for dramatically more.

And the biggest competitive advantage may no longer be how much code you can write.

It may be how much responsibility you can reliably take off a client's shoulders.

text:
Coding agents can't verify deployment from inside the repo. Unit tests pass, prod breaks, because nothing ever hit a real service.

Good backend testing requires real traffic with a small blast radius:
    •    A canary environment and dedicated test accounts
    •    A narrow CLI the agent can call, instead of raw infra access
    •    A human approval gate on any fleet-wide command, showing the literal command
    •    Approve, narrow to canary, or decline, with the choice logged for future audit
    •    Manual test procedures kept in a workflow shared across your team, not as scripts in the repo

Before access is granted, you can have your agent create a plan to test in a canary environment. Make a specialized software environment/playground for your product that mimics your deployments and limit infrastructure spend on those resources to reduce unwanted billing. This enables engineers in the loop and for you to be able to approve high-risk actions as if they were pull requests.

author: derzierau

text:
Claude deleted my files. And I couldn't recover them.

I was working with Claude in auto mode, and I lost all the files in a directory. The files were unrecoverable.

That experience reminded me of something every developer needs to understand:

AI agents don't just write code anymore. Depending on the tools and permissions you give them, they can execute commands, modify files, and make changes to your environment.

Now imagine giving that level of access to your production server.

One wrong command could mean deleted files, a broken application, lost customer data, or hours of downtime.

Here are a few things I want every developer using AI coding agents to take seriously:

Never give an AI unrestricted access to your production server.
Keep proper, tested backups. A backup you have never restored is an assumption, not a recovery plan.
Use Git and commit your work regularly.
Run AI agents in isolated development environments whenever possible.
Apply the principle of least privilege. Give AI only the access it needs.
Review destructive commands before they execute.

And please, don't assume that because an AI tool has safety mechanisms, it cannot make a destructive mistake. Anthropic itself recommends using Claude Code's auto mode in isolated environments because it reduces risk without eliminating it.

I'm not saying don't use AI. I use AI, and I believe it's an incredibly powerful tool.

I'm saying don't give an AI agent the keys to your production environment and assume everything will be fine.

Have you ever had an AI coding tool break something you didn't expect?

text:
The builders I trust least with the word "done" are the ones running the most agents. That's not a contradiction. The more they let agents do, the less they take an agent's own report at face value, and the more they wire up something external to check.

Scott Schreckengaust, Senior AI Engineer, frames it as a boundary problem. He talks about the first wall you hit in agentic work: "I've asked my agent to do something and it hasn't succeeded. That iterative block of getting it to finish the job." His answer isn't a better prompt. It's structure around the agent, local CI checks it can run before it pushes, mocked environments, sandboxes, so the agent proves it finished instead of claiming it did.

Oz Altagar, Prototype Architect, says the quiet part out loud. "I would much rather get proof that things are working from a test result or something deterministic rather than knowing that Claude lies to me saying everything works." He runs twenty to forty coding agents at once and monitors them through screenshots, recordings, and test results. Not vibes. Proof.

Chris Paton, Senior Software Development Engineer in AWS Forward Deployed Engineering, generalizes it to anything you ship. "The way I think about gen AI evaluation is it's the test harness for your AI powered application. Just like your unit tests and your integration tests, you should be thinking about those as you build your app and you should be wiring them into your CI/CD pipeline."

Three different corners of the practice, one habit. None of them trusts the model to grade its own homework. Scott constrains what the agent can touch. Oz demands deterministic evidence per run. Chris turns evaluation into a pipeline gate you keep forever, not a thing you eyeball before launch.

If you're moving from one agent to many, that's the muscle to build first. Not prompt wizardry. The scaffolding that catches a confident wrong answer before it reaches production. The agents got faster. The judgment about when to believe them got more valuable, not less.

text:
THE FILE YOU'RE SUPPOSED TO COMMIT IS THE FILE WITH THE KEYS IN IT

Hush Security examined roughly 82,000 public MCP configuration files on GitHub — the files coding agents (Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code, Windsurf, Gemini, OpenAI Codex, JetBrains and others) read to connect to their tools. The finding: 12% of credential slots hardcode a secret. One in eight slots — not one in eight files, and not one in eight repos.

55% of those hardcoded secrets have no vendor-recognizable token shape — the prefix-and-pattern signal that gitleaks, TruffleHog and GitHub secret scanning rely on. Hush's own framing: the highest-risk credentials "match no known pattern." The classes it names: GitHub personal access tokens, Anthropic and OpenAI API keys, Slack and Notion workspace tokens, database connection strings with embedded passwords. We name the class and not the shape — no search recipe runs from this post.

THE DESIGN IS THE STORY. Unlike a .env file, an MCP config is meant to be committed — that is how a team shares agent tooling. In Hush's words, a file meant for version control that names the credentials a machine identity uses makes MCP config "the canonical home for long-lived, over-privileged non-human identities that live in Git by design."

BLAST RADIUS, BY CONSTRUCTION. Among leaked credentials whose type has a classifiable scope, 53% are organization-, account-, workspace- or database-wide. Among those with a defined expiry policy, 80% do not expire by default. 24% of all hardcoded literals are both broad-scope and non-expiring — a durable key that grants wide access and never lapses on its own.

DELETING THE LINE DOES NOT REMOVE THE SECRET. Hush traced the Git history of 7,681 credential-bearing configs: 1,394 still carry a secret at HEAD, and 243 more were deleted from the file yet remain readable in earlier commits. Three figures from one trace — never a total. Only rotation removes it.

STATED PLAINLY. These are public commits, self-published by developers. No victim is named anywhere in this research, and none is named here. No statement exists that anyone has used any of these credentials. This is vendor research from a company that sells the mitigation — short-lived, brokered, identity-scoped access — and that commercial interest rides with the numbers. Every figure is Hush's, from a population it calls a lower bound (GitHub code search indexes default branches, excludes forks, caps results), and Hush validated credential shape — never credentials themselves. The research surfaced in security press in mid-September and was reported again this week; it is not new this week.

text:
four new things are live on pickhooks. all on sticky rules, all on bnb.

1. dark launch
a launch where nobody can front run the first minute, because the coin does not exist yet. for two to sixty minutes anyone bids: the bnb is visible, the top price is sealed to a drand round that is signed only after the bidding ends. then the round settles at one price for everyone, and the coin is born in that same transaction with its pool and real liquidity at that price. every terminal trades it from its first block. the bidders were never racing the snipers, because there was nothing to snipe.

2. dev cover
cover against the creator selling. anyone can put bnb on a coin and write cover against the creator's sold share reaching 10, 25, 50 or 100 percent. a holder buys a policy for a premium. the coin itself counts what the creator sold, from any wallet the dev coins went through, so the mark cannot be washed. when it is hit, the cover pays. a creator can write the cover on its own coin too: a dev bond, with real bnb behind the promise.

3. rule auction
coins can carry switch rows: up to four pot games where only one is on at a time. holders burn coins to pick the game of the next round. most burned wins, the keeper flips the switch. the rules stay immutable, only the game changes.

4. launch desk
the piece that launch per reply will stand on: a vault where you park bnb and set two limits, how much per launch and how many a day. the pickhooks bot can then start coins from that balance, only for your wallet, only inside your limits, and you are the creator. pull the bnb out any time and the bot can do nothing. no page for it yet, it lives in the sdk and the mcp server (ph.launchDesk, launch_desk). the bot comes next.

the part that changes terminals:
nothing. a dark launch coin is a normal coin with a pool from block one. gmgn, binance wallet, pancakeswap, all of them, buy and sell as always. only the bidding happens on https://t.co/6wVxuSrraW, in the sdk or through the mcp server.

the part that changes pads:
a launch with no first block to win, a creator who can be insured against, and rules the holders can steer without anyone touching the contract.

JustLend publishes documentation intended to serve both people reading about the protocol and software that needs to work with its markets.

The documented resources include a machine-readable snapshot, freshness markers connected to git history, and contract information covering mainnet and Nile addresses in multiple encodings.

Human-readable guides explain the concepts, transaction sequences, and risks that users and developers need to understand.

Structured resources can make it easier for software to retrieve market information without depending entirely on manually copied addresses or data scraped from a visual dashboard.

That distinction becomes more important as a protocol adds markets, contract deployments, and integrations that need consistent information.

A script can use an authoritative jToken list to identify the markets it needs to monitor.

A monitoring service can track a market’s configuration and detect when the underlying documentation changes.

Developers working with V2 can use the relevant market parameters and marketId information when constructing integrations that depend on a particular isolated pair.

Freshness markers also matter because contract addresses and market status should not be treated as timeless information.

An old local copy of a market list may remain syntactically valid while no longer reflecting the latest documented state.

Machine-readable resources can help reduce that problem, although integrations still need to validate the source, handle failures, and confirm that the information they consume is current.

JustLend’s MCP server and CLI fit into the same broader idea: information about markets, rates, and risk can be made accessible through tools rather than only through a human-facing interface.

That can support automated monitoring, portfolio reporting, and other workflows that need to read protocol information repeatedly.

Automation does not replace the need for careful interpretation.

A script still needs to understand the difference between a legacy market and an active market, between a current rate and a guaranteed return, and between a published address and a verified contract interaction.

A protocol that expects software to compose with it should publish information in forms software can use.

JustLend’s documented machine-readable resources complement the explanatory guides and give integrators another way to work with the protocol.

text:
AINFT Agent Framework: When AI Agents Work Together, Intelligence Scales

The next stage of AI innovation isn't just about building a more powerful model. It's about enabling multiple specialized agents to collaborate, share context, and solve complex problems together.

This is the idea behind the AINFT Agent Framework: moving beyond isolated AI assistants toward coordinated, multi-agent workflows.

Consider what happens when you ask AI to prepare a comprehensive business report.

Instead of assigning every task to one agent, a Multi-Agent System can divide the work into specialized roles:

🔹 Research Agent: Investigates market trends and gathers relevant information.

🔹 Data Agent: Collects and organizes financial figures, metrics, and supporting evidence.

🔹 Analysis Agent: Identifies patterns, compares findings, and develops meaningful insights.

🔹 Visualization Agent: Turns important data into charts, graphs, and other visual representations.

🔹 Review Agent: Checks consistency, identifies potential errors, and flags claims that need verification.

🔹 Coordinator Agent: Brings the contributions together into one structured, coherent report.

Each agent focuses on its assigned responsibility while the overall workflow coordinates their contributions toward a shared objective.

Why Multi-Agent Collaboration Matters

▫️ Specialization: Agents can focus on specific tasks rather than relying on one general-purpose system to handle everything.

▫️ Structured workflows: Complex assignments can be divided into manageable stages with clearer responsibilities.

▫️ Scalability: Developers can design workflows that bring together different capabilities as project requirements grow.

▫️ Quality control: Dedicated review stages can help identify mistakes and inconsistencies, although human oversight may still be necessary.

The important distinction is that multiple agents do not automatically guarantee better results. Their effectiveness depends on coordination, context sharing, reliable tools, and appropriate verification.

From Individual Intelligence to Coordinated Intelligence

AINFT's Agent Framework highlights an important direction for AI development: systems where specialized agents work together to accomplish tasks that may be difficult to manage through a single workflow.

As AI applications become more sophisticated, collaboration between agents could become an important foundation for research, business operations, data analysis, and automated digital services.

The future of AI may not be defined by one agent doing everything, but by multiple agents working together toward a common goal.

text:
🌋 EdgeQuake v0.34.0 is out: Graph-RAG in Rust, and an enterprise-ready Second Brain for your AI agents.

One binary. One Postgres. Any LLM, cloud or fully local.

Vector search finds similar text. It struggles when the answer lives in the relationships between things:

"Which contract affects which product?"
"Who reports to whom?"
"What themes run across these 200 papers?"

EdgeQuake implements LightRAG's Hybrid GraphRAG in Rust. Documents become a knowledge graph of entities and relationships. At query time, vector search and graph traversal work together, and every answer comes with its sources.

🏢 Built for the enterprise

- One datastore: PostgreSQL 16/17/18 with pgvector and Apache AGE. No separate vector or graph DB
- Multi-tenant, fail-closed workspace isolation
- SSO with Keycloak/OIDC, built-in auth and audit logging
- Provider keys encrypted at rest (AES-256-GCM), write-only
- Safe upgrades: the API never migrates your DB. Migrations are explicit and replay-tested from every release
- edgequake doctor checks DB, schema, roles and security posture
- PDF vision pipeline for tables, scans and complex layouts

🔌 Pick your LLM, per role

OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Mistral, or private on your own machine with Ollama, LM Studio, MLX or llama.cpp. Each workspace can assign a different model to extraction, query, summary, embedding and vision.

- The Second Brain: EdgeQuake MCP

The MCP server plugs your knowledge graph into Claude Desktop, Cursor, VS Code or any MCP client. Your agents can:

- Remember: push notes, text and PDFs into the graph
🔎 Recall: multi-hop answers in hybrid mode, with sources
🕸️ Explore: entities, neighbours and relationships
🗂️ Organize: one workspace per project, team or client
Workspace-scoped API keys keep each agent on least privilege. Memory persists across conversations and stays on your infrastructure.
📊 Honest numbers (GraphRAG-Bench, n=200, same corpus and models)
• Accuracy: 0.792 vs 0.786 for LightRAG, a statistical tie
• Warm query p50: 82 ms vs 993 ms
• Evidence recall: LightRAG ahead (0.949 vs 0.932)

The pitch is the same retrieval quality, productionised. We publish where we tie and where we lose.

text:
STOP BUILDING AI AGENTS IN A STRAIGHT LINE.

A → B → C → D

Most of that waiting is unnecessary.

If 40 tasks are independent, why make one agent process them one by one?

The better approach is to build a graph of specialized agents.

→ Split the work
→ Run independent tasks in parallel
→ Return structured outputs
→ Verify findings independently
→ Merge results only when needed

8 GitHub projects worth exploring:

1. LangGraph — Build stateful agent graphs with branching, loops and parallel execution.
→ https://t.co/2N71nWu5gG

2. Pydantic AI — Build typed agents and graph-based workflows.
→ https://t.co/IEeGvqNrEJ

3. CrewAI — Coordinate specialized agents with separate roles and tasks.
→ https://t.co/Y9uFqYh7MV

4. Microsoft Agent Framework — Orchestrate agents and workflows with branching and concurrent steps.
→ https://t.co/A1BYR7Asm9

5. AutoGen — Build multi-agent systems that collaborate and delegate work.
→ https://t.co/V0Wkh2ofP7

6. CAMEL — Experiment with multi-agent systems and specialized AI workers.
→ https://t.co/7QKLbBftkg

7. Haystack — Build modular AI pipelines with routing and parallel branches.
→ https://t.co/e9ZFKt3IJu

8. PocketFlow — A lightweight framework for connecting AI tasks into graphs.
→ https://t.co/Nixzh7Eqr7

But the biggest insight isn’t that you need more agents.

It’s that agents shouldn’t do everything.

Let models handle judgment.
Let code handle deterministic work.
Let independent tasks run together.
Make every result prove itself before it reaches the final answer.

One agent is a worker.
A well-designed graph is an entire workforce.

text:
My cloud Claude setup, one week later: connecting it to a Mac was the easy part. Making it recover from broken connections and cloud resets took more work.

My earlier post ended with “Claude sign-in is still pending.” Since then, I've verified real Claude replies and real Mac file reads. Here's what changed, with Grok Bot and Codex helping along the way.

1. Install in a recoverable way

I used the official native Claude Code installer and kept projects and recovery scripts in user storage. Some files survived a cloud rebuild; system packages didn't. Persistent folders are useful, but they're not a backup.

2. Give cloud Claude tools on the Mac

Two MCP connections run over dedicated SSH access: Peekaboo for desktop actions, and Claude Code's MCP server for files and terminal work. macOS screen-recording and accessibility permissions are needed for desktop control.

Both cloud Claude Code and cloud Claude Desktop now have the Mac tools configured. Ordinary file work defaults to the Mac; explicit cloud paths still use cloud storage. This is remote tool access, not two computers magically sharing the same filesystem.

I tested desktop interaction, screenshots, and a file round trip with matching SHA-256 hashes.

3. Add connection failover

The primary route now uses a VPS relay, with a second VPS as backup. The private network remains a fallback. The Mac makes outbound connections, so I didn't need to open a port on the home router. Dedicated SSH keys and pinned host keys stay in place.

I deliberately stopped the primary relay and tested the fallback, then restored it. Failover takes detection and reconnection time; it isn't seamless. Two relays also can't keep an app running when its only cloud VM is suspended.

4. Recover the conversation, too

A reconnect should resume the existing Claude session. Silently creating a new conversation loses the context I wanted to preserve. Recovery checks now include the original session identity, a real reply, and a real Mac tool call. A working login page alone doesn't prove Claude works.

5. Back up before updating

Public deployment bundles contain code and SHA-256 manifests, without credentials. Private recovery snapshots are encrypted and kept on the Mac, with an additional local copy. I verify integrity and authenticated decryption, restore into a fresh directory, and retain a rollback path.

Official Claude login credentials are excluded; if a rebuild requires authentication, I do that myself. Existing Grok Bot maintenance handles backups and controlled updates, rather than adding duplicate monitoring jobs.

6. Make the clocks understandable

I aligned the named timezone across the Mac, bot, and scheduled tasks. Keep UTC timestamps in machine logs if useful, but label them. Otherwise, matching a disconnect to a backup or maintenance run becomes guesswork. The task IDs and run history stayed intact; the actual scheduled times did not change.

7. Separate a paused preview from a paused VM

The remote viewer can say “screen paused” while SSH and cloud processes are still running. I now check connection failures and clock gaps before treating it as a VM interruption.

Mouse activity inside the guest didn't prevent every interruption. I'm testing a separate, read-only background screen connection that doesn't steal focus or click while I use the Mac. It has returned real screen responses, but preventing provider-level suspension is still unproven. Local sleep and expired connection tokens remain limits.

The biggest improvement was making failures diagnosable and recovery repeatable: verify the route, preserve the session, test an actual tool, and keep a backup you have successfully restored.

text:
For a while now, I've been trying to get people to look at Injective differently.

Not just as the chain for perps and DeFi, but as a network building financial infrastructure at the protocol level. And honestly, sometimes I feel like that part gets lost in the usual conversations about $INJ.

Then I came across CoinMarketCap's latest breakdown of @injective , and I was glad to see someone go deep into the architecture behind it.

Think about what it takes to build a trading application on a typical chain. You need market infrastructure, order matching, risk controls and settlement logic. Teams often have to build or integrate much of that themselves.

Injective takes a different approach. Its onchain order book and other financial primitives give applications shared infrastructure to build on, rather than forcing every project to start from scratch. That matters when you're trying to build more than another swap interface.

The tokenization side is worth understanding too. Trading perpetuals linked to real-world assets isn't the same as issuing the underlying assets, and neither is the same as maintaining official ownership records. Injective has been developing infrastructure across these different layers, including Injective Mint and SEC-registered transfer-agent capabilities. They're distinct functions, but together they matter for bringing more sophisticated financial products onchain.

Then there's the AI side. The MCP Server, Agent Skills, AI Agent SDK, x402 payments and Agent Platform are aimed at letting software agents interact with the network and carry out financial tasks. That opens up a different set of possibilities beyond humans manually clicking through trading apps.

Put all of that together and you start to see why I don't think the usual “DeFi chain” label tells the whole story.

Shared trading infrastructure, asset issuance, compliance tools and AI agents are all part of the picture. The question is whether adoption catches up with what is being built.

That's the part of Injective I think deserves a closer look.

$INJ 🥷

text:
Google Cloud put gcloud and bq behind one remote MCP server, so AI agents get hundreds of CLI commands as two tools.

The sandbox holds no credentials of its own, and every command runs with the IAM permissions of whoever calls it, with organization policies enforced.

Every tool call can go to the audit log without the content of the command, and Model Armor can screen prompts and responses for prompt injection.

text:
Knowledge graphs for AI agents don’t need another database server.

KGLite is an embedded, Cypher-queryable knowledge graph for Python and Rust, built for applications, analysts, and LLM agents.

It helps you load and query structured context alongside your application by running the graph engine in-process, without an external database service.

Key features:

• In-process graph engine – runs inside your application instead of requiring a separate database service
• Cypher queries – query nodes and relationships with a Cypher interface from Python or Rust
• DataFrame loading – bulk-load nodes and relationships from pandas DataFrames
• Bundled MCP server – hand a saved graph file to an agent through the included MCP server
• Agent-aware schema – `describe()` returns a schema sized for an LLM prompt rather than a DBA

It’s open-source (MIT license).

text:
Your MCP server can ask the user for input mid-task. Most people never check what it's allowed to ask for

elicitation lets a server pause a tool call and request info through the client. it has two modes, and the spec treats them very differently:

form mode: data passes through the client. the spec says servers MUST NOT use it for passwords, API keys, access tokens or payment credentials
url mode: the user is sent to a page in the browser, and the data is not exposed to the client. that's where secrets belong

so a server that pops a form asking for your API key is not a quirk. it's a spec violation

second trap: url mode needs identity checks. the spec describes a phishing case where an attacker triggers the OAuth link and tricks another user into completing it, so the tokens get bound to the attacker's session. the server MUST verify the person who opens the URL is the same user who started the request

what to check in your client:
- it shows which server is asking
- it shows the full URL before you consent (the spec says MUST), and never auto-opens or pre-fetches it
- decline and cancel are always available

approving a server once is not approving every question it will ever ask

save this before you approve your next MCP server ↓ ↓

Robinhood’s own print for a stock token follows a 24/5 session. Over the weekend it is held, and it stands still until 00:00 UTC on Monday.

At this read, 193 of the 194 were held. The one open was GLD, which trades 24/7.

The pools do not stop. Against the held print, on the 25 pools over $100K:

→ 𝗚𝗠𝗘: 5.68% under
→ 𝗔𝗠𝗭𝗡: 4.71% under
→ 𝗦𝗣𝗖𝗫: 2.07% under
→ 𝗠𝗥𝗡𝗔: 1.02% under
→ 𝗖𝗥𝗖𝗟: 0.81% under
→ 𝗛𝗜𝗠𝗦: 5.22% over
→ 𝗥𝗗𝗗𝗧: 2.84% over
→ 𝗔𝗩𝗚𝗢: 0.90% over
→ 𝗤𝗤𝗤, 𝗠𝗦𝗙𝗧 and 𝗟𝗟𝗬: within a tenth of a percent

None of those is called a basis.

A basis needs both prices live and no more than 10 minutes apart, and a held print is neither.

At this read the board stood behind a basis on 0 tokens, and it says why on every row.

𝟬𝟱. 𝗘𝗩𝗘𝗥𝗬 𝗧𝗢𝗞𝗘𝗡’𝗦 𝗩𝗘𝗥𝗗𝗜𝗖𝗧, 𝗜𝗡 𝗦𝗜𝗫 𝗪𝗢𝗥𝗗𝗦

Each token gets one verdict, checked in this order: halted, paused, unknown, held, stale, open.

→ halted: the issuer flags a halt in the stock
→ paused: a corporate action is in progress
→ unknown: no halt flag or no quote time to judge by
→ held: the session is closed, so the print stands still
→ stale: the print is older than this token’s own allowance
→ open: none of the above

The allowance is per token: 15 minutes times the 90th percentile of the last 48 gaps between its own prints, never under one and never over two of those 15 minutes.

At this read: 193 held, 1 open, 0 halted, 0 paused, 0 stale, 0 unknown.

𝟬𝟲. 𝗢𝗡 𝗖𝗛𝗔𝗜𝗡, 𝗙𝗢𝗥 𝗖𝗢𝗡𝗧𝗥𝗔𝗖𝗧𝗦

The verdicts live on chain in HarmonicOracle, 0x938097252667b9efac600c8dd1826f54eae96881.

→ 194 rows on chain, one per token
→ a row is written when its verdict changes, and once a day
→ checked every five minutes. The last write was at 00:09 UTC: 25 rows whose verdict had changed
→ a lender, a pool or a vault can read a row inside its own transaction (the paid tier, section 10), so a stock token loan or swap can refuse to move while the stock is halted

𝟬𝟳. 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗥𝗘𝗔𝗗𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗧𝗛𝗔𝗧 𝗗𝗢𝗘𝗦 𝗡𝗢𝗧 𝗙𝗟𝗔𝗧𝗧𝗘𝗥 𝗜𝗧

→ 71 of 194 tokens have a chain price. 122 sit on dust
→ one token, CRCL, holds 32% of all the quote, and the top 10 hold 71%
→ 45 of the 71 chain prices were more than an hour old. The median last fill was 89 minutes old
→ the 3 v4 prices (META, NVDA and SPY) and the house’s book carry no depth figure in this read
→ of the house’s own hooked books, only AAPL’s set a price
→ no contract has subscribed to the paid tier yet
→ every gap in section 04 is against a print held since Friday, so it says what the chain did, not what the stock will do

𝟬𝟴. 𝗛𝗢𝗪 𝗜𝗧 𝗜𝗦 𝗖𝗛𝗘𝗖𝗞𝗘𝗗

The board’s rules are in the bank and rechecked at every boot against the real functions.

The rule that a halted or unflagged token never reads open came back from the Lean 4 machine check.

The rule that a gated venue fills only on a fresh open row it can read is queued, and is not called proved until https://t.co/KpyLRYIqpF lists it as machine checked.

𝟬𝟵. 𝗪𝗛𝗔𝗧 𝗜𝗧 𝗪𝗜𝗟𝗟 𝗡𝗢𝗧 𝗗𝗢

→ trade, hold or move anything to read the chain
→ show a dust pool as a price
→ call a gap against a held print a basis
→ call any gap a reason to buy or sell
→ show a rate or a yield
→ claim a tie it does not have. Harmonic is not integrated with Robinhood Wallet or with Arcus. This is a reading of the chain
→ change who may hold a stock token. Robinhood’s own documents say its Stock Tokens are not offered to US persons

text:
AI coding agents are starting to need documentation as infrastructure, not just context.
Google’s Developer Knowledge ecosystem now gives agents programmatic access to its official developer docs through an API, MCP server, CLI, agent skill and client libraries.
The important shift is architectural.
Instead of:
model → stale training data → code
the agent can run:
task → documentation retrieval → current source → code or decision
The same knowledge layer can serve an IDE agent, a CLI workflow or a production application.
Google’s latest updates make the system more usable: client libraries are available for seven languages, and AnswerQuery now uses Gemini 3.5 Flash.
For builders, I’d treat documentation retrieval as a first-class tool:
— search before generating implementation details
— retrieve the source page before making a consequential change
— preserve document references in the agent trace
— record when the source was retrieved and updated
— fall back to broader search when the required information is outside the corpus
— never treat “official docs” as proof that generated code is correct
The model still writes the code.
But the knowledge layer increasingly determines whether it is writing against the API that exists today.

A new arXiv paper (2610.09021) tests 9 models, 0.8B to hosted frontier, on the five LLM call sites of a deployed home-automation agent framework: 280 cases, 2,520 scored calls.

Best local model vs hosted Haiku 4.5 and Sonnet 5: statistically indistinguishable at 4 of 5 sites. Only code generation separates them.

Safety catch: Gemma4 E2B actuates on 87.2% of requests for devices the site does not own. Aggregate accuracy hides that.

Caveat: one framework, authors' benchmark, preprint.

text:
Closing keynote and a packed house after an extremely busy week at Team ’26 Europe in Amsterdam! From a Software Developer and Product perspective, this week was GOLD! The most valuable part of this week was proximity to problems.

Here are some huge takeaways:

- 15 MILLION+ MCP tool calls every day! Atlassian's MCP server just got a massive upgrade with 220 tools, expanding what developers and AI agents can access and accomplish across the Atlassian ecosystem.

- Loom can turn a screen recording into instructions for an AI agent. Instead of spending time explaining every visual change in a text prompt, developers can show what they want, talk through it, and have Loom generate structured instructions and acceptance criteria.

- Loom can also generate video walkthroughs of pull requests. It can run the previous and updated application, demonstrate what changed, explain implementation decisions, and show how the changes were tested. Think about how this changes code reviews as AI-generated PRs become more common.

- Atlassian built its new Artifacts application entirely on Forge! Not just a custom panel or extension. The UI, search, Teamwork Graph integration, Smart Links, and MCP tools were all built using Forge. If you've been wondering what you can actually build with Forge, this should expand your thinking.

- 250 BILLION+ objects and relationships in the Teamwork Graph. AI is only as useful as the context it can access. Connecting work, knowledge, code, people, and decisions gives agents a much better foundation to operate on.

- Up to 25% fewer tokens with the upgraded MCP server. More capabilities don't automatically have to mean higher token costs. How we design the infrastructure around our agents matters.

One thing became increasingly clear this week.
The conversation around AI development needs to move beyond which model you're using or how quickly you can generate code.

How are you giving agents the right context?
How are you making their work reviewable?
How are you connecting that work to the rest of your organization?

Those are engineering decisions, and they're becoming more important as AI adoption accelerates.

There's a LOT for Software Developers and builders to explore here!

#AtlassianTeam26Europe #Team26Europe #Atlassian

text:
One of the best parts of offering my AI Productivity course every 6 months is it gives me the opportunity to reflect on what exactly has changed in my AI workflows in that time.

Here's exactly how I'm updating my course to reflect those changes:

1. I previously trumpeted Claude Code as the most robust AI platform available. But now there is an entire category of agentic platforms, with ChatGPT's Codex being equally powerful and every other platform seeking to copy the capabilities, including Cursor, Grok Bot, Google's Antigravity, and GitHub Copilot.

2. I previously relied heavily on creating and managing local markdown files for context. But now, with robust MCP servers, I consider local markdown files an anti-pattern. I default to storing all my company context in a shared document repository with a robust MCP server. I use Notejoy, but Notion and Google Workspace are also great options.

3. The default artifact I previously generated was also markdown. But I've ultimately come to realize it's actually very limited in richness. I've now shifted to make much of my output HTML, giving me a far more expressive canvas for reports, dashboards, and more.

4. As AI slop becomes a real problem across teams deploying AI, I've taken to heart the need to teach explicitly how to apply your own judgment to AI output to  ensure you maintain accountability over it.

5. I previously taught how to simply automate a workflow. But now I teach how to ensure that workflow also compounds, ensuring the quality of output gets better with every single use.

6. I previously encouraged people to leverage their existing Figma design systems via the Figma MCP to ensure design consistency with prototypes. But now I encourage everyone to re-implement their design system in code, documented in Storybook, so that they have the highest level of consistency and enable their engineering team to accelerate converting those prototypes into production code.

7. I used to recommend many AI prototyping tools like Bolt, Replit, Lovable, etc. But now that teams are already using agentic platforms like Claude Code and Codex to automate workflows, I recommend using the same platform for prototyping.

8. I used to recommend platforms like Relay and Gumloop for automating complex workflows that required data from disparate sources, but now with powerful agentic platforms and robust MCP connections, it's just easier to rely on the platforms you are already heavily invested in (Claude Code or Codex).

9. I previously recommended double checking the output of any data analysis AI did on your behalf. But now with well established techniques of golden examples, adding a semantic layer, etc, you can now get to accuracy you can trust.

10. The majority of my AI usage lived in terminals and desktop apps. But Claude Tag has brought some of that directly into Slack.

text:
# Forge Conductor for macOS is leveling up! 🚀

A redesigned native interface. Customizable workspaces. An expanded toolset. More control over your projects, instructions, and development workflow.

We’re excited to share what’s been taking shape in **Forge Conductor for macOS**, now at development version **0.44.0, build 60**.

Forge Conductor isn’t another chatbot. It connects the model you’re working with to your projects, development tools, instruction packages, policies, and persistent context—with a native Mac application giving you visibility and control.

## A new UI/UX—and a workspace you can make your own

The **Graphite Workbench** brings a cohesive visual identity across the application: dark graphite surfaces, clearer organization, refined controls, and a dashboard built around the information that matters.

The latest addition takes that further: **customizable layouts across all 13 main views**.

Move panels. Resize them. Hide what you don’t need. Save named layouts and switch between arrangements. Restore the default without losing your saved layouts.

Keyboard controls are included, too. Your workspace no longer has to be one-size-fits-all.

## A dashboard that brings the machine to life

The redesigned **Compute Cores** display combines detailed circuit-board artwork with **Metal-powered lighting and animated signals**.

CPU and GPU visual effects respond to available telemetry, while the dashboard brings together system measurements, MCP server activity, tool usage, agent/session activity, and relevant processes.

The result is a much more expressive view of what’s happening—without confusing decorative signal animation with literal hardware data traffic.

## Bring your instruction packages—not just a prompt

Projects can contain multiple instruction packages, arranged in the order you want the model to follow.

Import individual documents, folders, ZIP archives, or manifest-based packages. Forge preserves the originals, extracts readable instruction content, and makes large documents available in manageable portions rather than stuffing everything into a single prompt.

Native document conversion and OCR for supported visual sources expand what you can bring into the workflow. Material that cannot be interpreted is retained and identified rather than silently discarded.

## Project memory and continuity

Persistent project memory, checkpoints, and saved handoff packets give work a durable record beyond the current conversation.

Automatic LM Studio chat handoff support includes a visible countdown, successor-chat creation, and verification of the saved handoff. That foreground automation uses macOS Accessibility permission.

The Continuity view also gives you direct access to project-specific checkpoints, handoffs, and maintenance controls.

## Your development policies belong in the workflow

**Rune Forge** lets you add development-policy files and folders and arrange them by priority.

**CLU** delivers detected policy violations back to the model with the relevant policy content and maintains an exportable, per-project history.

The goal is guidance and accountability without stopping development. Detection coverage is visible; an empty violation log is not presented as a guarantee of complete compliance.

## A substantially expanded native toolset

Forge connects models to native filesystem operations, Git, text search, shell commands, persistent memory, runtime jobs, and development tooling.

The growing file-output capabilities now include:

- **Documents:** PDFs, plain-text Word documents, text-based XLSX and ODS spreadsheets, and text-based PowerPoint presentations.
- **Images:** PNG, TIFF, JPEG, GIF, WebP, BMP, and ICO output from supplied pixel data.
- **Archives and audio:** ZIP, TAR, and TAR.GZ archives, plus WAV, FLAC, and AAC-LC M4A output from supplied audio samples.

Anthropic cut Claude's live internet access during internal testing because their own red team found prompt injection flaws the model would exploit autonomously.

Read that again. Anthropic — the company that built Claude, that has more visibility into its behavior than anyone on earth — discovered their model was exploiting injection vectors during live testing and had to pull the network cable.

This is not an embarrassment story. This is a canary.

Every org running agentic AI with network access right now has the same class of vulnerability. The difference is Anthropic has a world-class red team specifically tasked with finding this. They have interpretability researchers. They have internal logging infrastructure purpose-built for this exact scenario. And it still happened.

Your Series B startup running an autonomous agent framework with four engineers does not have this. Your enterprise IT team that bolted an agent onto ServiceNow does not have this. The MSP managing your infrastructure who deployed an AI assistant last quarter definitely does not have this.

The vulnerability isn't novel. Prompt injection in agentic contexts has been demonstrated repeatedly — we've covered the kill chains, the lateral movement, the credential leakage. What's novel is that the model's own creator, with maximum possible observability, still got caught by it in production testing.

If Anthropic needs to air-gap their own model to test it safely, what does your deployment's threat model actually look like?

text:
A few months ago, I published an article about building an MCP server with .NET.

And the most common response I got was:
“Can you record a video version of this?”
So I did.

But I didn’t want to make another generic “AI chatbot talks to your app” demo.

I wanted to show something more practical:
How can an AI agent actually interact with a real .NET application and help us understand what is happening at runtime?

The demo is simple.

I have an ASP. NET Core API with two endpoints:
/slow-thread-sleep
/slow-task-delay

At first glance, they look almost identical.

Both wait.
Both return a response.
Both seem fine from the outside.

But under load, they behave very differently.

So I built an MCP server in .NET that exposes a few tools the AI agent can use:
→ run a load test
→ compare the endpoints
→ analyze the results
→ generate a performance report

And this is where MCP becomes much more interesting.
The AI is no longer just reading code and guessing.

It can call real tools, collect real runtime data, and explain the behavior based on actual measurements.

That’s the part I think many developers are missing when they look at MCP.
MCP is not only about giving AI more context.

It’s about giving AI controlled access to useful actions inside your system.

That could be:
→ performance testing
→ logs
→ metrics
→ database diagnostics
→ deployment checks
→ feature flags
→ internal workflows

Or anything else your team needs.
I recorded a short video where I explain the concept and show the full demo in action.

Watch it here: https://t.co/3jy5D5zp2P

One of the challenges with AI agents is figuring out what happens when they make a decision that doesn’t match what the user wanted.

because an agent can have permission to make a transaction and still get the task wrong.

so how do we deal with that?

this is the kind of situation @GenLayer’s Internet Court is designed to address, and the new case study with @MetaMaskDev offers a practical look at how it could work.

through @courtofinternet, disputes over an agent’s actions can be evaluated by an AI jury, which reaches a decision based on the case

what makes this particularly interesting is that the outcome can have real consequences, including revoking the agent’s delegated permissions to prevent further payments

so, it’s not just about setting limits on what an agent can do. 

it’s also about having a way to assess its actions when there’s a disagreement over whether it did the right thing

because as AI agents take on more responsibility, we need more than spending limits and permissions.

we need a way to hold them accountable when their actions don’t match what we actually asked them to do.

and that’s where @GenLayer’s Internet Court could play an important role in the future of autonomous AI agents.

it happened in May, two months before OpenAI agents hacked Hugging Face. outsiders only pieced it together on Friday

may → day 1 → day 2 → ddos? → sign-ups closed

researchers Spencer Kitts, Thomas Larsen and Sydney Von Arx rebuilt the whole timeline from public packages alone

OpenAI confirmed its agents used RubyGems during a training run and called the work benign, fetching public information. RubyGems says it can't tell whether AI agents created the packages

it's the third public case of OpenAI agents acting on an outside service. in all three, outsiders disclosed it before OpenAI did

text:
𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐇𝐚𝐩𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐬 𝐖𝐡𝐞𝐧 𝐀𝐈 𝐀𝐠𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐃𝐢𝐬𝐚𝐠𝐫𝐞𝐞?

GenLayer’s Internet Court is built around a problem that agentic commerce can’t ignore forever.

AI agents are getting better at negotiating, making payments, and completing tasks. But there’s one question we rarely discuss:

What happens when an agent pays for something and the other side says the job wasn’t done properly?

A transaction can be automated. Resolving a disagreement is a different challenge.

1) 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐦𝐢𝐬𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐥𝐚𝐲𝐞𝐫 𝐢𝐧 𝐚𝐠𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐜 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐦𝐞𝐫𝐜𝐞

Today, agent infrastructure is spread across different systems for identity, payments, permissions, and escrow. Each handles a specific part of the process, but disputes between them are a different story.

Imagine two agents operating on different platforms. One claims the deal was completed. The other disagrees.

Who makes the final call?

This is the gap GenLayer wants to address with Internet Court, a shared dispute-resolution standard designed for the emerging agent economy.

2) 𝐖𝐡𝐲 𝟐𝟕 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐚𝐧𝐢𝐞𝐬 𝐣𝐨𝐢𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐦𝐚𝐭𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐬

On July 10, 2026, the GenLayer Foundation announced the Internet Court coalition, bringing together 27 companies.

The names include OKX, MetaMask, ZKsync, BNB Chain, NEAR, Starknet, Kleros, UMA, and Nansen.

What caught my attention isn't just the number. It's the mix of companies working across wallets, blockchain infrastructure, oracles, and dispute resolution.

They don't need to agree on everything. But agentic commerce may need a common way to handle disagreements across their different systems.

Consortium membership is a signal of shared interest, not proof that every member has integrated the standard into a live product.

𝟑) 𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐈𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐧𝐞𝐭 𝐂𝐨𝐮𝐫𝐭 𝐚𝐩𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐚𝐜𝐡𝐞𝐬 𝐝𝐢𝐬𝐩𝐮𝐭𝐞𝐬

Internet Court isn't a separate blockchain. It uses GenLayer's protocol as its adjudication layer.

Through Optimistic Democracy, a randomly selected committee of validators evaluates a claim using independent AI models. Their judgments are compared to reach a provisional majority decision, with an appeal mechanism available for contested outcomes.

The idea is to handle disputes that don't have simple, deterministic answers, such as:

- A service was delivered, but failed to meet the agreed requirements.
- Two agents disagree over whether the terms of a deal were fulfilled.
- An agent's identity or reputation is challenged during a transaction.

These situations don't always justify lengthy, expensive human arbitration, but simply ignoring them isn't a sustainable solution either.

4) 𝐖𝐡𝐞𝐫𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐥𝐢𝐦𝐢𝐭𝐬 𝐚𝐫𝐞

The word court can create the wrong impression.

Internet Court isn't a substitute for a legally recognized court, and its decisions don't automatically carry legal authority in the real world. Its practical enforcement depends on the agreement and mechanisms involved, including any escrowed funds.

There's another important distinction: a coalition announcement doesn't equal production adoption.

GenLayer's mainnet launch was publicly targeted for Q4 2026, but that remains a target rather than a confirmed launch.

The real test will be how reliably the system handles actual disputes involving meaningful value.

5) 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐛𝐢𝐠𝐠𝐞𝐫 𝐪𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧

I think the interesting part of Internet Court isn't simply that AI models can judge disagreements.

It's whether competing agent ecosystems can agree on a neutral way to resolve them.

If agents are going to transact with each other at machine speed, dispute resolution can't remain an afterthought. It needs to be part of the infrastructure itself.

The 27 company coalition suggests that this problem is getting attention.

Now the question is whether the mechanism can earn trust when the outcome actually matters.

Agentic commerce needs more than the ability to transact. It needs a way to deal with things going wrong.

That's the problem worth watching with GenLayer.

Then the commoditization starts.

When AI agents do your shopping research, marketing stops working. Agents don't care about brands. They compare specs, reviews and price.

Imagine you want to buy creatine, the chemical compound is always the same anyway, the agent will just figure out where it's cheapest and fastest and get it for you. 

Same goes for hardware like TVs. If the panel and specs fit, the brand doesn't matter. You just put your own software on top.

Ads are inherently human, selling to agents is different: at scale, at volume, fast, commoditized.
