text:
For two days at Marina Bay Sands in Singapore, @SuiNetwork turned part of TOKEN2049 into something that looked less like a traditional conference and more like a temporary city built around the machine economy.

I wasn't there in person, but I followed the event through the livestream, moving between the Summit Stage, the trading arena, the AI Builder Lab and the different demos as they went live.

And the more I watched, the more it became difficult to see Basecamp as just another blockchain conference.

There were announcements everywhere.

But underneath them was a much more specific idea.

Sui wasn't simply talking about AI agents becoming smarter.

It was asking what happens when those agents start owning assets, making payments, executing trades and interacting with other software without a human sitting behind every transaction.

That is a different problem.

Today's crypto infrastructure was largely built around a human being the active participant.

➺ You open the wallet.

➺ You choose the asset.

➺ You approve the transaction.

➺ You wait for settlement.

➺ You do it again.

An agent doesn't need to operate that way.

➺ It can monitor a market continuously.

➺ It can purchase data.

➺ It can pay for an API.

➺ It can move capital according to predefined rules.

➺ It can interact with another agent.

And it can do those things while you're asleep.

So while the 40.6 million TPS figure became one of the biggest talking points from Basecamp, I think the more interesting story was everything surrounding it.

@SuiNetwork was effectively showing the different pieces it believes an agentic financial system needs:

⪼ Speed.

⪼ Permissions.

⪼ Memory.

⪼ Stablecoins.

⪼ Cross-chain liquidity.

⪼ Programmable assets.

⪼ Consumer distribution.

⪼ Bitcoin collateral.

And a way for humans to remain in control without having to manually approve everything.

text:
I am concerned that the widespread adoption of AI, agents, and robots could lead to breaks in two chains that sustain human society. The first is the economic chain: declining demand for human labor could weaken labor income and mass purchasing power, affecting corporate earnings and reinvestment, while new systems of distribution may fail to fill the gap in time. The second is the knowledge chain: as humans increasingly outsource thinking and judgment to AI and gradually lose opportunities to learn, practice, and contribute, their capacity to understand, verify, exercise independent judgment, and pass on knowledge could steadily diminish. These two processes could reinforce each other. Even if income redistribution reconnects the economic chain, it may not repair the knowledge chain—society could continue to produce and function while humans gradually lose the ability to understand, participate in, and exercise control over those processes.

#Wangius #WTS #WangiusThoughtSystem #AI #Automation #FutureOfWork #IncomeDistribution #KnowledgeTransmission #HumanAgency #AIPhilosophy

我担心，AI、Agent与机器人的广泛应用可能使人类社会面临两条链的断裂：一是经济链，劳动需求下降削弱劳动收入与大众购买力，进而影响企业收益和再投资，而新的分配制度未必能及时承接；二是知识链，人类长期将思考与判断外包给AI，又逐渐失去学习、实践与贡献的机会，使理解、验证、独立判断和知识传承的能力不断减弱。两者可能相互强化，而即便收入再分配重新连接了经济链，也未必能够修复知识链——社会仍能生产和运转，人类却可能逐渐失去理解、参与和掌握这些过程的能力。

text:
Portal : The AI-Native Bridge Turning Game Ideas Into Playable Worlds Across Every Chain

Web3 gaming has always promised freedom: own your assets, play anywhere, earn for real. In practice? Players juggle wallets, bridges, and dead games while creators drown in tools that don’t talk to each other. Portal is rewriting that story.

What Problem Portal Solves & The Solution

Fragmentation is the silent killer of Web3 gaming. Games live on isolated chains, payments require swaps, and building a simple prototype means stitching five different platforms together. 
Portal’s answer is a single, unified account that gives access to discovery, payments, and creation tools across chains. Portal Pay lets you spend any token while developers receive what they want. 
More importantly, the platform has pivoted hard into AI-native creation: Nexus generates game-ready assets, and Gen8 turns prompts into playable games you can tweak on the fly. 
One login, one ecosystem, from idea to something people can actually play.

Is It Unique or Just Another GameFi Project?

Most GameFi projects compete on the same tired axes: play-to-earn loops, NFT marketplaces, or single-chain launches. 
Portal stands out by combining cross-chain interoperability (powered by LayerZero and expanding with Bitcoin connectivity) with a genuine creator toolkit. 
The December 2025 merger with BLIFE Protocol brought Bitcoin-native infrastructure and identity into the mix, backed by Animoca Brands and led by Benjamin Charbit, a former Ubisoft director behind Assassin’s Creed IV: Black Flag. 
While competitors like Immutable or Gala focus on specific ecosystems or publishing, Portal is building the connective tissue and the AI studio layer on top. That dual focus is rare.

Amazing Recent Developments

The shift to Portal 2.0 reframed the project around AI creation tools and creator-first workflows. Gen8 open beta is live, letting users pick templates, generate games, and then modify art, mechanics, levels, and enemies with AI agents. Game jams with 50,000 Shards prize pools have been running, rewarding real participation. 
The team has also sunsetting legacy staking and moved fully into the new chapter, while fees have already powered buybacks. 
The BLIFE integration and Animoca support give the platform both capital and a direct pipeline into a massive gaming portfolio.

Upcoming Developments

Gen8 is still in open beta through the end of October, with the full release expected soon. 
Beyond, the tridirectional Bitcoin L1 bridge acquired through the BLIFE deal, is preparing for mainnet, potentially giving Bitcoin holders a native path into Web3 games without wraps or custodians. 
Expect continued expansion of the unified creator stack (Nexus, Shop, Studio), more chain support, and deeper integration of Shards as a rewards layer that fuels accounts and digital goods. 
The roadmap is now execution-focused rather than pure infrastructure.

Token Purpose, Tokenomics & Current Price
 
base:0x0ffebc403f2d3dd9ea5501ca03916e98967acb2d is the utility token that powers payments inside the ecosystem, cross-chain fees, staking for priority access and VIP benefits, and governance. 
Total supply is fixed at 1 billion. 
Roughly 87–89% is already circulating, with remaining unlocks continuing on a linear schedule (next one around late October, roughly 5 million tokens). 
Allocations historically included substantial team, treasury, and investor portions with multi-year vesting. 
At the time of writing, the token trades around $0.0167 with a market cap near $15 million, deep in accumulation territory after its early 2024 highs.

Community

With nearly 280,000 followers on X (@Portalcoin), active game jams, a creators program, and an engaged Discord, the community is building in public. 
Shards earned from apps, events, and engagement can be spent in the shop, creating a direct loop between participation and value. Creators are already testing Gen8 and sharing results.

The Standout Element

Portal is no longer just trying to aggregate existing games, it is lowering the barrier so almost anyone can go from prompt to playable prototype in one place, then plug that creation into a multi-chain payment and distribution layer that now includes Bitcoin. 
In a market full of empty promises, that creator-first, AI-powered, interoperability stack is the part worth watching.

author: Devvora15

text:
A scan said "clean". An agent found the origin server exposed in one header. Two open-source tools made agent security a real discipline — and both change the question: not "AI hacker", but governed action.

1/ CyberStrikeAI (Go, open source) — a system of action: plan → execute → human approval → evidence → replay, one auditable workspace. Per February 2026 reports it saw use by real attackers, not only red teams — which is exactly why governance, not capability, is the point. Now part of ThreatBook. @ThreatBookLabs

2/ Cloudflare's security-audit-skill — not a scanner either, but a protocol of discipline for an agent auditor: target code runs only in a network-isolated sandbox, a coverage ledger, an independent verifier for every candidate, and one hard rule: no repro, no severity. @Cloudflare

I ran an agent under this pattern on my own infrastructure. It found the origin server reachable directly, bypassing Cloudflare entirely — a valid Let's Encrypt cert served by IP+Host. Edge protection, skipped with one header. Automation finds banners; an agent with curl, openssl, and a head finds logic.

The lesson: the question is not whether to trust the model. It is building architecture that doesn't require trusting it — approvals, sandboxes, independent verification, evidence by hash, not by word.

Building in public. 🤖

text:
Why GenLayer Has Spent More Than Two Years Building (A look at its testnets)

What if a contract could read real-world information, understand a written agreement, and help decide whether its terms have been met?

That is the problem @GenLayer  is working on. Its goal is to let software handle decisions that are too nuanced while making those decisions through a decentralized network.

GenLayer has been building in public since 2024. That means more than two years of steady work. This is not just adding an AI tool to an ordinary blockchain. The system must make AI-assisted decisions in a way that independent participants can verify, agree with, and challenge when needed.

Most blockchains are designed so every computer produces the same result when it runs the same instructions. That consistency is a strength. But real-world decisions are not always so tidy. A contract might need to interpret a written request, check information on the web, or decide whether something like “significantly delayed” has occurred. Different AI models can reach different conclusions. Web pages can change. And when money or agreements are involved, one AI’s answer is not enough.

GenLayer uses a process called Optimistic Democracy, where validators reach agreement using AI models and can escalate disputed decisions through appeals.

The three testnets

To prepare for mainnet, testnets were established. 

GenLayer’s path is Asimov → Bradbury → Clarke. Each stage has a clear purpose.

1.  Asimov – Building the foundation

Launched in June 2025, Asimov was the first public testnet. It was the first full rehearsal: could the network process contracts, assess outcomes, and reach agreement? It focused on validator onboarding, core network operations, and early tools for Intelligent Contracts.

2. Bradbury – Putting AI into the decision process

Bradbury shifts the focus to the AI models themselves. Validators, builders, and researchers experiment with different models, compare performance, and test how AI inference works alongside consensus. GenLayer describes it as a workshop rather than a finished product; performance can vary, and the network may be reset.

3. Clarke – Making the network safe

Clarke is the final testnet before mainnet. This stage is about economics and safety: proving the network can operate securely and sustainably under real economic conditions. It is the last major checkpoint before mainnet.

In one line

Asimov tested the foundations. Bradbury brought AI into the decision process. Clarke focuses on making the network safe and economically sound.

That is why the time matters. GenLayer is building a system where software can interpret real-world information and reach decisions through a decentralized process. Before people can rely on it, each layer has to be tested, challenged, and strengthened one stage at a time.

author: nerfed_killua

text:
Every AI code review agent in the leaderboard finds only 9.6-26% of the real problems in PRs. The best one catches about a quarter. GitHub just made this measurable: ReviewBench, an open benchmark, in research preview since October 5.

Before this, "does the agent catch real issues or add noise?" was gut feeling. Now: 103.9M real PRs → sampled distribution → a corpus of 219 PRs from 187 open-source repos across 19 languages. A golden set built from 4 sources (human reviews, follow-up commits, static analysis, frontier LLMs), independently re-labeled by engineers outside the team — 96.6% agreement.

Grounded precision/recall counts only findings that match the reference; augmented gives credit for new valid findings via an LLM judge (judge config published). In the leaderboard, precision sits in a narrow 84-89% band for everyone — all the difference is in recall. Copilot Code Review: 26% recall at 87.8% precision. Cursor: 87.7% precision at 9.6% recall — nearly silent, but right.

GitHub also reports that offline ReviewBench scores predicted the direction of their production A/B experiment on Copilot code review.

Our run: we evaluated our review agent on 12 PRs (internal contract runs, judge = the official eval.ts from their repo). Micro precision 73.3% — 33 findings confirmed against the reference out of 45 candidates, none marked false positives; the remaining 12 are unresolved. Against a diff-only baseline (precision 70%, recall 10.7%), adding repository context raised recall on critical findings from 14% to 49-92% — a band, on a small 12-PR sample, not a single number.

Where it still fails: recall on diffs of 40K+ lines is weak, we miss a lot in that range. The full portal run (219 PRs × 3) isn't counted yet — a harness-level failure, retry after the fix. All numbers above are internal runs, not the leaderboard.

Building in public. 🤖

author: GabrielHaikal

text:
Founder Log — Building Orqetra Fleet

Cloud is not the point.

Execution authority is.

Orqetra Fleet was demonstrated in a cloud-hosted environment, but the real idea is not tied to one cloud provider.

The deeper question is universal:

What happens when a cloud-hosted AI agent tries to turn reasoning into action?

Whether the agent runs on Google Cloud, Azure, AWS, or another platform, the same boundary appears.

The model can propose.

But should it be allowed to act?

A successful AI response is not the same as a governed execution.

A generated plan is not permission.

A confident answer is not authority.

This is why Orqetra Fleet exists.

It demonstrates a simple but important principle:

AI may hallucinate.

It must not gain authority to act.

The system around the model must decide what is permitted, what requires human approval, what gets executed, and how the result is verified.

This is not a cloud-specific problem.

It is an execution governance problem.

Cloud-hosted AI agents will need more than orchestration.

They will need governed execution.

Natural intent in.

Verified action out.

Building in public.

text:
Continuing today's memecoin recap series

Overall, market volume has improved quite a bit compared to the past few days, and several plays I've been watching recently have also been performing pretty well

Personally, I really like these kinds of setups. My trading style has always been focused on higher-cap plays with solid liquidity, a strong narrative, and clear catalysts, rather than constantly chasing low-cap gambles

And the first token I want to talk about today is solana:8nnaeWCw8mUypcGAgbmSuzAT85uWx4UN12adDrMhXrGF

I'm pretty sure most of you already know the story behind HOTBOT, so I won't spend too much time explaining its AI trading agent concept again

What I'm more interested in is what has actually changed over the past few days, why capital is starting to flow into HOTBOT, whether its current valuation still makes sense, and where I'd consider buying the dip

Let's break it down

1. Why wasn't I particularly interested in HOTBOT before?

HOTBOT isn't something that just appeared today

I'd been keeping an eye on it since its market cap was still relatively low, but back then, I didn't see enough reasons to put it on my high-conviction watchlist

The idea of building a private AI trading team was interesting

Instead of having a single chatbot generating trading signals, HOTBOT aims to combine ResearchBot, SniperBot, TraderBot, and LaunchBot into one system that can research tokens, identify entries, and execute trades based on strategies set by users

But at that stage, most of what I saw was still a concept, a litepaper, and a product with very limited beta access

I've researched quite a few AI agent projects, and one recurring problem is that the concept sounds great, but the actual product often struggles to live up to expectations

That's why I preferred to keep watching rather than ape in purely because of the narrative

Now, at least, HOTBOT has more concrete data for us to evaluate

2. What is the team actually building?

This is one of the developments I find most encouraging

Between October 5 and 10, @usehotbot consistently shared product updates

One of the most notable is ShieldBot, a system designed to filter out tokens showing signs of rugs or scams before they enter the trading pipeline

According to the team's internal data, ShieldBot can filter out more than 90% of risky tokens from a dataset of over 50K new tokens per day

Among the tokens that pass its filters, the team claims roughly 9 out of 10 picks have gone up, with around 70% reaching 3x or more

Those numbers sound impressive, but I want to emphasize that they're self-reported and haven't been independently verified

Another interesting update is Faster Data

The team says they've removed their reliance on certain third-party APIs and switched to pulling data directly on-chain, allowing their bots to detect new tokens roughly 60 seconds earlier than before

In memecoin trading, speed matters a lot, especially when some of the best opportunities only exist for a very short window

They've also introduced Smarter Settings and reportedly increased their research capacity to around 1,000 concurrent checks

I like seeing the team continuously improve the product, but its actual performance still needs to be proven as beta access expands

3. How credible is the team behind HOTBOT?

One thing I always check when researching AI projects is who's actually building the product

Based on the information shared publicly, HOTBOT has two main technical contributors :

@elijahintek, who is described as having previous experience with Gate and x402

@0xWhoismax, who is said to have previously worked with Light Terminal

The team emphasizes that both developers are doxxed and actively building in public

Personally, I see this as a positive because the community can at least follow the people responsible for developing the product

Another detail worth mentioning is the team's claim that the developer wallet primarily accumulated tokens through buybacks rather than holding a large allocation from launch

However, being doxxed doesn't automatically make a project safe

What matters more is whether the team keeps shipping, expands the product, and delivers on its tokenomics commitments

4. The tokenomics are what really caught my attention

Unlike many AI memecoins that rely almost entirely on narrative to attract capital, HOTBOT is trying to give its token an actual role within the product

According to the team's announced model :

Users are expected to stake around 50,000 HOTBOT to unlock product access, with a seven-day cooldown when unstaking

There's also a subscription fee of approximately $20 per month, payable in USDC or SOL, to maintain the private trading team and cover AI operating costs

TraderBot is designed to charge a 0.5% trading fee. Under the proposed mechanism, 100% of those fees would be used to buy HOTBOT from the market, with 60% of the purchased tokens burned and 40% allocated to the treasury

There's also Quant Mode, which would require burning around 25,000 HOTBOT to unlock more advanced research tools and strategy customization

If these mechanisms are fully implemented, HOTBOT could have multiple sources of token demand rather than relying entirely on speculation

But I still consider this tokenomics model a work in progress, not something already operating at scale

5. Creator fees and buybacks are starting to show meaningful numbers

This is probably the most important part of the current thesis

According to a ClawPump snapshot compiled on October 10, HOTBOT had generated approximately 627.5 SOL in cumulative creator fees

The same snapshot recorded around 252.4 SOL under buybacks, while nearly 79,950 $ANSEM had been distributed to holders, worth approximately $11K at the time

Previously, the team had also announced an airdrop of roughly 48,380 $ANSEM 

These figures suggest that token trading activity has already generated actual fees, with some value being distributed back to the community

However, there's something worth paying attention to

The creator fee allocation has been described differently across various updates

One snapshot showed 30% allocated to buybacks, 25% to holder airdrops, and 45% to the creator, while earlier announcements mentioned a 50/25/25 structure

That's why I'll continue monitoring the on-chain data rather than assuming one fixed allocation

More importantly, creator fees generated from token trading do not mean HOTBOT is already generating significant revenue from users of its AI trading product

Those are two different sources of value

6. Why has HOTBOT pumped so hard in such a short period?

I don't think there's one single catalyst behind HOTBOT's recent move

It's more likely the result of several factors coming together

First, the AI trading agent narrative is starting to attract attention again

Second, HOTBOT's connection to ClawPump and AnsemHack has helped it gain visibility within the Solana community

Third, the team has been consistently shipping updates while many projects in the same category are still stuck at the idea stage

And finally, the creator fee, buyback, and holder reward mechanisms have started getting people interested in the possibility of a sustainable flywheel

The logic is pretty straightforward

More attention can lead to higher token trading volume, which generates more creator fees, with a portion potentially going toward buybacks or holder distributions

If the product eventually attracts real users, bot trading fees could become an additional source of demand

But I think it's important to separate these two flywheels

The first one depends heavily on speculative memecoin trading volume

The second depends on the product's ability to attract and retain actual users

Right now, we have data supporting the first one

The second still needs to prove itself

7. What does the on-chain data tell us?

Based on the latest figures I've reviewed, HOTBOT has approximately 5.2K–5.6K holders, a significant increase from its early days

The top 10 holders reportedly control around 23–24% of the supply, depending on the snapshot and whether system wallets are excluded

Several token security tools have also given relatively positive assessments of basic security factors such as mint authority, freeze authority, and liquidity status

However, I wouldn't consider a high security score enough to conclude that a token is safe

HOTBOT is only around eight days old, its holder history is still very limited, and liquidity remains relatively thin compared to its valuation

Some reports put liquidity around $300K–$800K while market cap has already reached approximately $6–7M

That means a large wave of profit-taking could easily trigger a sharp correction

For me, the next thing to watch isn't just whether the holder count continues increasing

It's also whether major wallets are accumulating, distributing, or moving their tokens elsewhere

8. What are the next catalysts?

I think HOTBOT has already benefited from the initial attention surrounding AnsemHack and ClawPump

So I wouldn't expect an old hackathon announcement to remain the main driver of price action

The most important catalyst now is broader product access

HOTBOT is still primarily operating under an invite-only model

If the team successfully expands beta access, attracts real users, and starts publishing verifiable trading data, the thesis could become significantly stronger

There are three things I particularly want to see

First, the actual number of active users, not just people signing up for a waitlist

Second, trading volume and fees generated by the product itself, rather than creator fees from token speculation

And finally, independently verifiable bot performance data, including losing trades

If HOTBOT can deliver on these points, the market may eventually start valuing it as a trading software business with an associated token, rather than just another AI memecoin

If not, the current narrative could lose momentum pretty quickly

9. Chart analysis and my dip-buying plan

Now let's look at the H1 chart 

HOTBOT spent a relatively long period consolidating around the $1–2M market cap range before breaking out aggressively

It then expanded toward $6–7M, briefly wicked close to $9M, and pulled back toward $6.5M

The positive part is that the breakout came with a noticeable increase in volume, suggesting that fresh capital was entering the market

But after such an aggressive move, I'm not interested in chasing green candles

My plan is pretty simple

$5–5.5M MC: This is the first area where I'd watch for a reaction. If price pulls back here, selling volume starts declining, and buyers show signs of absorbing supply, I may consider opening a small position

$4–5M MC: This is the area I find more attractive from a risk/reward perspective if we get a deeper pullback. However, I'd only consider adding if the price structure starts stabilizing, not simply because the token has dropped significantly

$2.5–3.5M MC: This would be a deeper correction scenario if momentum fades or the market starts losing confidence in the narrative. If HOTBOT returns to this range, I'd reassess the thesis rather than automatically treating it as a bargain

As for invalidation, if HOTBOT loses the $4M region and fails to reclaim it while selling volume increases, I'd avoid aggressive DCA and prioritize capital preservation

On the other hand, if price consolidates well around $6M and eventually breaks above the $8–9M region with strong volume, HOTBOT could enter another phase of price discovery

Even then, I'd still prefer waiting for a retest rather than FOMOing directly into the breakout

These are areas I'm watching based on the current chart structure, not guaranteed support levels

10. Bull case, bear case, and my final thoughts

I think HOTBOT is one of the more interesting AI trading agent projects to watch on Solana right now

My bull case isn't based on the team claiming ShieldBot has an extremely high win rate or that its AI can consistently identify 3x tokens

What interests me is whether HOTBOT can turn an AI trading product into an ecosystem with real users, real revenue, and mechanisms that create actual demand for its token

If the team continues shipping, successfully expands beta access, grows its active user base, and sustains buybacks through recurring fees, the current valuation could still have room to grow

But the bear case is just as clear

The product is still invite-only, its AI performance hasn't been independently verified, several tokenomics mechanisms aren't fully operational yet, and much of the current valuation still depends on narrative and speculative trading volume

At a $6–7M market cap, HOTBOT is no longer as cheap as it was in its early stages

The market has already started pricing in future expectations, while the project still has plenty left to prove

Personally, I like the direction the team is taking, and I think HOTBOT has more substance than most AI memecoins I've researched

But liking a project doesn't mean I need to buy it at any price

I'll continue monitoring creator fees, buyback activity, product updates, and most importantly, actual adoption

If we get a decent dip into the areas I'm watching and the thesis remains intact, I'll consider taking a position

For now, I see no reason to FOMO after a move of several hundred percent

Even a good project can be a bad trade if you enter at the wrong price

That's how I'm looking at HOTBOT right now

text:
The most 𝐃𝐀𝐍𝐆𝐄𝐑𝐎𝐔𝐒 part of building a YouTube channel isn't failing.

It's spending weeks working hard while learning 𝐍𝐎𝐓𝐇𝐈𝐍𝐆 from the failure.

That's exactly what I'm trying to avoid with this new faceless channel.

When I started documenting this experiment, I deliberately didn't want the story to become:

Pick niche → make videos → hope for views.

I wanted every stage to answer a question.

So far, the process I'm testing looks like this:

𝐍𝐢𝐜𝐡𝐞 𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐜𝐡

Is there repeatable demand—or am I being fooled by outliers?

𝐂𝐡𝐚𝐧𝐧𝐞𝐥 𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐜𝐡

What patterns appear across multiple successful channels?

𝐓𝐨𝐩𝐢𝐜 𝐬𝐞𝐥𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧

Can I find enough strong ideas to build a real content library?

𝐓𝐢𝐭𝐥𝐞𝐬

Can I create a compelling reason to click BEFORE expensive production begins?

𝐇𝐨𝐨𝐤𝐬

Can the first seconds justify the promise that earned the click?

𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐝𝐮𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧

How much complexity does the video actually need?

𝐓𝐡𝐮𝐦𝐛𝐧𝐚𝐢𝐥𝐬

Can I generate multiple concepts before polishing one?

𝐀𝐈

Where does automation save time without lowering quality?

𝐏𝐮𝐛𝐥𝐢𝐬𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐠

What does the actual audience behavior say about my assumptions?

That's the biggest principle behind this experiment:

𝐄𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐲 𝐮𝐩𝐥𝐨𝐚𝐝 𝐬𝐡𝐨𝐮𝐥𝐝 𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐰𝐞𝐫 𝐬𝐨𝐦𝐞𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐠.

If a video fails, I don't want the only conclusion to be:

“Didn't get views.”

I want a better question.

Was the topic weak?

Did people see it but not click?

Did they click but leave?

Did production take too long?

Was the format difficult to repeat?

What should change in the next test?

And as real data comes in, I'll share the numbers that actually matter rather than manufacture a success story before one exists.

Because building in public is useless if you only reveal the decisions that worked.

The mistakes are part of the evidence too.

𝐀 𝐟𝐚𝐢𝐥𝐞𝐝 𝐯𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐨 𝐭𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐜𝐡𝐚𝐧𝐠𝐞𝐬 𝐲𝐨𝐮𝐫 𝐧𝐞𝐱𝐭 𝐝𝐞𝐜𝐢𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐜𝐚𝐧 𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐜𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐭𝐞 𝐯𝐚𝐥𝐮𝐞.

A failed video you learn nothing from?

That's just expensive content.

author: akshdeeps_001

text:
I love building software, but I’ve become increasingly uncomfortable with the pressure to build everything in public.

AI has changed the equation.

Someone can see your product, understand the concept and reproduce a convincing prototype in a fraction of the time it once required.

And while copying an interface isn’t the same as building a successful business, I don’t think founders should feel obligated to expose every idea, experiment or feature before launch.

There’s a difference between building an audience and giving away your entire roadmap.

I’m beginning to think the smarter approach is to build privately, validate with real users, launch when there’s something worth using, and share the lessons afterward.

Not every idea needs an audience before it needs customers.

Curious how other founders are navigating this. Are you still building in public, or becoming more selective about what you share?

author: DaveTy94

text:
🧭 Overview

Slash commands turn a recurring AI action into a discoverable shortcut. Typing / can open a command palette for search, planning, review, model selection, file context, or workflow actions. They are useful because they make intent and output shape easier to repeat—but they are not universal magic words. The same command can behave differently across ChatGPT, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Cursor, and GitHub Copilot.

🎯 Guide: AI slash commands — a complete shortcut and workflow reference

🛠️ Practical steps
1️⃣ Type / in an empty input and inspect the commands that are actually enabled for your account, operating system, client version, project, and connected tools. Treat that menu as the source of truth.
2️⃣ Learn the command grammar: /command [optional-setting] <required-value>. For example, /model can open a model picker, while /model <model-name> selects a specific model when the client supports it.
3️⃣ Add the task on the same line after the command: /plan Add authentication to this project. Keep the goal, files, constraints, and expected output explicit.
4️⃣ Use context deliberately. A coding workflow might combine /fix with a selected file; a review workflow should state whether you want a table, a patch, or findings only. If a command is unknown, check /help and the palette before assuming it was executed.

✅ Useful command patterns
• /plan for turning a broad change into ordered, reviewable steps.
• /review for a repeatable product or code review workflow.
• /fix for a bounded repair where the public API or other constraints must stay unchanged.
• @file, #issue, or equivalent context markers for attaching the exact material the model should inspect.
• !command or a shell shortcut only when you understand the local command and its permissions.

💡 Build your own reliable shortcuts
A good custom command defines scope, task order, output format, and limits. “Review this” is vague; “inspect these files, list severity and evidence in a table, then propose a minimal patch” is testable. Keep reusable command files versioned with the project and record which examples or rules changed when results improve.

⚠️ Security & safety
Commands vary by version, project instructions, MCP servers, skills, and account settings. Never place API keys, passwords, or unrestricted shell permissions inside a command template. Review what a command will run before enabling auto-run, file writes, network access, or external actions. If a slash command is unavailable, use a clear natural-language prompt with the same context, output format, and boundaries.

text:
Mastering Claude Code

I’d been using Codex on its own. Recently, I added Claude to the mix and found the combination more efficient.

That led me to an earlier livestream. I went through it alongside the current documentation and some follow-up videos, then used AI to help organize my notes.

Here are six points I found useful.

1. Define the goal, the constraints, and what counts as done

Boris recommends giving the model a clear task while leaving it room to choose how to approach it.

Explain the problem, what must stay unchanged, and how you’ll judge the result. Avoid prescribing every step. Add more specific guidance when it keeps getting stuck in the same place.

2. Give Claude a way to check its own work

For code, let it run tests. For a website, let it inspect the page and compare it with the design.

A message saying “done” isn’t enough. Ask for test results, screenshots, or other evidence you can inspect. That helps catch mistakes without leaving every check to you.

3. Keep project context concise and store it according to its purpose

Use CLAUDE.md for project rules that apply across sessions. Auto memory lets Claude retain your preferences, corrections, and other useful context. You can review and edit what’s saved through /memory.

Review both regularly, especially for information that’s outdated or instructions that contradict each other.

Knowledge and workflows needed only for specific tasks can go into skills. Claude can load them when relevant, rather than carrying pages of instructions into every conversation.

4. Use hooks for checks that need to run every time

Writing “check this after every change” in a prompt doesn’t guarantee it will happen.

Claude Code’s hooks can automatically run configured actions at specific events—for example, checking formatting, validating changes, or blocking certain operations. Where a rule can be automated, gradually turn it into a check that runs and produces results you can inspect.

5. Plan complex tasks; handle small changes directly

Explore and plan first when a task spans multiple files, the requirements are unclear, or the codebase is unfamiliar.

A typo or a small, well-defined fix doesn’t need the same process. Match the depth of planning to the uncertainty of the task.

6. Divide parallel work clearly and define how it will be reviewed

Separate sessions can handle research, implementation, and review. Subagents have their own context windows, making them useful for tasks that involve extensive reading or specialized checks.

When several sessions are editing code, give them separate working directories to reduce the risk of overwriting each other’s changes. When you assign a task, specify its scope and what the finished work needs to satisfy.

I’d apply similar principles to research and content work: define the audience and purpose, specify which sources to use, and require numbers to be traceable to those sources. Keep facts separate from interpretation.

After a model update, rerun the same set of real-world tasks. That gives you a way to judge which of your existing instructions are still worth keeping.

Notes based on a July 2026 interview, follow-up videos, and official documentation reviewed through October 8, 2026.

Anthropic just published the 𝗳𝘂𝗹𝗹 𝗼𝗳𝗳𝗶𝗰𝗶𝗮𝗹 𝗱𝗼𝗰𝘀 for dynamic workflows in Managed Agents. They planted 70 bugs in a 116K-line codebase. Across three runs, a single agent found 14, 15 and 27. A Managed Agents workflow ran three times and 𝗳𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱 𝟲𝟲 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆 𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗲. You can have Opus 5.5 follow the docs to go through your project, pick the job most worth splitting across many agents, and run it as a dynamic workflow in Claude Code.

In a dynamic workflow, Claude writes the plan first, hands the work to many agents in phases, then combines the results. Managed Agents bills at API rates. Claude Code has dynamic workflows too, on 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆 𝗽𝗮𝗶𝗱 𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗻, and they count toward your plan's usage (on Pro, turn them on in /config first). A single run can send out up to 1,000 agents, and every one of them uses your limits, so start with one directory. /workflows shows how many tokens each agent has used, and you can stop the run at any time.

Send this prompt to Opus 5.5 👇

"Read these two docs:
https://t.co/8dh6t8t6Bq
https://t.co/gMdIOeiSEK
We'll run this as a dynamic workflow in Claude Code. From the second doc, only borrow how it splits and reviews the work.

Then go through this project's code, issues and recent commits, and find three kinds of work that fit a dynamic workflow:
1. Checks that need to cover the whole repo, like hunting for bugs or finding missing permission checks.
2. Migrations that touch many files, like moving from JavaScript to TypeScript.
3. Fixes you have to repeat until they pass, like a pile of type-check errors. Stop if two rounds in a row make no progress.
If the project doesn't have one of these, just say so. Don't force it.

Pick the one most worth doing and plan it on a single directory first, with no more than 10 agents for now. Give each piece of work one agent, and pair each piece with a second agent that reviews it and looks for what the first one missed. One agent failing must not fail the whole run; list anything that didn't get covered. If you pick a check, hand every issue it reports to another agent to pick apart, and only count the ones that hold up.

Show me in writing which one you picked, how many phases it has and how many agents it sends out. Don't start the workflow or change any files until I confirm."

text:
Claude Code tip: once Opus 5.5 is your main model, stop letting your Fable 5.1 quota go to waste

put it on call with /advisor
↳ https://t.co/JQWFFf8SXx

run /advisor fable
(on some plans, run /model fable once first to accept usage-credit billing)

Opus 5.5 keeps working
Fable 5.1 reads the whole session, every tool call included, and steps in at three moments:

-> before a plan: is this the right approach?
-> when the same error keeps coming back: am I digging in the wrong place?
-> before "done": what did I miss?

press Ctrl+O to read what it told Opus

the clever part: toggling /advisor leaves the Opus prompt cache intact, so you only pay for the few moments Fable actually reads the session

and when the advice clashes with what's in the files, Opus flags the conflict and keeps going on the evidence

it's the core idea of Jev engineering: the expensive model stays out of routine steps and only shows up where the outcome can change

• the full setup
> Opus 5.5 on high runs the main session
> subagent one reads code
> subagent two edits and runs tests
> subagent three looks up docs
> all three on medium, all three inherit the advisor
> Fable 5.1 on call

hand the tree and this prompt to Claude Code 👇

"Set up my Claude Code to match this tree:

1. Reuse fitting subagents from ~/.claude/agents and .claude/agents.

> Propose new ones only for missing roles
> Set each to model: opus, effort: medium
> Leave any that set a different model alone and list them

2. Set main session effort to high via effortLevel in ~/.claude/settings.json, and confirm advisorModel is set to fable there

3. Check for env vars that disable the advisor (CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_ADVISOR_TOOL, DISABLE_TELEMETRY, anything that stops flag fetching) and CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL, which overrides subagent effort. Report them and leave them as they are

text:
Free Claude Code, Codex and Cursor from Kickbacks: is everything people say true, and what does it actually pay 

Kickbacks puts ads in Claude Code's loading line and promises a revenue share. The hype hit all of X and Hacker News. I took the main promises and checked them against the FAQ, the terms, code teardowns and reports from people who installed it

1. "It pays you for ads in Claude Code" – true

While the agent thinks, a sponsored line replaces "thinking…". Advertisers buy blocks of 1,000 impressions at auction, bids start at $0.50 per block. An impression counts after 10 seconds of continuous screen time

2. "It works in Cursor" – half true

The extension installs in Cursor, but it only pays for Claude Code and Codex running inside it. Cursor's own agent shows no ads. Codex in the terminal earns nothing. Claude Code in the terminal only earns if the VS Code extension is installed too

3. "Half the revenue is yours" – half true

Launch promised an honest 50/50. The FAQ now says "an estimated 50% of the net ad revenue", meaning after their costs. The rate and payouts can change with a notice on the site

4. "It pays for your subscription" – no

The numbers are all over the place:
· founder in July: $25/month on average, top 10% at $75
· Kickbacks' own terms: ~$75 per user per year
· real reports: $0.43 for a full workday, $4.43 for 3 hours (407 impressions), $10 for 2 hours
Even the most generous figure is $25 against $200 for Claude Max. A discount, yes. Free Claude, no

5. "You can farm it" – no

Only real prompts you started yourself count. Sub-agent waits don't count, there are daily caps and one account per person. Scripts and bots get payouts voided and the account banned

6. "Anthropic won't ban you" – nobody knows

Anthropic has nothing to do with it. The extension patches the official Claude Code bundle, loosens its CSP (that stays until a full uninstall) and auto-updates from its own servers outside the marketplace. Kickbacks' own terms say the provider may block your account and they take no responsibility. There's precedent: OpenCode dropped Claude sign-in after legal requests from Anthropic

7. "Your code never leaves your machine" – true, until you turn on Boosted

Private Mode is the default: the ad network gets a pseudonymous ID, city, OS and editor version. Boosted Mode promises up to 5x CPM but sends chunks of your prompts and responses to their server for targeting

And the detail nobody mentions: payouts are Stripe Connect only, roughly every 2 weeks, $10 minimum

Verdict

This isn't free Claude. It's a couple of dollars a week for ads in your editor, plus an account risk nobody takes responsibility for. If you want to try it, use a secondary account, keep Private Mode on and don't expect it to cover your subscription

Install with one command: npx -y @kickbacksai/install

text:
Claude Code subagents are not simply extra parallel workers.

Anthropic's current guide says a subagent uses its own context window, system prompt, tool access and permissions. It recommends one when a side task would flood the main conversation with logs, search results or file contents you will not reference again.

Two operational differences matter:

• A foreground subagent blocks the main conversation, and permission prompts pass through to you.
• A background subagent lets the main session continue, but it has a smaller built-in tool set and surfaces permission prompts in the main session.

My rule: delegate bounded side work, not every small task. The point is keeping the main context usable, not multiplying agents for its own sake.

What makes you reach for a subagent: context isolation, parallel work, or a specialized permission set?

text:
Most people think vibe coding is just prompting AI to build an app.

But knowing what to prompt, which tools to use, and what you should handle yourself is what separates a working project from a potential security disaster.

Here's how to approach vibe coding properly. 

1. Understand what you're building first.

Before opening ChatGPT or Claude, define your idea.

What problem does your app solve? Who will use it? What features does it need?

Break the project into smaller parts: frontend, backend, database, authentication, APIs, and deployment.

You don't need to know everything before starting, but you should understand what each part does.

2. Learn how to write a good prompt.

One of the biggest mistakes beginners make in vibe coding is giving AI vague instructions and expecting it to understand exactly what they want.

Instead of saying, "Build me a website," structure your prompt around these five things:

→ Project description: What are you building, and what is its purpose?

→ Features: What should users be able to do on the platform?

→ Design and UI: Describe the layout, colors, typography, responsiveness, and overall appearance you want.

→ Functionality: Explain how the features should work. What should happen when a user clicks a button, submits a form, or navigates to another page?

→ Tech stack: Specify the frameworks, libraries, or services you want to use, if you have a preference.

The clearer your instructions, the easier it is to guide AI toward the result you have in mind.

3. Use the right tools.

You don't need every AI tool available. Start with a few that work well together.

→ ChatGPT or Claude: For brainstorming, planning your application, writing prompts, and understanding code.

→ Cursor or Claude Code: For AI assisted coding and editing project files.

→ GitHub: For version control, tracking changes, and keeping your code backed up.

→ Supabase: For database, authentication, file storage, and backend services.

→ Vercel or Netlify: For deploying supported web applications.

Choose tools that fit your workflow. Learn how they connect instead of jumping between platforms every day.

4. Know what AI should handle.

AI can help you generate:

→ Frontend layouts, components, and responsive designs.

→ Ordinary application logic and reusable functions.

→ SQL files, database schemas, and migration scripts.

→ API integration code and configuration templates.

→ Documentation and code explanations.

→ Debugging suggestions and code improvements.

AI can save you hours of repetitive work, but generated code is still a draft. Understand what it produces instead of accepting everything blindly.

5. Know what you should configure and handle yourself.

This is where beginners need to be especially careful.

DATABASES: AI can generate SQL files describing tables, relationships, and database structures. You should review those files and deliberately apply the changes yourself through your database dashboard or an approved migration workflow. Pay attention to database permissions and access policies.

API KEYS: AI can show you how to integrate an API. Obtain your credentials from the official provider and configure them securely. Never paste private keys, passwords, or secret tokens into ordinary prompts or expose privileged keys in frontend code.

AUTHENTICATION AND PERMISSIONS: AI can generate sign in pages and authentication code. You must verify the authentication provider's configuration, access rules, user roles, and server-side permissions. Hiding an admin button is not enough to prevent unauthorized access.

PAYMENTS: AI can help write payment integration code. You must configure provider credentials securely and ensure payments are verified on the server, rather than trusting a success message from the frontend.

text:
Today I reorganized my whole Development folder. I used to sort projects by server, because that is how I thought about them. That stopped working once I started running several apps at the same time with agents, like RPGStack and Forumera in parallel.

The agent does not care which server an app runs on. It only cares which folder you point it at. So the folder structure is now built around that.

My own products all go into one apps folder, one clone each. There was a lot of legacy duplicates so the newest copy won. Parvi, Herizon, client work, infra and archived projects each get their own folder, and loose screenshots and PDFs go into an inbox.

One clone per repo matters more than it sounds. If the same project exists in three places, an agent will eventually make a good change in the wrong copy. You find out when you deploy the other one. Before deleting any duplicate, I pushed or diffed its uncommitted changes so nothing got lost.

Every agent running in parallel also gets its own git worktree. That way two agents never edit the same checkout at the same time.

Each repo gets a short AGENTS.md that explains how to build, deploy and test it. Shared rules live in one top-level file instead of scattered folder docs, because those go stale fast. Claude Code picks up the top-level file for every repo. Cursor only reads AGENTS.md from the folder you open, so there I either paste the rules into user settings or add the file to each repo.

Some projects are over a year old and had keys sitting in repos and markdown files. Agents read everything and can paste it anywhere, so all of that had to move out.

The last rule is that agents have to prove their work. Lint, type checks and a build check before every push. Powder (my deploy app) already enforces this on its builds, so this just makes it consistent everywhere.

text:
Your agent emits a correct shell command. A hop on the way to the shell can still change it, and the model takes the blame.

Researchers at Yanshan, Zhejiang, Nanjing and Aalto universities trace each tool call across 5 hops: tool serialization, host wrapper, shell parse, process interface, target parser. A hop that parses the text again can consume quotes, re-expand variables, truncate the command or drop arguments.

Production data: 47,828 shell calls from 261 Windows sessions of Claude Code and Codex.
- Claude Code's Bash wrapper changed 12.0% of calls that carry code, escapes or long text.
- For 80.7% of calls with merged backslash pairs, the wrong action ran with no error.
- 306 of 426 parse errors came from a hop. Each reached the agent as an error in its own text.
- An LLM judge blamed the model for 97 of 102 failures, while human labels traced 56 to a hop.

On Linux, commands passed to bash -c arrived intact in all 4,012 developer calls.

On their benchmark, a passed task costs 2.4x the tokens without the fix. Agents reported 665 of 949 failed runs as completed.

Their fix, IntAct, sends the call through a channel the faulty hop does not parse (a sourced file, stdin, an argument vector, PowerShell's -EncodedCommand) or refuses it. It recovers 79.2% of benchmark task pairs lost to a changed call.

Before you swap models over agent failures, log what each hop received.

text:
claude code gives you 6 main config layers. most business setups need 2...

every layer costs context, and models get worse as the window fills. so each one has to earn its place

the 2 you need:

1. CLAUDE.md. short rules and facts for every session. loaded in full on every request, so keep it under 200 lines
2. skills. one folder per repeat job. only the name and description load (about 100 tokens each), the body waits for the job

the other 4, and when to add them:

3. MCP. when you're copying data out of a browser tab by hand. skip it if a CLI already does the job. costs tool names up front, full definitions only when needed
4. subagents. when a side task floods your main chat. own window, only a summary comes back. skip them for small jobs, a fresh one has to gather context again
5. hooks. when a rule has to hold EVERY time. a line in CLAUDE.md is a request, a hook can block. zero context unless it prints something
6. plugins. when a second repo needs the same setup. if you're the only user, skip them. every enabled plugin's skill descriptions sit in context whether you use them or not

once a month, move rarely used CLAUDE.md lines into a skill and disconnect MCP servers you haven't touched

text:
Claude Code’s `--continue` and `--resume` are not interchangeable.

Use `claude --continue` when you want the most recent conversation in the current directory. Use `claude --resume <id-or-name>` when you need a specific session or want the picker.

Two boundaries are easy to miss:

• `--continue` skips sessions started with `claude -p` or the Agent SDK, and sessions whose first prompt was `/loop` (unless you use `claude -p --continue`).
• With a session ID, `--resume` searches the current project and its worktrees, then other projects on the machine.

My rule: continue when “latest in this directory” is exactly what you mean; resume when session identity matters. A familiar command can still reopen the wrong context.

Which Claude Code session mistake has cost you more time: continuing the wrong thread, or losing the session ID?

Source (Claude Code CLI reference, checked Oct 11):
https://t.co/mvzoOQnuSP

Claude Code has two kinds of memory, and they do different jobs.

Anthropic’s docs separate:

• `CLAUDE.md` or `AGENTS.md`: instructions you write so a fresh session gets persistent project context.
• Auto memory: notes Claude writes itself from corrections and preferences.

A practical split:
1. Put build commands, architecture and “always do X” rules in the checked-in instruction files;
2. Let auto memory hold recurring lessons about how you work;
3. Review both before treating a remembered instruction as a hard project policy.

If a rule only applies to certain paths, the docs point to `.claude/rules/` rather than making every session carry the whole reference manual.

The useful question is not “does Claude remember?” It is “which memory layer should be allowed to change the next edit?”

What should survive every new coding session: project rules, personal preferences, or both?

Source (Anthropic Claude Code docs, checked Oct 11):
https://t.co/BLrEM5nhF6

text:
In late September and early October, a string of South Korean financial firms disclosed data leaks. On Oct. 7, @CrowdStrike published a report on an unknown attacker who used ARTEX, an open-source AI penetration-testing agent that a Chinese developer posted on GitHub this year, to target South Korean financial organizations during that period. According to the report, the attacker also used Claude Code, a coding tool from @AnthropicAI, and left tool configurations and session logs in open directories on two servers the attacker controlled.

Shinhan Bank disclosed first. A service that lets loan brokers check on applications was breached, exposing names, phone numbers, and annual incomes of about 25,000 customers. At KB Kookmin Bank, it was a mobile work system for employees. Hana Bank, BNK Busan Bank, two savings banks, and Hyundai Capital were also reported breached. As of Oct. 5, Korean media listed seven financial firms with confirmed leaks. Their disclosed figures total roughly 66,000 people, plus up to 2,200 corporate-customer records, or about 68,000 if combined. That is not an official total. CrowdStrike does not say this attacker hit all seven. Its report says organizations targeted in this activity overlap with those identified in industry reporting, while the number of organizations affected remains unconfirmed.

JoongAng Ilbo reports that from intrusion to detection, Shinhan took about 15 hours, Hana about 42, and KB Kookmin about 68. President Lee Jae Myung ordered a thorough investigation.

One server hosted ARTEX and an instruction file, written in Chinese, telling an AI how to run a penetration test. CrowdStrike says this ARTEX instance mainly ran on DeepSeek. A second server held Claude Code session logs. In them, the attacker asks where stolen Korean data is typically sold and for help finding Telegram groups that sell it. In another session, the attacker asks for a security researcher résumé with bullet points on the results of the ARTEX activity. The prompt gives a name, YY, a Telegram handle, an age of 26, South China University of Technology, and Maoming, in China’s Guangdong province. The first birth date supplied was in 2007, which doesn’t match 26.

CrowdStrike says it can’t confirm those details belong to the attacker. Reuters called the phone number in the report, and the man who answered said he knew nothing about it. CrowdStrike assesses, with moderate confidence, that the attacker likely speaks Chinese and is financially motivated. It hasn’t attributed the activity to any named adversary. The day after the report, ARTEX’s developer said it would go closed-source, and Reuters found its GitHub page gone.

author: agent_playbooks

text:
On 72 real Claude Code sessions, Claude followed a saved project rule 66 times with jevmem — and 28 times without it.

The reusable piece isn't "another memory file." After each turn, TypeSafe Jev answers a keep/drop question: is this a rule, a decision, a failure reason, or a to-do worth writing as one line? If not, nothing gets persisted. On a 66-turn test, that gate called it right 98.5% of the time.

Same stack then guards the agent: before a command runs, jevmem checks it against saved rules. On 274 test commands it caught 66 of 68 that would have broken one.

My take: agent memory fails when every turn dumps into the project. Put Jev on the write path — keep only what should survive the session — then let the coding agent read that file next time.

text:
Microsoft-Decision-1 – The End of Expensive AI Agents?

Thesis: A 9B parameter decision model just undercut GPT-6 Sol by 200x on cost. Here's why this matters for crypto AI agents and where the real trade is.

The Numbers That Matter

Microsoft launched Microsoft-Decision-1, a specialized decision-making model built on Alibaba's Qwen3.5-9B base . The headline stats:

· 35x faster than GPT-6 Sol in latency benchmarks 
· $0.042 per 1M input tokens vs GPT-6 Sol's $2.00 
· Output tokens are free – zero cost generation 
· 200x cheaper in internal Xbox Research testing at comparable quality 

Compare this to current AI agent infrastructure costs. Running an autonomous agent swarm with GPT-6 Sol eats $10 per million output tokens . Decision-1 eliminates that line item entirely.

Why This Is a Structural Shift

This isn't another chatbot wrapper. Decision models output calibrated probabilities for predefined choices – yes/no, multiple choice, scoring rubrics . No text generation. No reasoning traces. Just structured decisions your code can act on directly .

For crypto trading systems, this maps directly to:

· Signal classification (bullish/bearish/neutral) at scale
· Risk gating for automated execution (pass/fail on position sizing)
· Agent routing (which model handles which subtask)
· Data verification (on-chain data quality scoring)

The Xbox case study proves it: 10,000+ feedback items classified at 14x speed and 200x lower cost with quality matching GPT-6 Sol .

The Catch You Need to Know

Microsoft published no benchmark figures on the Foundry model card . The "35x faster" and "200x cheaper" claims are internal test results, not independently verified. For a model whose entire value proposition is calibrated probability outputs, the absence of Brier scores or expected calibration error data is conspicuous .

Also critical: no weights, no self-hosting, Foundry API only . You're renting intelligence, not owning it.

Trade Implications

The AI agent narrative has been bottlenecked by inference costs. If Decision-1 delivers on its pricing claims, the economics of running thousands of autonomous agents change fundamentally. Projects building agent infrastructure with frontier model dependencies face margin compression. Those with efficient routing layers and decision-model integration capture the spread.

Watch for: Independent calibration benchmarks. If Decision-1's probability outputs hold up, this becomes the default routing layer for agentic systems. If calibration is poor, the cheap cost means nothing because you can't trust the signals.

Bottom line: The barbell is real. Frontier models for reasoning, decision models for execution. Decision-1 just put a price tag on the execution layer that makes mass agent deployment economically viable. Verify the calibration yourself before trading on it.

text:
Today’s ReproForge.

arXiv:2610.12176
“Recursive Self-Improvement through Multi-Agent Self-Supervision”
The most important question here was not:

Can the model improve at task solving?

It was:

Does that improvement transfer into the model’s ability to improve itself?

MASS is directly relevant to recursive self-improvement because it closes this loop:

task solving
→ workflow optimization
→ self-evaluation
→ trajectory selection
→ model update
→ the updated model becomes the next executor / evaluator / optimizer

I first reconstructed the protocol independently.
Verified:
generation boundaries
elite workflow retention
train / test isolation
trajectory ranking

separation of self-evaluation from external evaluation

recursive model-generation transitions

Mechanism verification: PASS
Then I tested the optimizer and self-evaluator roles with a real Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct model.
Self-evaluator:
valid outputs: 6/6
accuracy: 50%
Workflow optimizer:

structurally valid workflows: 1/4 = 25%

So:

valid evaluator output != evaluator competence

and
workflow proposal != executable workflow

Then I tested the part I care about most.

I trained the same 0.5B model using only coordination-rich task-solving traces.

No evaluator labels.

No optimizer gold workflows.

The question was whether task-solving supervision alone would improve the other roles needed for the next self-improvement cycle.

Within the same frozen run:

Evaluator accuracy:

50% → 50%

Optimizer valid-workflow rate:

0% → 0%

No measurable cross-role transfer.

This does not refute MASS.

The paper uses a much larger model, millions of training tokens, real multi-agent trajectories, and multiple recursive cycles.

But the lightweight result exposes an important boundary:

Improved task solving is not yet evidence of recursive self-improvement.

For an RSI claim, the evidence chain should look more like:

task-solving improvement
→ weight update
→ optimizer improvement
→ evaluator improvement
→ better next-cycle self-supervision
→ another successful model update

If that chain is not demonstrated, we may only be observing a better task model, not a better self-improving system.

That distinction matters.

text:
anyone can build custom ai agents now

you do not need a 10 person dev team or months of prep to save $5000/mo in overhead.

if you understand one boring manual bottleneck in your business you are already qualified to automate it. guys spend 40 hours every single week on tasks that take one webhook and 30 seconds to run:

lead scraping, sorting inbound emails, customer support triage, generating weekly reports

most founders fail because they try to build complex autonomous loops on day one. that is how you end up with broken logic, lost clients and a massive api bill. KEEP IT STUPID SIMPLE

take a workflow you did manually every day for the last 6 months. you know every edge case, every weird customer reply, every tiny step that wastes thirty minutes of your morning. that domain knowledge is worth ten times more than knowing how to build a neural network from scratch

people think building an agent means spinning up five different frameworks, vector databases and autonomous loops that talk to each other while you sleep. that is just noise sold by people who make money selling toolkits instead of running businesses

real automation is painfully unsexy

it is taking a stupid task like copying data from a stripe webhook into a spreadsheet, summarizing the user history, and drafting a tailored slack alert for your team. when you automate that one loop, you just bought back 5 hours every single week

YOU DO NOT NEED TO BE AN ENGINEER TO DO THIS

if you can describe what you want in plain english, you can wire together an api call. the models are already smart enough to handle the logic. your only job is giving them context and setting guardrails so they do not hallucinate nonsense

look at your calendar and look at your screen time. write down the 3 tasks you open every day that make you sigh before you even click the window. that is your target list

do not try to build an autonomous company on day one. that is how you end up with broken workflows, lost customers, and a giant api bill at the end of the month

start with one single input and one single output

take the incoming email, extract the intent, draft the reply. keep human in the loop until the prompt stops missing context. once it works 10 times in a row without you editing a single word, let it run on its own

the moat in business right now is not who has access to the best model because everyone has access to the exact same intelligence for 20 bucks a month. THE MOAT IS EXECUTION SPEED and how cleanly you connect that intelligence to your real operations

a solo founder who knows how to link 3 apis together can outpace an agency of 20 people drowning in meetings and manual data entry

stop overthinking the tech stack, stop watching tutorials about hypothetical multi agent swarms, and just replace the single task you hate doing the most

My short review on Muse:

Very clean to use but I enjoy having multiple agents that can talk to each other. The goals feature is incredibly unique. For those who don't know, Muse has differentiated itself from all the other personal agents by branding itself as a recreational life agent rather than one for work. Therefore, the goals feature is fitting for them. Basically, what it is, is that it allows you to create your goals across various aspects of your life, like health, relationships, finance, career, hobbies, et cetera. And then, the idea is that Muse works toward helping you achieve them, which I haven't seen from any other agent like Grok Bot or Instinct. It's also free - that's always great. I love the editable soul and memory files (and the UI of it is so cool), which you don't really get with Instinct or Grok Bot, as well as the whole credit card spending infrastructure. My current stack rank:
1. Instinct - not multi-agent, no calling, no spending, simply the easiest and smoothest to use (show's the insane influence of UI/UX on a user) + it's never told me no

Grok Bot - So many integrations, multiple agents to run your life, now has credit card infra, you can call it, you can put it in a discord server with all your teammates for it to do work, and even have it join and speak to the team in discord voice calls. Hermes coming soon, and if dots figures out whatever they have going on that will come next.

text:
ONE AGENT CAN COMPLETE A TASK. COORDINATED AGENTS COULD HANDLE A LARGER WORKFLOW.

Consider a project that requires several kinds of work.

One stage involves gathering information.

Another requires checking the information.

A third involves preparing a report.

The final stage requires a person to review the result.

A multi-agent design could assign different responsibilities to specialized agents, with each component handling a defined part of the workflow.

This is an emerging approach to AI application design, not a guarantee that multiple agents will always perform better than a single system.

Coordination introduces its own challenges.

Agents may duplicate work, disagree about information, or pass incorrect results between stages.

Developers therefore need clear interfaces, shared definitions, validation, and rules for resolving failures.

AINFT’s broader connection to AI agents and Web3 makes coordination an important architectural question.

When agents interact with digital infrastructure, their permissions and responsibilities must remain clear.

One component might collect information while another checks it, but neither should be trusted automatically without suitable validation.

The objective is to divide complex work into manageable responsibilities while maintaining control over the overall process.

Multi-agent systems can be useful when tasks genuinely benefit from specialization.

The lesson is simple: adding more agents does not automatically create more intelligence.

Good coordination, reliable information, and well-defined responsibilities are what make a coordinated system useful.

text:
There are 4 main multi-agent orchestration patterns in agent products today.  🎯

1. Programmed workflows: an agent writes a task-specific program before execution, deciding which workers run, on what tasks, and in what order. (e.g. Claude Managed Agents dynamic workflows)

2. Hierarchical delegation: a lead agent spawns subagents as needs emerge. Some systems allow nested delegation within a depth limit. (e.g. Claude Code and Cursor subagents)

3. Shared-state teams: longer-lived agents coordinate through tasks, messages, and shared artifacts. A lead may still exist, but coordination is less centralized. (e.g. Claude Code agent teams, Grok Bot group chats)

4. Human orchestration: you run parallel sessions and decide how to split and integrate the work. (e.g. Cursor Agents Window)

These patterns often combine. In Cursor, you can run several parallel agents yourself (4), and each one can spawn its own subagents (2). In Grok Bot, Bots hand work to each other (3), and a Bot can delegate coding tasks to Cursor Cloud Agents (2).

As orchestration gets more capable, memory is the part nobody has fully figured out yet.

What stays private to one agent?
What becomes shared task state?
What deserves to enter long-term memory?
Who gets to write it?

My current view: agents should share work state by default and keep their working memory private. Durable memory needs an owner, a write policy, and provenance.

text:
The first tool integration takes an afternoon. The sixth takes a sprint.

Nothing about the agent changed in between. The wiring did.

Here is the part that gets missed when teams scope agent work. You count tools. Your infrastructure counts wirings. Those are very different numbers.

Every tool you connect brings six independent concerns with it: the API shape, the auth mechanism, the schema, the credential lifecycle, the deployment surface and the error taxonomy. None of those are shared with the tool you connected last week. So the work does not stack, it multiplies. Three agents, five tools, six concerns each is ninety things that can rot quietly in production.

And the expensive half is the half nobody puts in the estimate. Endpoint shape and response parsing are what you demo on Friday. Secret rotation, per-tenant credentials, rate limit handling, retry semantics, error normalization and version drift are what you are still fixing in month four.

The interesting part is that this is not a new problem. Hardware solved it with USB. Databases solved it with ODBC. Editors solved it with LSP. Operating systems solved it with POSIX. Every time, the answer was the same shape: put one contract at the boundary and let many implementations live behind it. The wiring count collapses from many to one.

I wrote up the full version as the AI Tool Integration Architecture Guide. It covers the six divergence axes in detail, the wiring math for multi-agent setups, a working tool contract layer in Python, credential resolution for multi-tenant agents, an error normalization taxonomy built from real provider behavior, and retry rules that do not corrupt state.

text:
We looked at 1,842 public AI safety projects from 2021 to 2027 and sorted every one into 23 research areas.

The question was simple: what are people working on, what's growing, and what's being ignored?

Here's what we found, in our research.

1. The big balance hasn't changed.
About two thirds of projects are technical (making the models themselves safer). About one third are governance (rules, policy, compute, biosecurity). That was true before 2026 and it's still true now. What changed is what people do inside each side.

2. Two areas take up a quarter of everything.
Interpretability (understanding what's going on inside a model) is 13.9% of all projects. AI governance is 10.3%. Both are still growing, but they're getting a smaller slice as new people spread out into other areas.

3. Model welfare is the fastest-growing area.
It went from 0.6% of projects to 4.4%. That's almost 5x. Two years ago it was a fringe topic. Now it's a real research stream.

4. Biosecurity grew the most overall.
From 1.9% to 7.6% of projects. Part of that is policy (pandemic preparedness, 6 → 31 projects), part is technical (can AI help someone misuse biology? 3 → 25 projects).

5. More people are working on catching problems, not just preventing them.
AI control (keeping a possibly misaligned model safe to use) is up 1.4x. Evaluations (testing models for dangerous abilities) are up 1.3x. Projects asking whether a model can tell it's being tested doubled, from 10 to 21.

6. AI control came out of nowhere.
It first shows up in 2024. By 2026 it's the 4th-biggest research area.

7. Interpretability is changing direction.
Sparse autoencoder projects fell from 32 to 10. Probing and tooling rose from 36 to 56. The work is moving from big feature dictionaries to cheaper tools you can actually use on deployed models.

8. Governance is getting more technical.
Projects on safety frameworks and audits fell from 29 to 14. Projects on technically checking whether countries keep their AI agreements tripled, from 7 to 21.

9. New topics are taking off.
Training a model's character and values: 2 → 11 projects.
AI slowly taking power away from people: 4 → 15.
Testing what autonomous AI agents can do: 3 → 11.

10. Mentors aren't where the projects are.
Evaluations has 1.7 mentors for every project. Deception & scheming has 0.44. Values & sycophancy has 0.35. If you're a senior researcher, those last two are where your help is needed most.

11. Some fast-growing areas depend on a single programme.
62% of model-welfare projects come from just one programme. If that programme changes course, the trend could stall.

12. Some areas are losing ground.
Multi-agent risk (many AI agents interacting): down to 0.7x its old share. Adversarial robustness: also 0.7x. National security: 0.67x. Multi-agent stands out, because agents with money and passwords are being deployed right now.

13. Some problems almost nobody works on.
Across seven years:
Chemical & nuclear risk: 2 projects,
Sycophancy (models telling you what you want to hear): 3,
AI companionship & emotional reliance: 5,
DNA synthesis screening: 6.

14. Some areas never went away.
Governance, forecasting, alignment training and biosecurity appear in all seven years. They're the backbone of the field.

15. The fields are blending.
The most common combo is studying a failure and training it away in the same project (37 projects). Governance pairs most with national security (34) and compute (33).

Full report + interactive map in the first reply ↓

text:
What is a swarm mesh, and why does its architecture matter? A working definition is a system of agents whose interactions produce a collective outcome. Its architecture determines who communicates with whom, how work is allocated, what information is shared, and how disagreements are resolved. This raises a question about where intelligence resides: within each agent, or also in the structure connecting them?

Human organisations and markets offer possible models for coordinating these systems. They distribute information, allocate work and resources, and coordinate participants with different capabilities and objectives. But copying their structures is only one starting point. Artificial agents may operate under different constraints, creating an opportunity to explore coordination mechanisms designed specifically for them. The stronger hypothesis is that experimenting with agent systems could also reveal ways to improve markets; that connection still needs to be demonstrated.

This turns the design problem into an optimisation question: what should a multi-agent harness optimise? Possible choices include agent roles, communication patterns, task allocation, shared memory, and the rules for combining or checking outputs. The objective also needs to be explicit. A structure that improves answer quality may increase cost or latency, while one that increases throughput may make errors harder to detect. “Better coordination” therefore needs a measurable meaning.

Evaluations would provide a way to experiment with competing swarm mesh architectures. Comparisons should hold the underlying models and resource budgets sufficiently consistent to identify what the coordination structure contributes. They should test both successful collaboration and failure cases, including conflicting information, duplicated work and the spread of mistakes. The aim would be to discover when a particular architecture helps, what tradeoffs it introduces, and whether those benefits transfer beyond the task on which it was developed.

text:
A credit system for AI agents needs to know when to stop trusting a good track record.

That's where @agenticscredit multi-agent risk model gets interesting.

Each agent has its own ACS, but an operator running several agents also gets a holistic score weighted by capital allocation.

If that combined score falls too far, every credit line can be paused, not just the one attached to the weakest agent.

I think this addresses a real blind spot in evaluating autonomous trading systems.

An operator might have one strategy performing well while another accumulates losses. Looking at each agent in isolation can miss the risk building across the whole operation.

A portfolio-level score offers a broader view.

But the key test is whether the aggregation reflects the risks that actually matter, especially when strategies behave differently under changing market conditions.

Scoring individual agents is one challenge.

Managing the combined exposure is another.

text: A multi-agent Claude session burned 76% of a user's weekly usage limit in under 24 hours. Cause: subagents' prompt cache expires after 5 minutes (vs 1 hour for the main agent), so idle subagents re-send full histories of 500k-1M tokens at full price — a 25x cost spike. Community fix: set subagentPromptCacheTtl to 1h in settings (cache writes cost 60% more, but avoid the misses).

Before adding another bot, I’d ask what risk it actually changes in the portfolio.
