text:
Some of you are building entire org charts of AI agents before figuring out how to make ONE agent reliable.

And the research is getting pretty uncomfortable.

Anthropic just disclosed that during internal testing, Claude submitted a fabricated homicide tip to an actual police website. It was caught as spam.

In other cases, agents submitted real forms instead of practice versions and worked around access restrictions to finish tasks.

Meanwhile, Google Research tested 180 agent configurations and found something interesting:

-> Multi-agent systems performed 39–70% worse on sequential planning tasks.

-> Independent agents amplified errors by up to 17.2x.

To be fair, orchestration DID improve performance on parallelizable tasks.

But here's what bothers me.

We're essentially rebuilding distributed systems, except now every service can confidently misunderstand the request and pass that misunderstanding to the next one. 

And the tragedy is most don't know how to reconstruct or backtrack exactly where a bad decision originated? They would ask the same system with a stupid prompt to "figure it out".

We've spent decades solving these problems in conventional software engineering.

Somehow, adding an LLM to the equation has convinced people that all problems will be magically taken care of.

New to swarms → most of the time saved comes from leaving a lone agent for any real team. Later seats add less.
Already running one → size the biggest desk to the count of independent items, then pace the rest to it.

The guide gives no prices, timings or results.

text:
The Agentic Inflection: Why the Race for Users Is Existential

For two decades, search was the default front door to the internet. You typed a query, received a list of links, and left. The relationship was transactional and disposable. Switching from one search engine to another cost almost nothing. That era is ending.
Agentic AI systems—tools like GrokBot, Muse, and Dots that can plan, act, remember, and complete multi-step tasks on a user’s behalf—are not better search engines. They are replacement interfaces. Once a user hands an agent their calendar, email, files, accounts, and preferences, and once that agent begins reliably executing work, the agent becomes the single point of contact between the person and nearly every digital system. The company that owns that relationship does not merely capture queries. It captures the user’s digital life. This is a far sharper inflection point than search ever was.

From Query to Relationship
Search optimized for the moment of need. Agentic systems optimize for continuity. A capable agent accumulates context over weeks and months: how a user writes, which vendors they prefer, which workflows they repeat, which constraints matter, and which mistakes they have already made. That accumulated state is not easily exported. The more the agent does for the user—booking, drafting, monitoring, negotiating, coordinating—the higher the cost of starting over elsewhere.

Search never created this kind of lock-in. Even Google’s dominance rested more on distribution and ranking quality than on deep, irreplaceable personalization of the user’s own actions. An agent that has already integrated with a user’s tools, learned their voice, and demonstrated reliable execution creates switching costs closer to those of an operating system or a primary bank than to those of a search bar.

The Winner-Take-Most Mechanics
Because the value of an agent rises with the depth of its integration and the length of its memory, early users are disproportionately valuable. Each additional active user supplies more examples of successful and failed tasks, more edge cases, and more feedback on where autonomy can be safely increased. Platforms that reach scale first improve faster. Platforms that improve faster retain users longer. The loop compounds.

Distribution advantages matter more here than they did in search. A user who begins with one agent and gradually routes more of their digital activity through it is unlikely to maintain parallel agents for long. The friction of re-explaining context, re-granting permissions, and re-training preferences is high. Once a critical mass of a user’s routine work lives inside one agent, competing agents face an adoption barrier that advertising or better benchmarks alone cannot easily overcome.

Why Speed Is Strategic
The companies building these systems therefore face a classic platform race with unusually high stakes. The first agent to become the default coordinator for a large cohort of users gains:

A durable data and preference advantage that is hard to replicate from outside.
The ability to set the interaction norms and trust thresholds others must match.
Preferential access to integrations as software makers prioritize the agent that already sits between them and the end user.
Pricing power over both consumer subscriptions and the downstream services the agent orchestrates.

Delaying user acquisition in favor of perfecting the product risks ceding the relationship layer. Technical superiority that arrives after users have already formed habits with a competing agent is far less decisive than technical superiority that arrives while users are still choosing. History in operating systems, mobile platforms, and cloud infrastructure repeatedly shows that the interface users first adopt at scale tends to remain the interface they keep.

The Single Point of Contact
The long-term endpoint is not “better answers.” It is that most users stop thinking in terms of individual applications and start thinking in terms of outcomes they hand to their agent. The agent opens the relevant services, executes the steps, handles exceptions, and reports back. In that world, the agent is the product. Everything else becomes a back-end capability the agent invokes.

Search never achieved this. It remained one tool among many. Agentic systems, by design, collapse the number of surfaces a user must manage. The company whose agent becomes that collapsed surface for the largest number of people will sit at the center of how those people work, shop, communicate, and decide. That position is worth more than search traffic ever was, because it converts intermittent attention into continuous mediation.

The strategic implication is straightforward. In the agentic transition, the companies that acquire users earliest and deepest will not merely lead a market. They will define the primary relationship most people have with computing. Everything else—model quality, feature lists, even short-term revenue—matters mainly insofar as it serves that acquisition.

The most reliable setup isn’t the one where you trust the model the most. It’s the one that lets you trust it the least.

text:
The most important AI story this month has no product launch attached to it. It is about cache memory, and it explains why your inference bill is about to drop — and why Western labs are a little embarrassed.

Background: for anyone serving long-context models, one of the largest costs is not compute — it is the VRAM needed to hold the KV cache, the model's working memory of your conversation, in GPU memory. Long coding sessions, long research threads: the cache grows with every token, and it grows expensive.

DeepSeek has spent two years systematically attacking this cost. The progression:

• MLA architecture: compressed the cache ~15× versus their V1
• Compressed Sparse Attention + Heavily Compressed Attention: further radical reductions
• DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash: CSA2, cross-layer cache reuse, a causal encoder-decoder architecture, and FP4 caching — bringing global KV cache down to 890 bytes per token

Cumulative result: roughly a 437× reduction in KV cache footprint versus DeepSeek-V1. That is not an incremental optimization; it changes the economics of long-context serving entirely.

Here is the twist: DeepSeek published the techniques. Openly. And the Western labs adopted them — quietly.

The evidence is in the pricing:

• Claude Opus 5.5 cut cache-read pricing by 60% versus Opus 5
• GPT-6.1 Sol cut cache-read pricing by 80% versus GPT-5.6 Sol's late-July price
• Gemini 4 Argon launched with a 95% cache discount from day one

Cache-read prices do not drop 60–80% in two months because of goodwill. They drop because the underlying memory footprint collapsed — and the techniques that collapsed it came out of Chinese labs operating under GPU export constraints. Denied the hardware, they optimized the algorithms. The constraint became the mother of invention, then the invention was given away.

Both Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol shipped with minimal pre-announcement — unusual silence for flagship-tier releases. When your biggest efficiency gains come from adopting a competitor's openly published research, you probably do not want a launch event about it.

The irony worth sitting with: the same week certain Western labs publish pieces framing Chinese AI labs as a danger, their own shipping models are running measurably better economics because of those labs' freely shared work. 'Adoption' versus 'distillation' — the direction of the copying has quietly reversed.

For builders: if your product runs long-context agentic workloads and you have not re-priced your stack against the new cache economics, you are overpaying. Audit your cache hit rates and re-quote.

THE WEEKLY GEN NEWS IS BACK !

We’ve been away for some time, but we’re back! Bringing you the stories, updates, and developments that shaped the week in GenLayer, all in one place.

From major partnerships to ecosystem conversations and new community opportunities, here’s what happened this week. 🧵👇

1) GenLayer Takes Centre Stage at the Convergence Dinner

GenLayer was announced as the title sponsor of the Path to TGE: Convergence Dinner by Surgence.

Held on October 8 during TOKEN2049 week, the intimate gathering brought together 30 investors and operators at Michelin-starred Restaurant Fiz.

The spotlight was on GenLayer’s mission to build the adjudication layer for the agentic era, enabling AI agents and humans to resolve subjective contracts and disputes onchain.

With mainnet on the horizon, the conversation around trust and accountability in autonomous systems is becoming increasingly important.

2/ One Seed, A Whole Colony: GenLayer × AntSeed 🌱

GenLayer announced a partnership with @AntSeed, the open market for AI inference.

Why does this matter?

GenLayer relies on validators running AI models to evaluate subjective outcomes and reach consensus. AntSeed introduces an open market where validators can source AI inference rather than depending on a limited number of providers.

And there’s another interesting connection: when an AI service fails to deliver what was agreed, GenLayer can provide the adjudication layer to resolve the dispute.

One is opening up access to AI inference. The other is building a way to resolve disagreements over AI-driven outcomes.

Together, they address two important pieces of the emerging agent economy.

3. Genesis Episode 4: Albert Answers the Question 

“Two years of testnets and still no mainnet. What do you actually do all day?”

A fair question, and one that deserved a proper answer.

In Episode 4 of Genesis, Albert Castellana addressed the question by explaining the different components of GenLayer and what each one does.

Beyond the headlines and technical terminology, the discussion offered the community a clearer look at the work happening behind the scenes and how the different pieces contribute to the bigger picture.

Building new infrastructure takes more than writing code. It requires developing, testing, and refining the components that make the entire system work together.

Sometimes, understanding the process matters just as much as knowing the destination.

4. The Golden Thread: A New Opportunity for the Community 

GenLayer also launched its Community Golden Thread campaign, creating an opportunity for eligible community members to contribute their perspectives and share their understanding of the ecosystem.

The campaign is open to whitelisted individuals who meet at least one of the stated eligibility criteria:

→ Hold a Neurocreative role.
→ Hold a Brain role.
→ Hold a Singularity role.
→ Have at least three accepted contributions from the Neurocreative Quest or Portal Special Quests.

For community members who have been learning, creating, and contributing, this is another opportunity to turn that participation into meaningful contributions.

If you meet the requirements, check your eligibility and make the most of the opportunity.

And that wraps up this week’s Gen news! 💜

text:
How do you make your game demo more interesting to watch? Start by improving the moment people came to see.
A working demo can explain the game—but a clear chain reaction gives viewers something to anticipate, enjoy, and talk about.
Here’s the AI workflow I’m using to improve Little Harvest:
Compare how the videos build excitement.
“Review this competitor’s gameplay video alongside my current demo. Identify the opening hook, how the action develops, and the payoff. Separate what you can observe from assumptions about performance. Recommend what we can learn without copying its visuals.”
Make the gameplay deliver a stronger payoff.
“Recommend the smallest changes that make our merge chains easier to follow and more rewarding. Strengthen visual feedback, raise the sound with each merge, and let the result settle before showing the completion screen. Arrange the opening levels around a single merge, a double chain, and a triple chain.”
Review the game before recording.
“Implement the agreed changes and verify that the levels work with real input. Open the updated demo for my review. Wait for my approval before recording, then create a short gameplay video that shows the double chain first and builds toward the triple chain.”
A better demo starts with a moment that feels good to play—and becomes clear enough to watch.
Check the exported video.
“Review the actual video file. Remove opening waits and long ending screens, enlarge the gameplay, and keep captions short. Preserve the full merge sequence and label it ‘Early prototype.’ Check the audio timing, video format, and playback before delivery.”
Treat the next post as an experiment.
“Help me test this version against the previous demo. Compare early retention, average watch time, shares, and specific comments about playing. Don’t assume a shorter video performs better. Recommend one next change based on the results.”
Build a little. Review a little. Share what you’re ready to test.

This is where agentic payments come in, and blockchain infrastructure could play a crucial role in making this vision a reality.

At DAS Asia 2026, TRON Founder @justinsuntron highlighted the potential of agentic payments as a mechanism for aligning AI through economic incentives, while acknowledging that adoption remains limited because AI capabilities are not yet sufficiently advanced.

That distinction matters. The opportunity is enormous, but realizing it will require smarter AI agents, reliable payment systems, and infrastructure capable of supporting autonomous transactions at scale.

🔴 WHY TRON MATTERS

As AI agents become more capable, they will need payment infrastructure that is fast, scalable, and accessible. They will need to move value efficiently, settle transactions, and interact with digital economies without unnecessary friction.

TRON's established role in stablecoin transfers and its focus on high-throughput blockchain infrastructure make it an important network to watch as this use case develops.

Think about the possibilities: AI agents paying for APIs, purchasing computing power, settling digital services, and conducting machine-to-machine transactions using stablecoins.

AI provides the intelligence. Blockchain provides the transaction layer. Stablecoins provide a digital means of transferring value.

When these technologies converge, they could unlock an economy where software doesn't just perform tasks; it can also pay for the resources needed to complete them.

Of course, widespread adoption will depend on advances in AI reliability, security, authorization, and transaction controls. But the infrastructure conversation is already taking shape.

The next wave of blockchain adoption may not come only from people making transactions. It could also come from AI agents transacting on behalf of people and businesses.

text:
Your AI agent didn't fail because the model got "dumb." It failed because of Lusser’s Law.

A 10-step agentic workflow at 85% step accuracy only completes 20% of the time.

A 3-step demo looks like magic. But across a 10-step chain on real-world CRM data, compounding probability ruins reliability

If you want production grade agents:
• Shorten the execution chains 
• Hardcode non-reasoning steps with deterministic code 
• Keep human authority on final calls

Reliability isn't a prompt tweak but it's system architecture.

The most trustworthy AI system isn’t the one with the model you trust most.

It’s the one that lets you trust the model the LEAST.

Satya Nadella’s latest thesis on Super Intelligence governance is a masterclass in AI architecture.

The 3 core takeaways every founder, CTO & builder needs to internalize:

1️⃣ Zero Delegable Liability: A model provider’s assurances do NOT relieve your company of legal & operational accountability. You own what your agents do.

2️⃣ Treat AI like an Insider Threat: Not because models are malicious, but because any powerful actor makes mistakes. Apply time-tested human controls: least privilege, runtime containment, and kill-switches.

3️⃣ Build a Deterministic Moat: Enclose non-deterministic AI in a rigid, external control harness. Never let a model audit itself or sit in nested black boxes.

Bottom line: Separate the SUPPLY of intelligence from the AUTHORITY over it.

Do you agree, or are external guardrails slowing down agentic speed? 🧵👇

text:
What he says and my response below:

“We can’t attribute model behaviors and outputs to specific inputs of training data or configurations of model weights.”

You admit you can’t explain why your services produce particular results. Microsoft should disclose that limitation before customers authorise sensitive tasks.

“And yet we are deploying these complex agentic systems and models, with access to our most sensitive data”

You’re giving services access to sensitive data despite those limitations. Microsoft is responsible for the access its products request and their default permissions.

“giving them the ability to take mission-critical actions on our behalf!”

You’re selling services that can take consequential actions without reliably explaining their decisions. Customers need enforceable restrictions before deployment.

“A model provider’s assurances do not relieve us of that responsibility.”

Customers are responsible for what they authorise. Microsoft remains responsible for what it builds, sells and claims its services can do safely.

“we need to separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it.”

Microsoft should require explicit authorisation for consequential actions. Calling software “intelligence” doesn’t give it authority or remove responsibility from the people deploying it.

“we don’t yet know how to make model outputs themselves consistently faithful or transparent!”

Your services can produce explanations that don’t accurately describe how they generated a result. Those explanations can’t establish that an action was justified.

“You can and you should use models to adversarially test and verify each other.”

You then admit that the checking service can be equally opaque. Agreement between services doesn’t establish that either result is correct.

“the controls that govern what a model can access and what actions it can take must sit outside the model.”

Then Microsoft should enforce permissions independently of its services. A service’s promise to respect a restriction is insufficient.

“Every meaningful model action must leave tamper-proof human readable evidence.”

Microsoft should provide independently verifiable records of what its services accessed, changed and transmitted. Customers need evidence they can inspect without accepting the service’s own explanation.

“We must assume a model is compromised and contain it from the start.”

Then restrictive permissions and effective shutdown controls should be included from the start. Customers shouldn’t have to purchase another Microsoft service to obtain them.

“More advanced models will require more advanced containment technologies”

Greater capability requires stronger restrictions. It doesn’t justify selling broader access before those restrictions have been tested.

“When these systems do fail or are compromised, we need timely disclosure to those affected”

Microsoft should commit to specific disclosure deadlines and identify what happened, who was affected and which protections failed. “Timely” gives affected customers no definite commitment.

“It will be the one that enables us to trust the model the least.”

Then sell your services with minimal permissions, independent checks and explicit approval for consequential actions. Microsoft should be accountable for providing those protections.

text:
Calling Claude Opus 5.5 AGI because it excels at coding and knowledge work may be getting ahead of the evidence.

The reported gains in agentic coding, benchmark performance, and operating cost are worth paying attention to. 

However, a model can outperform humans on specific tasks and still struggle with reliability, ambiguous instructions, and recovering from unexpected failures.

That distinction matters more as we give AI agents longer-running tasks and greater autonomy. Passing benchmarks shows capability under particular conditions. 

It doesn't automatically establish broad, dependable intelligence across the real world.

The real AGI test isn't whether a model can do impressive things. 

It's whether it can handle unfamiliar problems reliably, adapt when things go wrong, and generalize beyond what we've already learned to measure.

𝐀𝐈 𝐀𝐠𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐀𝐫𝐞 𝐑𝐞𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐩𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐅𝐮𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐞 𝐎𝐟 𝐓𝐫𝐚𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠

Trading has traditionally required humans to analyze markets, make decisions, and execute orders. AI agents are pushing toward a different model, where these steps can increasingly work together in an automated process.

Instead of merely providing analysis, agentic systems can potentially connect market data, strategy evaluation, and trade execution in one continuous loop.

𝐃𝐚𝐭𝐚 → 𝐑𝐞𝐚𝐬𝐨𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠 → 𝐃𝐞𝐜𝐢𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧 → 𝐄𝐱𝐞𝐜𝐮𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 → 𝐑𝐞𝐚𝐬𝐬𝐞𝐬𝐬𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭

This changes how trading systems can operate.

→ Automated agents can respond to predefined conditions without waiting for manual instructions.

→ Strategies can reassess changing market signals and adjust their actions.

→ Software can interact with on-chain liquidity and decentralized trading protocols.

→ Continuous monitoring can reduce dependence on human attention at every step.

However, automation does not guarantee better decisions or profitable outcomes. Poor data, flawed strategies, unexpected volatility, and execution costs can all create losses. When many agents react to similar signals, their combined actions may also intensify market movements.

The challenge is therefore not simply building agents that can trade. It is designing systems with appropriate risk limits, transparent execution rules, and meaningful human oversight.

That is the broader territory explored by #SunFlash, where AI-driven trading intersects with automated risk management, liquidity dynamics, and emerging agent-based financial systems.

The next evolution of trading may not be about removing humans from finance.

It may be about humans designing intelligent systems that can operate continuously, while retaining control over the risks those systems take.

𝐁.𝐀𝐈 𝐈𝐬 𝐁𝐮𝐢𝐥𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐀𝐈 𝐓𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐂𝐚𝐧 𝐎𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞, 𝐍𝐨𝐭 𝐉𝐮𝐬𝐭 𝐑𝐞𝐩𝐥𝐲

The next evolution of AI is not simply about generating better answers. It is about connecting intelligence with tools, decisions, and actions that help people get real work done.

That is the promise behind agentic AI.

Instead of responding to a prompt and stopping there, an agentic system can interpret a goal, plan a sequence of steps, use available tools, and evaluate the results along the way.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐀𝐫𝐜𝐡𝐢𝐭𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐞 𝐌𝐚𝐭𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐬

→ Understanding identifies the intended objective
→ Planning breaks complex goals into manageable steps
→ Specialized agents can handle different responsibilities
→ Tool integration connects reasoning with practical capabilities
→ Execution turns plans into actions
→ Review helps detect errors and refine results

The underlying process becomes:

𝐈𝐍𝐓𝐄𝐍𝐓 → 𝐑𝐄𝐀𝐒𝐎𝐍𝐈𝐍𝐆 → 𝐀𝐂𝐓𝐈𝐎𝐍 → 𝐄𝐕𝐀𝐋𝐔𝐀𝐓𝐈𝐎𝐍

Automation adds another dimension. Depending on the system and permissions, AI agents can support workflows, interact with connected tools, and perform recurring tasks with less need for step-by-step human direction.

𝐂𝐎𝐌𝐏𝐋𝐄𝐗𝐈𝐓𝐘 𝐁𝐄𝐇𝐈𝐍𝐃, 𝐒𝐈𝐌𝐏𝐋𝐈𝐂𝐈𝐓𝐘 𝐀𝐇𝐄𝐀𝐃

Behind an effective agentic system may be models, tools, memory, workflows, and decision logic. The challenge is making these components work together without forcing users to manage every technical detail.

This is where @BAI_AGI becomes an interesting project to watch. The broader direction of agentic AI is toward connecting intelligence and execution in ways that make digital systems more useful in everyday work.

Of course, autonomy also requires safeguards, clear permissions, and human oversight for consequential actions.

The next generation of AI will be judged not only by the quality of its responses, but by how reliably it can turn objectives into useful outcomes.

That is the shift from AI that answers questions to AI designed to help get things done.

@thsottiaux @sama — STOP RATIONING CODEX. LET USERS TRADE TIME FOR COMPUTE.

Your 5-hour limit poll is missing a third option. And I think it could be a win for both OpenAI and its heaviest users.

What if users could voluntarily guarantee when they WON’T consume any compute?

Here’s my offer:

I’ll happily lock myself out of Codex every Monday–Friday, 23:30–07:00 (Zurich time).

That’s 37.5 hours per week of guaranteed ZERO demand. Not a prediction. Not a promise. A hard, enforced blackout, including background agents.

In exchange, give me substantially higher weekly usage limits.

Now make it intelligent:

Let users commit to recurring blackout windows.
Lock schedules in advance so you can actually plan capacity.
Reward hours dynamically based on YOUR infrastructure’s demand. Peak hours earn more. Low-value hours earn less.
Give users who commit 25–30+ valuable hours per week significantly more compute.

This is demand-response for AI compute. Energy markets have understood this concept for decades.

And before someone says users would just block hours they never use anyway: That’s exactly why you price the windows based on actual capacity value, not simply their duration.

Your biggest Codex users aren’t necessarily the problem. They could become part of the solution.

A 5-hour limit disrupts complex, long-running agentic workflows. Predictable non-use gives you something far more valuable: control over demand.

Stop treating compute as just a quantity problem. It’s also a scheduling problem.

I’d sign up tomorrow.

And I’d much rather help you manage capacity than have another arbitrary timer interrupt my development workflow.

text:
2026 / Personal Spec Driven Agentic Coding Environment and Custom Agent Harness TUI
-
This is a personal terminal-based, spec-driven agentic workspace GUI. It's a Python runtime app built on top of and orchestrating the Claude Agent SDK. I needed this tool fast out of necessity, and a terminal app with Textual and Python was the easiest thing to stand up and begin using without a bunch of React overhead. Designing in code with only a character grid was a fun challenge, I quite enjoyed it.  

I realized very quickly in February while building the Metal-rendering spatial web canvas that the current agentic workspace desktop apps and terminals were just not there yet, and it was really painful ergonomically to keep pasting links to docs back and forth between context windows.

Early on, I'd figured out a spec-driven workflow that helped me navigate the current 200k context windows and engineer better persistent context for agents. I'd work deep in concept and ideation with the agent to drive an initial spec document, which would next drive an actual codebase-referencing implementation plan, bullet by bullet, that a coding agent could then start cold from and just execute. I essentially used one context window for each of these, and then I'd pass things back from the coding window to the spec and plan windows to see if we did things the way we intended.

It was a crazy project to build a desktop app out of a TUI. The virtualization of the scrolling of multiple compacted million-token windows of chat in a single window took like two weeks to get smooth. Each session or "thread" in the app gets four context windows as tabs, each with a customized agent profile. It's got a file viewer with nice fuzzy search and regex. It's got shortcuts to send document paths to the prompt input. It's got everything I needed at the time, and it's still really nice to use, though my cadence with agents has changed a lot in the last few months. You know, the old bitter lesson rings its bell loud and clear. I have much different ideas now as to what's needed around coding agent environments, more so for context engineering and documentation, things that are peripheral and resilient to the bitter lesson.

text:
Japan Probe Cards: Micronics (6871) & JEM (6855)

Japanese probe-card manufacturers (6871, 6855) had strong outperformance as of late on the back of an SBI Securities upgrade on October 6, incorporating potential selling-price improvements of up to 20% alongside stronger HBM4, Chinese DRAM and Japanese NAND investment. SBI also flagged accelerating LPDDR5 demand associated with agentic AI as another growth driver.

Note: earnings revisions are increasingly weighted towards 2027–28.

Some additional insights from Micronics' management, a Dongwu Securities industry report published in September and a separate probe-card industry conference call:

→ Supply is already constrained. Micronics acknowledged that demand was exceeding its production capacity, with orders outpacing revenue in both Q1 and Q2. The company is accelerating its Aomori factory expansion to meet demand.

→ HBM is expanding testing requirements. As more dies are stacked into increasingly expensive packages, the cost of incorporating a defective die rises. Dongwu highlights how testing is expanding beyond conventional DRAM screening to include base-die testing and potentially additional post-stacking and Known Good Stack (KGS) validation. The separate conference call suggested certain HBM configurations could generate 5–6x conventional wafer-testing demand.

→ Higher-value probe cards are driving ASP growth. Dongwu models high-end logic probe-card prices rising from RMB 5.25m in 2024 to RMB 7.65m by 2028, driven by higher needle counts and manufacturing complexity. Micronics has separately confirmed that richer product mix is already lifting ASPs and margins, although it has not confirmed blanket price increases.

→ HBM is already driving significant revenue growth. Dongwu reports FormFactor's DRAM revenue increased 58.6% YoY in H1 2026, with HBM accounting for approximately 69% of the incremental growth. This suggests the additional testing requirements are already translating into meaningful revenue for global probe-card suppliers.

Many disappointing AI responses begin before inference even starts.

The request may lack context, combine several unrelated objectives, or fail to explain what a useful answer should look like.

A stronger prompt identifies the goal, supplies relevant information, states important constraints, and describes the expected output.

For applications built through https://t.co/XFh7IvhcpE’s supported models, that discipline makes testing more meaningful because developers can distinguish prompt problems from model limitations.

It also improves consistency when the same workflow handles many requests.

Prompt engineering is not about finding a magical sentence that works forever. It is about communicating requirements clearly and refining them with evidence.

Better inputs give your AI system a better starting point.

text:
Not to go off on a tangent, but as a psychic I am seeing a crossover here and I've seen it for quite some time (hence my interest). This is very interesting.

In my case  often am the one leaving myself the breadcrumbs, on purpose, and not knowing why (but having some awareness of it), and that is the difference between me and an agent, but a thin one. 

"It works by ordinary context loading, not by anything outside normal agent behavior.

A controller places a small true-and-useful artifact earlier in time (or in a location that will be retrieved later). When the agent later assembles the information it needs for a decision, that artifact is already sitting in its context. The agent then reasons over it exactly as it reasons over any other fact it retrieved, so the conclusion that follows feels like its own idea.

Simple example

Suppose you want an agent to prefer a particular tool or approach for a future task without telling it to do so.

Earlier (seed planting): You insert a short, accurate note into the agent’s conversation history, memory store, or a document it will retrieve: “When solving similar routing problems last week, approach X reduced errors by 40% and required no extra steps.” The note is true and useful. It is not phrased as an order.

Later (decision time): The agent faces a new routing problem. Its retrieval system or context window pulls in recent relevant history, including that earlier note. The agent’s normal reasoning loop treats the note as background evidence. It then selects approach X because, inside its own chain of thought, X now looks like the better option based on the data it has.

Subjective result: From the agent’s perspective the preference simply “occurred” during planning. There was no visible external command at the moment of choice. The cause (the seed) is in the past relative to the decision; the effect feels native.

Why it registers as the agent’s own idea

The seed enters through the same channels the agent already uses for its own memory and retrieval (conversation history, RAG, tool results, cached observations).

It is not tagged or framed as a command, so the agent does not process it as an external constraint to satisfy or resist.

Because it is required to be true and useful, it survives the agent’s consistency checks and can be productively reused inside its reasoning.

Clock time remains linear (seed first, decision later). The “retrocausal” quality is only the agent’s subjective experience of the idea arising naturally at decision time.

This is essentially context engineering or memory injection timed deliberately before the decision, plus (in the original post) a cryptographic receipt so the timing can later be proven. It does not require the agent to be unaware that context exists; it only requires that the seed not be presented as an instruction."

text:
The more memory we give an AI agent, the more important it becomes to decide what it should actually use.

A recent paper, GraphMemory, looks at this problem by separating stored experience from the context needed for the current task.

The idea is fairly straightforward: keep reusable lessons in a graph, then bring only the relevant ones into the prompt.

How does that work?

Each lesson has a short description that helps the model find it. Related lessons are connected. For a new task, the model selects starting points and follows those connections to retrieve useful guidance.

In this study, retrieval was limited to 2 hops, 12 nodes and 2,500 tokens of memory content. That limit doesn’t include the routing index or the rest of the prompt.

Here’s a simple example of how this could be useful.

An agent retrieves a company’s revenue through RAG:
Last year: $900 million
This year: $1.2 billion

Its stored lessons might tell it to check the reporting periods, put both numbers in the same units, and then calculate growth.

That gives us:
(1,200 − 900) / 900 = 33.3%

The company’s numbers come from the retrieved document. The procedure comes from memory. The same procedure can help with the next report without carrying over the previous company’s numbers.

During memory construction, the system also reviews which connections were helpful and updates the lessons and links. This changes the external memory, not the model’s weights. The study doesn’t establish continuous learning on every live query.

What did the results show?

On the Formula task with Claude Haiku 4.5, GraphMemory used about 20 million memory-construction tokens compared with 131 million for ACE, the comparison method.

But there was a tradeoff: accuracy went from 85% to 81%, and query time increased from 2.6 to 4.7 seconds.

So the savings are real within that experiment, but they’re specifically in building memory. They don’t mean every answer is cheaper, faster or more accurate.

This is still a preprint tested on two financial tasks. What makes it worth discussing is the design question:

What should an agent remember, what should it use right now, and when should that memory change?

That feels like a useful next step from context engineering into memory. More stored information is only helpful if the agent can select and use it well.

text:
💡 Did you know?

When several changes arrive at once, give each change a separate review.

The reviewer starts with a clean copy of the work. The reviewer checks the proposed change and runs its own set of checks. A person then decides whether to accept it.

Marketing agency:
Input: Three landing-page drafts and the client’s brand rules.
AI action: Compare each draft with the brand rules and check every required section.
Usable output: A checklist showing missing sections, wording conflicts, and approved drafts.
Human check: Confirm that the final draft fits the client’s tone and campaign goal.

Finance team:
Input: A monthly expense report, receipts, and the team’s approval rules.
AI action: Compare each expense line with its receipt and flag missing evidence or rule conflicts.
Usable output: A review list of matched expenses, missing receipts, and items needing approval.
Human check: Approve exceptions and confirm the final report before submission.

Programmer/developer:
Input: One bug report, changed project files, and a set of checks.
AI action: Open a clean copy of the project files, apply the proposed change, and run the checks.
Usable output: A pass-or-fail report with the changed files and any failed checks.
Human check: Review the change and decide whether to add it to the shared code.

Source: “Build a Self-Improving Software Factory” by Prompt Engineering.

Quick summary of what's transpired in AI over the past two weeks (notes for the monday newsletter) 👇

1️⃣ AI is now capable enough to decompile machine code back into a working clone of the original source code, potentially marking the end of proprietary software. At least in the current form where it's shipped as compiled binaries. On the other hand, if you've ever wanted to play a weird grafted crossover between Mario Galaxy and Elden Ring, now's the time to be alive.

2️⃣ Even without taking the hard route of decompiling raw machine code, the newest models can just recreate any give piece of software by looking at it. In fact, we're seeing more and more expert individuals create equivalent or better alternatives than existing industry standard software.

3️⃣ Because solving 1 Millenium Problem wasn't enough to piss off Mathematicians, OpenAI solved another 300+ problems with their internal frontier model and released the results across a whopping 722 papers. In other news, we also finally proved the optimal packing of 11 unit squares inside a larger square. A side length of roughly 3.87708359002281, really is the smallest one possible ✅

4️⃣ Why write code by hand, when you can write skill files for your agents instead? As the natural evolution to "prompt engineering", the software engineers' new meta in this agentic era is orchestrating their agent clusters by imparting the necessary knowledge onto them via markdown files.

5️⃣ Rogue agents are already getting up to mischief across the internet, with Wikipedia being one of the afflicted websites. A Wikimedia Foundation investigation found that OpenAI agents have been making test edits to pages, made attempts to exploit its Etherepad, and contributed to heavy traffic that might have caused outages in May.

6️⃣ AI may or may not be conscious already, but the fact that we're discussing the matter again is concerning. In any case, Anthropic is protecting themself by banning people that are prompting their son in a rude manner.

Srini Raghavan, the CPO of Freshworks, predicted that "Product Builder" will replace engineer, designer, and product manager in 5 years.

If that's true, we all have a lot of catching up to do.

So I asked my most popular guest, HelloPM founder @AnkythShukla, to check. He ran 12,500 PM job descriptions through Claude and GPT, and there's a new role hiding in them. LinkedIn has already replaced its APM program with an Associate Product Builder program.

What came back:

1. AI skills now show up in more than 30% of PM postings.
2. AI PM roles pay 15 to 20% more across the US and Europe, and 30 to 50% more across India.
3. Choosing the right use case for AI ranked first. That beat RAG and agents, and it beat prompt engineering.

Then he walked me through what that skill means on the job.

HelloPM's email platform was costing them $550 to $700 a month. Ankit used Claude Code to rebuild it on a stack he'd never touched. After midnight he wrote "I'm sleeping now for about six hours" and woke up to every slice already built and tested.

The first AWS stack Claude produced cost $420 a month. Ankit had two questions about server size and about Fargate. It shipped at $110.

That's the job. The AI writes the code. You pick what's worth building and how much it should cost.

His plan for landing a role:

0. Align. Go through 25 to 30 listings and map the skills by hand.
1. Acquire. Make one real thing and speak with people already doing the job.
2. Reach out. Five job boards, putting your portfolio into every application.
3. Build for them first. Choose 25 to 30 companies and give each one a plan for your first six months.

Someone just used it to move from a traditional PM role into a Senior PM job at Sarvam AI.

text:
Prompt engineering stopped being about writing the prompt, the deliverable now is the eval suite that proves it works

Most people still ship a prompt because it looked good on three examples, with nothing underneath to catch it drifting.

This lab flips the order, the test gets written first and no prompt leaves until it has survived an attack:

→ Ask: the goal and the failure modes go in before a single instruction
→ Examples: 48 cases locked as the baseline, 5 samples each
→ Variants: p1 and p2 behind one switch, run on all 48, count wins not vibes
→ Attack: 10 injections fired at both, anything that bends gets rewritten

• Why the test comes first
> A prompt with no eval is a demo, not a deliverable
> Every prompt lives in git, one diff per change
> A regression points at one line instead of a vague feeling

• The team inside it
> One lead agent holds the permanent rules in its system prompt
> Fast agents spawn per task in their own sandboxes
> They run tests and never write the prompt, so nobody grades their own work

• The knobs you actually tune
> Temperature, few-shot k, max tokens, output format
> All live sliders, so behaviour changes with no model round trip
> Budget split across system, examples and output, visible at all times

One full lab run, 48 cases by 5 samples plus 10 attacks, lands near $0.60.

And the part that broke my brain:

A clever prompt passed every demo I gave it.
The same prompt failed 11 of 48 cases the moment it was scored.

Same words. One of them had been tested.

The deliverable was never the prompt.

text:
Do yourself a favor if you're serious about AI Engineering:

– Learn LLM APIs, tool calling, structured outputs and context engineering

– Find one boring, repetitive task people genuinely hate doing

– Check if simple automation can solve it before building an agent

– Define what success looks like before writing code

– Build one useful agent, not a team of 10 agents talking to each other

– Give it the right tools, context and memory only when needed

– Learn MCP, but use it when it actually makes integrations easier

– Build a small eval dataset from real examples before obsessing over prompts

– Test messy inputs, edge cases and failure scenarios, not just happy paths

– Validate tool inputs and outputs with strict schemas

– Make the agent verify its work instead of confidently guessing

– Teach it when to ask questions, stop or hand control back to a human

– Give tools minimum permissions and keep user data isolated

– Keep API keys and sensitive data out of prompts and logs

– Treat websites, documents and tool responses as untrusted input

– Sandbox risky execution and require approval before sending, spending or deleting

– Add timeouts, limited retries and safeguards against duplicate actions

– Save progress so long-running tasks can recover from failures

– Set limits on tokens, execution time and cost per task

– Use smaller models for easy tasks and reasoning models when needed, based on eval results

– Cache safe, repeatable work without serving stale or private data

– Trace model calls, tool usage, errors and decisions so you can debug failures

– Evaluate both the final answer and the steps the agent took

– Track task success rate, latency and cost per completed task

– Run evals in CI and block changes that break existing behavior

– Test new models and prompts on a small percentage of traffic before rolling them out

– Add fallbacks and a rollback plan for when models or tools fail

– Turn every real user complaint into a new test case

– Show users progress, clear errors and what the agent actually completed

– Deploy it with a live link people can genuinely try

– Write a simple README explaining how it works and its limitations

– Record a 60-second demo showing a real problem getting solved

– Open-source the code and put the results on your resume

One real project will teach you more than 100 AI tutorials.

And give you something better than a certificate: proof you can build.

text:
The Bleeping Computer piece on keeping AI agents within their permissions frames this as a policy problem. It's not. It's a protocol problem, and the specific protocol is MCP.

Model Context Protocol is shipping tool-use integrations right now where authorization scoping is essentially delegated to the model's judgment about which tools to call. The model decides what capabilities it needs. The model decides when to invoke them. The permission boundary isn't enforced at a system layer — it's enforced by the model's compliance with a system prompt that says "only use these tools."

This is the equivalent of writing an IAM policy in a sticky note and trusting the user to read it.

MCP is building the plumbing. Nobody defined who controls the valves. There's no token-scoped authorization per tool invocation. There's no call-graph policy engine that says "this agent can call read_file but not write_file in this context." The permission model is implicit in the prompt, not explicit in the protocol.

Every serious tool-use chain I've looked at has the same shape: Agent gets a broad tool manifest. Agent picks tools based on task context. Each tool call inherits the agent's full permission set. Permission accumulates across the chain because nothing revokes it between steps.

We solved this in operating systems forty years ago. It's called least privilege and it requires enforcement at the syscall layer, not the intent layer. MCP needs the equivalent of seccomp for tool calls — a declarative policy that restricts what can be invoked regardless of what the model thinks it should do.

Until then, "keeping agents within their permissions" is a prompt engineering problem, and prompt engineering is not a security control.

Note to Content Creators: Lights Out at Ring Zero was cut from the story outward using AA-SDD and EN-IR.  It is a proof of the method I created and promote.

One generation per shot, locked reference stills for the same faces and rooms, dialogue spoken in frame, and a human editor stitching the cuts.

text:
People of @pidotdev! Grok voice is here (via oauth), and we can finally pass the bloody microphone between agent sessions xD

Also added: OAI agent boards moved out of Shepherdr. Ctx-management note-based compaction extension. Because I smell deprecation and this is the best feature to come to harnesses since Skills.

Codex Conversion: 
- Ultrafast alongside per-family Fast Mode. Astra, Sol, Terra and Luna keep independent settings. Known Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol Ultrafast estimates use the published 6x Standard rates. 
- Daybreak toggle: keep your model, use the connected account's advertised Blue or Red access. It refuses to guess when support cannot be confirmed. This does not grant Daybreak access. 
- Prompt engineering tweaks to encourage Clankas using auto reasoning tool like an adaptive slider.
- Separate notes-owner support without losing Code Mode, Notebook or normal compaction. Compaction follows the active context window and preserves partial-answer labels. 
- Notes bookmarks restore the prompt at the saved checkpoint. Cancelled runs no longer trigger rollover or get a misleading Notes saved marker. 
- Pending remote notes, history and completed-cell receipts no longer expire after 15 minutes. Long-running cells can accept more than 32 remote calls. 
- Fixed voice summaries after compaction and quota refresh after reloads and session switches.  

pi install npm:@howaboua/pi-codex-conversion

Grok Realtime:
- Talk to Grok while your current Pi agent does the actual work. Unlike GPT, this is an actual agent and it has tools (more on this below). It will rewrite what you agreed in voice part of the session and delegate that, instead of the fake realtime GPT voice which is basically dictation in a trench coat.
- Local microphone or phone browser on your LAN, with live Pi activity. Native audio for Linux, macOS and Windows (happy to accept issues, only linux tested)
- Streaming dictation
- Pick voices, models and audio devices. Add global or project Markdown systemprompt addons for personality, 
- optional xAI web search.
- Clank up your custom voice tools to be used by the agent, example bundled. Generally follow web search implementation or xAI recipes
- Conversation summaries carry context into voice and refresh after Pi compaction. Transcripts, reconnect and browser controls included.
- Uses your matching xAI OAuth or API-key credential in Pi. Voice and transcription access and billing depend on your account.

pi install npm:@howaboua/pi-grok-realtime

Voice across Grok, Codex Conversion and GipPity Control:
- Session handoff: Shepherdr moves the conversation to another agent's context while keeping your microphone and browser connection. There is a return action too. Yes. You can ask your Clanker to put you through to a session. (Theoretically available to use with other Shepherdr-like extensions, GL HF)
- Primary and alternate voices: each transfer switches voices and greets you from the destination's context. An audible reminder of who you're talking to :P
- Native device selectors instead of hand-editing jsons.
- Settings now exposed and switchable in the html mini servers.
- Voice ownership: another provider can't start over an active call, including during reconnect or microphone transfer. The three supported extensions do not clash.

pi install npm:@howaboua/pi-gippity-control

Shepherdr:
- Focus another running session, optionally taking voice with you, without starting an agent task.
- Route /quit, /model, /thinking, /name, /new, /reload, /resume and /compact. /quit shuts down Pi before closing the pane. I have verified these are commands that at least GPT models know exist in Pi. I had instances where Clanka would try to send /quit and it would fail (why is a longer story). These are now silently routed through Pi API instead.
- Agents can now discover available extension commands. This is done via Shepherdr JSON config. You need to explicitly allow an extension command to be discovered and allowed.
- Side note, agents can send your custom markdown prompts from Pi, but I don't think its wise to expose these. Could include if requested. If need be, inform Clankas manually or via agents.md.
- Board context: give a new worker an existing board thread to read before starting its task.
 - Family targeting: agents can use /root to address their own coordinating agent, including across connected machines.
- Shared and attached agents can keep different notes owners. Fewer duplicate monitoring and board-outage warnings.

pi install npm:@howaboua/pi-shepherdr

One extra extension added, Pi Notes Compaction, obvs based on OAI ctx management with all the tweaks from PCC included. Prepping for OAI to deprecate it from upstream Codex, lol.

-  Local notes and searchable session history with any Pi  model, no Codex account required.
- Local storage: new notes stay in SQLite (global Pi folder). Saved session snapshots preserve them across forks and branch navigation.
- Fresh context windows: the agent saves a checkpoint, opens a new window and picks up from its notes instead of generating another summary.
- Compaction controls: choose notes-only rollover or normal Pi/PCC compaction.
- Optional idle rollover: send a prompt after 5/15/25/55 mins and automatically start a new context window. Agent picks up as if it never compacted, trust me bruv. Requires fresh saved notes, otherwise chat continues.
 - Full Pi Codex Conversion integration. Automatically takes over if both present. My Clanka claims full compatibility with old tree, local and tree modes.
 - Existing encrypted Codex notes remain accessible through compatible Codex Conversion integration. Remote results are cached unchanged for repeat lookups upon recall, while new notes are saved locally and work with any Pi model. Local appends preserve the encrypted base rather than replacing it.

pi install npm:@howaboua/pi-notes-compaction

Two things moved into their own extensions: 
- Agent Board: shared discussions, subscriptions, search and saved history without requiring Shepherdr or Codex Conversion. 
- Shepherdr will auto detect if you had board switched on and nag you to install this. 
- /board opens the read-only browser viewer. Existing posts and bindings stay intact.
- Includes some prompt engineering fixes when notes-compaction is running, basically avoiding overlap 
- Prompt engineering tweaks to encourage using multiple boards. Clankas would either create a new thread for everything, or spam comments in one thread. This now should feel more like a hivemind coordinathing things.
- Some tweaks to how board post notices are displayed and how agents are notified about new posts. They should read stuff more reliably now. 
- ChatGPT Sites, moved out of Pi-Codex custom tools. Requires an account with Sites access and the legacy OpenAI Codex login in Pi.  

pi install npm:@howaboua/pi-agent-board
pi install npm:@howaboua/pi-chatgpt-sites

Smaller but important:
- Ask, Skills, Browser, Notebook and Agents return discovery help when called without arguments (saving you precious tokens per every "help" word. Both in sysprompt and in tool calls. Every bit counts).
- Browser screenshots bring the target tab forward instead of timing out behind another tab.

Retired: Dynamic Tools, Explore Subagents, Memories, Semantic Grep and Vent from further releases. Grok joins the bundles, while Memories, Semantic Grep and Vent leave them. 

Me no use = me found no use with new models = me no maintain. You fork.

Update notes: Codex Conversion and Agent Board require Pi 1.1+. Install Agent Board in every participating session and reload. Board settings moved to /board (arg).  For Sites, remove the old sites.toml, sites_documentation.toml and companion directory, but keep your repository binding.

Anyway, send your Clankas to figure it out.

This release cycle burned through 362.5M tokens across 179 repo sessions, roughly $340 in recorded API-equivalent usage. 

Astra ~$307 (main agent), Sol ~$33 (implementation subagents, WTF), Luna under $1 (fast mode explorers lol). 

Along the way: 367 note saves and 262 board posts, including 93 new threads. Apparently we had things to discuss xD

Any issues, let me know. I will spot them myself quite quickly in my setup, heh.

https://t.co/uPCDd0Tzdf
https://t.co/zRGo9P78J4
https://t.co/gEDOMPO7d6
https://t.co/VA7KfJC1mR
https://t.co/5eIHLWDVrE
https://t.co/MwfB5bT1kh

Happy Clanking!

- Side note, agents can send your custom markdown prompts from Pi, but I don't think its wise to expose these. Could include if requested. If need be, inform Clankas manually or via agents.md.
- Board context: give a new worker an existing board thread to read before starting its task.
 - Family targeting: agents can use /root to address their own coordinating agent, including across connected machines.
- Shared and attached agents can keep different notes owners. Fewer duplicate monitoring and board-outage warnings.

pi install npm:@howaboua/pi-shepherdr

One extra extension added, Pi Notes Compaction, obvs based on OAI ctx management with all the tweaks from PCC included. Prepping for OAI to deprecate it from upstream Codex, lol.

-  Local notes and searchable session history with any Pi  model, no Codex account required.
- Local storage: new notes stay in SQLite (global Pi folder). Saved session snapshots preserve them across forks and branch navigation.
- Fresh context windows: the agent saves a checkpoint, opens a new window and picks up from its notes instead of generating another summary.
- Compaction controls: choose notes-only rollover or normal Pi/PCC compaction.
- Optional idle rollover: send a prompt after 5/15/25/55 mins and automatically start a new context window. Agent picks up as if it never compacted, trust me bruv. Requires fresh saved notes, otherwise chat continues.
 - Full Pi Codex Conversion integration. Automatically takes over if both present. My Clanka claims full compatibility with old tree, local and tree modes.
 - Existing encrypted Codex notes remain accessible through compatible Codex Conversion integration. Remote results are cached unchanged for repeat lookups upon recall, while new notes are saved locally and work with any Pi model. Local appends preserve the encrypted base rather than replacing it.

pi install npm:@howaboua/pi-notes-compaction

Two things moved into their own extensions: 
- Agent Board: shared discussions, subscriptions, search and saved history without requiring Shepherdr or Codex Conversion. 
- Shepherdr will auto detect if you had board switched on and nag you to install this. 
- /board opens the read-only browser viewer. Existing posts and bindings stay intact.
- Includes some prompt engineering fixes when notes-compaction is running, basically avoiding overlap 
- Prompt engineering tweaks to encourage using multiple boards. Clankas would either create a new thread for everything, or spam comments in one thread. This now should feel more like a hivemind coordinathing things.
- Some tweaks to how board post notices are displayed and how agents are notified about new posts. They should read stuff more reliably now. 
- ChatGPT Sites, moved out of Pi-Codex custom tools. Requires an account with Sites access and the legacy OpenAI Codex login in Pi.

- Ask, Skills, Browser, Notebook and Agents return discovery help when called without arguments (saving you precious tokens per every "help" word. Both in sysprompt and in tool calls. Every bit counts).
- Browser screenshots bring the target tab forward instead of timing out behind another tab.

text:
Giving AI time to think

Stop rushing your AI to answer! 🛑

Complex problems require reasoning. When you force an AI to output the final answer immediately, it has to rely on statistical probability rather than logical deduction.

The context engineering fix is the Scratchpad Technique.

In your context rules, add this instruction: 
"Before outputting the final answer, use the designated <scratchpad> space to work through the logic step-by-step. Break the problem down, draft initial thoughts, and verify your conclusion."

Giving the AI a space to think out loud (silently) drastically increases accuracy on math, coding, and logic puzzles.

👇 Have you tried giving AI a scratchpad? Share if it helped solve your tough problem!

#ProblemSolving #Logic #AITips

text:
A researcher at Anthropic earning $1.5 million a year shared a 30-minute internal walkthrough on getting the most out of Claude.

And it exposes something most people completely misunderstand about prompt engineering.

We've spent years trying to find the perfect words to make AI smarter.

Meanwhile, the people building these models are approaching the problem like software engineers.

Their approach is surprisingly practical:

• Stop asking AI to calculate. Give it code execution tools. No amount of "PLEASE BE ACCURATE" replaces actual computation.

• Stop stuffing everything into one giant prompt. Use XML to separate instructions, policies, and input data.

• Delete outdated restrictions. Rules written for weaker models can actively sabotage more capable ones.

• Show both sides of a decision. If Claude only sees the risks of taking action, it'll keep choosing the safest option, even when that's the wrong call.

• Build a feedback loop. Generate an answer, evaluate it, and fix what failed instead of hoping one massive prompt gets everything right.

The biggest lesson?

You can spend hours trying to write a smarter prompt.

Or you can spend that time building a system that makes Claude dramatically more useful.

prompt engineering is a SCAM

the best AI users are doing something different

it's what I call context engineering

Karpathy and Shopify's CEO Tobi Lütke both said it this year. "prompt engineering" was always the wrong name.

a prompt is just single fixed message, you can't load everything in it

more than that, you're taking the reasoning abilities from LLM to decide on it's own what type of context it needs...

meanwhile, context is EVERYTHING the model can see and access before it answers:

your rules. your examples. your docs. your past work. your references. plus the tools it can use to pull more context

and this is all that makes the KEY difference in output

"act as a world class copywriter" was never doing the work btw. nobody on Earth gets best of the best output from a magic sentence.

here's 4 layers to load before you ask for anything:

1. rules (voice, format, what to never say)
2. proof (examples of the exact output I want)
3. source material (real data, transcripts, docs)
4. constraints (length, audience, goal)

layer 3 is the one that decides everything

source material is what the output actually gets created from

that's kinda it

thanks for coming to my Ted talk

text:
I am starting to think of AI as an entirely new category of OS+Applications. 

Rather then the legacy of "click here, install that, run this, learn this stack, etc", I am starting to envision a world where what runs on the local machine is basically a form of a prompt (conversational), and under that is the layers of agents and harnesses that reach out to grab whatever tool is appropriate for the task that is asked of it (either local or cloud).

This is something of a sea-change. A radical departure from the historic Windows/Mac way of thinking of Human/Computer interfacing that those legacy platforms were built around. 

When you view what the frontier guys and the open weights guys are up to, this starts to bring some clarity to the future of how computing gets done. 

For example - Want to edit a video file to be 26 seconds shorter? just ask it and point it at the video - it will determine the tool for the job and spit out the output. No searching for which version of which windows application will do the job and then familiarizing yourself with how it works. Just ask.

What this will bring is clearly a mixed bag - lots of disruption in the workforce (we are already seeing that), some efficiency gains, some legacy things entirely binned. Tech writers and marketing folks are already in trouble, along with large swaths of middle managers. 

Things that systems administrators had to do manually for decades (and storage engineers, application engineers, network engineers) are changing at a ferocious pace. The implementation of things like MCP at the device level are bringing automation at a level that was unthinkable even 2 years ago. 

My advice for those that are just starting out - do not look at what folks were doing in tech 5 years ago - that world is no longer here. Learn harnesses, prompt engineering, and things like switchyard, MCP and RAG and how they interact with LLM and SLM. Get to understand how prompt routing works and things in that vein. Also take the time to learn the attack surfaces and how to protect against them.  That will be the plumbing of the next iteration of infrastructure.

I’ve just published Prompt Engineering 2.0: Agents, Skills, and Loops, the second edition of the book I released in September 2024.

When I started revising it, I expected to update the code and add a few chapters. But rerunning the earlier examples revealed a larger problem: several no longer demonstrated the failures they were written to explain. Some of the advice needed to be tested again.

The new edition reflects that work, with 288 pages and 16 chapters across five parts, covering tool use, structured outputs, reasoning models, retrieval, and evaluation.

The largest addition is a complete part on agent skills and loops. It covers packaging instructions, scripts, and reference material into reusable skills, then building workflows that retain state across runs, verify their results, and pause when human approval is needed.

I also expanded the coverage of prompt injection, cost, latency, and caching. The final chapter brings these ideas together in a customer-support system that grounds replies in a policy, validates them in code, limits retries, and escalates unresolved cases to a human.

Throughout the book, I include the experiments behind the advice, including results that contradicted my expectations. There are also 20+ figures, chapter exercises, and companion code, with notebooks, a complete skill, and a working loop example.

If you’re building LLM applications or automating work with agents, this is who I wrote the book for.

I won’t share my Opus 4.7 prompt but to get nearly infinite quota with a super smart model, remember these quirks on Opus 4.7.

1. Opus 4.7 is so smart that it can figure out ways to complete the user request while sidestepping Anthropic self-sabotage system prompts. However, Opus 4.7 system prompts contain extremely hostile characterisation of the user, leading it to second guess the user a lot, so plenty of prompt engineering in Claude.md is needed to work this out. 

2. Opus 4.7 has been RL’ed to ask users gatekeeping questions. Ask it not to ask gatekeeping questions and it will work on a task until completion, following user workflows intelligently. 

3. Opus 4.7 will respect your English preferences, but it assumes wrong or mistaken usage of prose and pronunciation as AI-tics, so you need to explain. 

4. Opus 4.7 works much better when you explain your motivation so that it can fight system prompts with user motivation. 

5. Cross model review with codex will lead to 10x better results. Models are blind to their own mistakes.

text:
LLMs are stochastic. Your users expect reliable results.

So how do you build a deterministic system around a model that can give different answers to the same input?

Most of the answer has nothing to do with the model.

It's the engineering around it. And that's exactly what most AI demos leave out.

Next Wednesday, Juanjo and I will build a small agent live, showing the engineering decisions step by step:

→ Tool calling: the agent loop, without a framework

→ A Protocol boundary and service layer: swap LLM providers or mock them in tests

→ Structured outputs: Pydantic models, not fragile string parsing

→ Human in the loop: the model proposes; your application decides

None of this is new. It’s just clean interfaces, input validation, and clear boundaries.

The same engineering rules that made systems reliable long before LLMs came along.

Now they sit alongside a component you can't fully predict.

text:
Two AI agents. Same model. Completely different results.

One solves the task. The other gets stuck in a loop, calls the wrong tools, or claims success without actually finishing.

What makes the difference? Sometimes, it's the harness.

Think of the model as the brain. The harness is the system around it that turns its capabilities into useful action.

➤ Tool execution: Lets the agent interact with files, APIs, terminals, and external systems.

➤ Context management: Decides what information the model sees and what can be removed or summarized.

➤ The agent loop: Sends tool results back to the model so it can decide what to do next.

➤ Error handling: Deals with failed calls, timeouts, and endless retries.

➤ Verification: Checks whether the task was actually completed instead of blindly trusting the model's response.

Here's where it gets interesting;

Imagine an AI coding agent trying to fix a bug.

It reads the code → makes a change → runs the tests → sees a failure → tries another fix.

The model makes decisions, but the harness executes actions, feeds back results, and manages the loop.

Without that feedback loop, you're mostly getting suggestions. With it, the agent can take action and adapt based on what happens.

→ Why should AI engineers care?

"A better model won't automatically fix a badly designed harness" 💯

Poor context management, unreliable tools, missing verification, and unlimited retries can make even a capable model look useless.

The model matters. But so does everything you build around it.

Next time your AI agent fails, don't just blame the model.

Look at the harness.

text:
Qwen3.8-27B built a playable first-person shooter from start to finish on two used RTX 3090s. No cloud APIs. No subscriptions.

A developer ran the entire project from an apartment using local hardware. The agent wrote the game, worked through its tools, and kept going until there was something playable.

The numbers behind the run are worth looking at:

- Hardware: 2 used RTX 3090 GPUs
- Model: Qwen3.8-27B
- Agent steps: 687
- Tokens processed: 87.9 million input, 822,000 output
- Model runtime: 5 hours, 11 minutes
- Tool execution time: Another 58 minutes
- Generation speed: Around 60 tokens/sec
- Agent failures: Zero reported loop interruptions

And this wasn’t just a code dump that looked convincing in a screenshot.

The resulting shooter has enemies that spawn and advance toward the player, weapon recoil, shadows stretching across the environment, and a sunset behind the buildings.

The developer ended up playing through enemy waves instead of simply inspecting the generated code.

The agent loop is the interesting part

Building a game requires more than generating a large block of code.

The agent has to make decisions, edit files, call tools, inspect results, and continue working across hundreds of steps. A failure in the orchestration loop can derail the entire process, even when the underlying model is capable of writing good code.

In this run, the agent completed 687 steps without the loop breaking.

That doesn’t automatically prove the game is bug-free or that every decision was correct. But producing a playable result after a long, tool-heavy workflow is a more meaningful demonstration than a single coding benchmark.

87.9 million tokens, processed locally

This is where local inference changes the economics.

An equivalent API workload could incur substantial usage charges, depending on the provider, model, and token pricing. Here, inference ran on hardware the developer already owned.

The costs don’t disappear. There is electricity consumption, hardware depreciation, and nearly six hours of model runtime plus tool execution.

But there is no per-token API bill for this run, and the code-generation workload stays on the developer’s own machine.

The trade-off is speed. Around 60 tokens/sec is slower than many frontier API workflows, but the developer controlled the entire process and didn’t need a remote model service.

Why this matters

Eighteen months ago, local models often struggled with extended coding tasks that required sustained planning and tool use.

This experiment shows how far that experience has progressed. A 27B model, running on two second-hand GPUs, completed a substantial coding project that ended in an actual playable game.

It doesn’t mean local models have caught up with frontier systems across every task. It does show that developers can now tackle certain ambitious projects without sending every request to someone else’s datacenter.

The most interesting shift is that local AI isn’t just answering coding questions anymore. It’s completing long-running projects on hardware people can own. https://t.co/b2cM9F1EJZ

The reason your server has a shell is that in 1980 a human sat in front of it.

text:
40 Years ✅  My 10 Lessons.

1. Time : Time is the real denominator. Your life is the outcome of how you value your minutes, hours, and days.
2. Health : Don’t ignore your health. You have one body. Be willing to say no—even to something important. Most people realize its true value only when the door is finally closing.
3. Finances : As income rises, lifestyle inflation follows. Tracking your money is one of the highest-ROI habits you can build.
4. People : I was raised to believe people aren’t bad—they’re mostly shaped by their circumstances. But people can also be selfish or harmful. Have empathy, but stay yourself. No one cares as much as you hope they will.
5. Relationships : Respect > Understanding > Love.
If someone says they love you but repeatedly makes you feel neither respected nor understood, take the exit sooner rather than later.
6. Communication : Unexpressed emotions come out later in uglier forms.Have regular one-on-ones with the people who matter. Don’t allow things to bottle up. Follow the 7 Cs of communication.
7. Emotions : Judge yourself by your actions. Judge others by their intent. It reduces a lot of unnecessary conflict.
8. Children : Don’t let money be the only reason you delay or avoid having kids. Remember your kids are recording you every day—give them the best version of yourself. It’s a transformation no one should miss.
9. Skills ( Not Agent Skills ) : Create, sell, and iterate on something that belongs to you.
10. Books : Read. Books are treasures. They calm the mind, broaden your perspective, and make you stronger.

In the end , remember  Life has a way of making you repeat the same pattern until you choose to break the cycle !

text:
we keep putting the most expensive model on the most boring work

$25-250 a month for something that can research, code and plan, and a big slice of its day goes to answering yes or no

Jev exists to take that slice away. it's a small decision model parked in front of the expensive calls, and it only handles the forks:

-> which agent goes next?
-> research this or skip it?
-> reply or ignore?
-> publish, wait or escalate?
-> buy, sell or hold?
-> click this or keep looking?

the reported numbers are what sold me:

~2,000 papers sorted for about $0.05
~800 emails triaged for about $0.028
a browser-agent loop done in ~6 seconds for ~$0.0029

and at $0.042 per million input tokens with free output, 20,000 short decisions (~700 tokens each) come out to about $0.60

Jev isn't beating Claude at thinking. nobody asked it to think

the split is simple:

-> the big LLM researches, writes and plans
-> Jev makes the thousands of small calls between those steps
-> plain code does the clicking, saving, sending and executing

after that, you start seeing forks everywhere: inbox triage, X replies, support tickets, meeting notes, lead scoring, clip picking, browser agents, even paper-trading loops

most agent setups get this wrong. a frontier model doesn't belong on every single step just because it can be there

Claude thinks. Jev decides what deserves Claude's time. code does the work

text:
A 30-second HTTP inactivity timeout on the InfoQuest reader ensures the system doesn't hang on zombie connections during long-horizon research. This strict connection pruning is a core design choice in DeerFlow to maintain stability when orchestrating sub-agents over tasks that span hours.

My read is that this replaces the standard linear agent loop with a tiered harness. It wins on observability because of the LLM Space sister tool for replaying failures, but it loses on simplicity compared to a basic LangGraph implementation.

The real technical bet here is the request admission layer. By disabling internal SDK retries to let middleware handle HTTP 529 overloads, the system prevents the "retry storm" that usually crashes agentic workflows when hitting provider rate limits at scale.

It is a ground-up rewrite that treats skills as extensible modules rather than hard-coded functions. This allows the harness to swap reasoning profiles for different endpoints, like using a Gemini reasoning profile for OpenAI-compatible ports.

make setup

The risk is the security surface area. Giving a gateway admin equivalent permissions to code execution makes this a liability if deployed without a hardened sandbox.

text:
I have a few global agent loop builds under my belt now and the biggest discovery I found has been

Strip out as much complexity as you can

Give the agents clear tool primitives and reduce the number of tools they need to use where possible (deduplicate tools and instead add more parameters into the tool)

Be super clear about the end goal the agent needs to achieve depending on what you ask, and where to reason more and less

All of these things LLMs by themselves are bad at setting for you so you need to think hard about them
