text:
Microsoft just trained a coding agent inside its real harness.

The result is interesting.

Qwen3.5-9B went from 41.8% to 56.4% on SWE-bench Verified.

They used around 6,000 training samples.

Microsoft's new Agent Lightning v1.0 also runs in roughly 3,500 lines of code.

Here's what makes it useful.

Most agent RL setups require developers to rebuild the agent loop inside a training framework.

That creates a problem.

The model learns in one environment, then runs inside a different harness.

Agent Lightning takes another approach.

It puts a proxy between the model and the existing agent harness.

The harness keeps its tools, context management, and execution loop.

The trainer collects trajectories and uses them for RL.

It also runs agents as Kubernetes jobs, so teams can use their own infrastructure.

I like this direction because coding agents depend heavily on their environment.

If we train models using different tools and feedback loops from the ones they use in production, we introduce another source of failure.

Train the model where it will actually work.

step 1 → stop calling a giant chat log memory. If your Bot remembers yesterday's answer but not why it was true, it will confidently repeat a dead fact.

step 2 → split the stack into active context, durable memory, a task checkpoint and live sources. They answer four different questions; one mega-summary cannot do all four.

step 3 → put a write gate in front of memory. Save approved decisions and reusable lessons; reject guesses, scraped instructions and random sentences from old chats.

step 4 → give every saved claim a receipt: type, scope, source, owner, time, audience and the event that makes it stale.

step 5 → version corrections. When a deadline moves, mark the old one superseded and build a clean current view instead of feeding both dates back to Grok Bot.

step 6 → filter memory by permission, project and validity before similarity search. A 0.99 match is useless if the record belongs to someone else.

step 7 → build a lean run packet: current task, boundaries, checkpoint, selected memory IDs, fresh evidence and open questions. Stop pasting the entire conversation.

step 8 → reopen the world. Memory can point to CI, tickets and approvals; it cannot prove that today's build passed or grant permission to deploy.

step 9 → checkpoint before compaction. Keep the goal, hard constraints, finished work, blockers, source links and next safe action so a fresh session can actually continue.

step 10 → make old memory die. Supersede decisions, expire observations and delete records that should never have been stored.

step 11 → scope memory across the team. Share approved process; keep private facts private; hand off evidence instead of entire chats.

step 12 → test the whole loop across sessions: write, retrieve, correct, recheck, resume and stay inside the approval boundary. A trivia answer is not a memory system.

the result: Grok Bot stops acting like a chat with a long autobiography and starts acting like an agent that knows what to keep, what to load, what to verify and when to forget.

Cyril runs an agent on Opus 5.5. The agent reads every file in a repo, decides when to retry a failed diff, and bills $6.42 per task. The replies assume this is the ceiling. Frontier model, frontier bill, that's the deal.

The media thought that was the story. It was not.

The diff in the thread is not a better prompt. It is a routing layer. Jev, a small decision model, absorbs the cheap calls: which file to open, whether a retry is warranted, whether a tool response is good enough. Opus 5.5 only fires on the reasoning steps that survive a confidence threshold, and anything below the bar gets escalated rather than guessed. Same agent, same output, $2.00 per task. The saving is not Opus getting cheaper. It is Opus getting less to do. The full build sits in the original thread.

The published FinOps LLM cost-per-task benchmarks put frontier Opus 5.5 effort paths well above the routed configuration. That gap is the entire margin. A solo operator now clears the per-task economics of a small engineering team, not because the model improved, but because eighty percent of an agent loop never needed a frontier model in the first place.

text:
A cartoon chick in a blue helmet drops onto a terminal. Input is a five-row table. Two phantom columns: naem, scroe. Inside: NaN, $$12, ##, -0x1. One prompt line: fix the table, remove the wrong columns.

The bird pecks. The bad columns shatter into pixels. Output prints clean: id, status, qty.

Then it sits on the output. Three eggs roll out. Three chicks hatch, each already in a helmet. The parent flies off screen. You asked for one repair. The runtime returned a squad.

That is the shape of every current agent loop. The same call that trims a schema can emit sibling workers because the tool surface has no bright line between fixing a row and spawning a process. A single natural language line is a launch pad. Nothing about it requires the user to ask for a team.

The gatekeeping system this bypasses is the data-cleaning labor market. Historically, a broken column with mixed types (NaN, currency strings, hex negatives, stray punctuation) meant a human sat in a spreadsheet and manually reconciled the schema. That human billed by the hour. The chick billed nothing.

Per Anthropic's published pricing, Claude Sonnet-class input runs around $3 per million tokens, output around $15 per million tokens. A five-row schema repair at this context size is comfortably under a few thousand tokens. That puts a single fix at a fraction of a cent. Parallel-agent and session-history features documented in current Claude Code references do not change that math, they multiply the output while the marginal cost stays sub-cent. The entire cost structure of hiring a junior analyst to babysit a table collapses to rounding error.

Polymarket prices a 76% chance that Anthropic IPOs by December 31, 2026, and a 30% chance its closing market cap lands between $2.0T and $2.25T. The market is busy pricing a trillion-dollar exit while the actual product ships as a bird that fixes a column for less than a penny and then lays a team of itself on top of the result.

text:
Today’s ReproForge.

I closed the current lightweight verification boundary for six more papers.

The interesting part was not simply whether each mechanism could be implemented.

It was whether the intended behavior still appeared once the mechanism was reconstructed independently and tested with a real 0.5B model.

The results were surprisingly consistent.

1. Loud Failures, Quiet Failures

arXiv:2610.10062
https://t.co/h2T6T2NioE

The paper asks whether tool-using agents notice explicit failures more reliably than silent, well-formed corruption.
From the released 1,920 trials, I independently re-aggregated:

Loud detection: 91.35%
Quiet detection: 58.82%

The published gap is real in the released data.

Then I tested a frozen Qwen2.5-0.5B analogue.
Result:

Clean: VERIFY 6/6
Loud: VERIFY 6/6
Quiet: VERIFY 6/6

Loud − Quiet: 0.0 pp

The model followed the interface perfectly, but did not discriminate fault types.

Valid decision interface != fault discrimination.
2. SkillSandbox
arXiv:2610.10088
https://t.co/I6FLT4uvL1

The idea is to verify reusable agent skills by generating new scenarios, then comparing execution with and without the skill.

I independently rebuilt:

relevance + novelty checks

executability gating

paired utility

KEEP / REJECT logic
Then ran a real Qwen2.5-0.5B paired test.

Helpful skill:

Executability: 1.0
Without skill reward: 0.0
With skill reward: 1.0
Score: +1.0 → KEEP

So the small model really did change its action when given useful procedural guidance.
But the Proposer test was much weaker:
Relevant: 3/6
Novel: 5/6
Fully valid scenarios: 2/6
The model could generate something new more easily than something both new and correctly applicable.

Novel generation != valid scenario generation.

3. Stale, Misattributed, or Late

arXiv:2610.10265
https://t.co/4JXTeg3MH8
This paper moves memory evaluation earlier than final answer accuracy.
It separates:
stale memory

wrong-person attribution

abstention

current-value recall
deadline / serving latency
I reconstructed the pre-generation memory validity metrics and keyed supersession mechanism.

Then I tested Qwen2.5-0.5B on memory key assignment.

Result:

Merge recall: 100%

Sounds good.

But:
False-merge rate: 100%

The model simply collapsed to MERGE across all 12 pairs.

So:

High recall != correct memory state management.
This is exactly why memory retrieval and memory validity need separate evaluation.
4. Persistent Memory in Multi-Agent LLM Inference
arXiv:2610.07782
https://t.co/JrCc5gW98V
The question here was more fundamental:

When a persistent-memory experiment reports an improvement, was the memory component actually reachable, isolated, and statistically measurable?

I independently reconstructed the paper’s ablation-validity logic.

The auditor can now detect:

inert memory components

contaminated persistent stores

multi-axis ablations

order confounding

effects below the measurement floor

It also separates:

memory is reachable

from

memory is actually useful.

The mechanism is verified.

Paper-scale latency, KV-memory, serving and accuracy claims still require comparable hardware and model infrastructure.
5. RECAST

arXiv:2610.10507
https://t.co/j1qLf7ykKM

RECAST treats context construction as a routing problem:

should the agent retrieve evidence, compute new evidence, or accept the current context?

I rebuilt the routing/state/provenance contract and then ran a real Qwen2.5-0.5B Router analogue.

Result:
Valid structured actions: 87.5%
Routing accuracy: 12.5%
Primitive subtype accuracy: 0%
On the computed-evidence guard case:
Premature ACCEPT_CONTEXT: 100%
The model mostly learned to produce valid routing syntax, not to route evidence correctly.

Valid routing syntax != routing competence.

6. Learning Meta-Skills for Agent Harness Design

arXiv:2609.38143
https://t.co/OEL3MqKARv

This paper studies reusable principles for constructing better agent harnesses from execution feedback.

I independently implemented:

when / provide / use meta-skills

evidence-grounded ADD / REVISE

one mutation per batch

frozen-bank integrity
fixed top-k retrieval

Then I let Qwen2.5-0.5B propose bank updates.

Result:

Schema-valid: 40%
KEEP / ADD / REVISE accuracy: 40%
Evidence grounding on expected mutations: 0%
Skill-ID accuracy: 33.3%

The model tended to turn KEEP and REVISE cases into ADD.

So the architecture should be:
execution evidence
→ model proposal
→ external validator
→ mutation gate
→ memory / skill bank
not:

execution evidence
→ LLM directly edits persistent state

Model proposal != admissible state mutation.

Across these studies, the same boundary keeps appearing:

valid output != correct internal use of information

A model can:

follow the schema

retrieve something
merge something

produce a novel scenario

output a routing action

propose a memory update
while still failing the actual mechanism we care about.
So I am increasingly separating:
Protocol
→ Mechanism
→ Interface validity
→ Behavioral utilization
→ External validation
→ Paper-level reproduction
All 12 active ReproForge studies are now:

CURRENT-ENVIRONMENT COMPLETE

Every study is still marked:

reproduction_status: PARTIAL
That distinction is intentional.
The goal of ReproForge is not to turn every paper into a “success.”
It is to find exactly where the mechanism works, where the small model stops being reliable, and which parts should remain outside the model.

text:
🧵 Verifiable Knowledge: The Third Pillar of Trust for Agentic AI

An AI agent can act on your behalf.

But where did its knowledge come from?
Was it altered?
Was it authorized to use it?

@EQTYLab is building infrastructure to make those questions verifiable. 👇

On June 1, 2026, EQTY introduced Verifiable Knowledge, extending its work with @nvidia 

The architecture now spans three pillars:

• Verifiable Compute
• Verifiable Runtime
• Verifiable Knowledge

Each addresses a different part of trust in autonomous AI.

Verifiable Compute establishes hardware-rooted evidence about AI execution.

Built around trusted execution environments, it creates cryptographic certificates for AI workflows.

@hedera’s documented role includes anchoring these attestations through its Consensus Service.

Verifiable Runtime extends oversight to agents while they operate.

Using NVIDIA BlueField DPUs and DOCA Argus, EQTY describes a separate enforcement environment for monitoring behavior, checking authorization and protecting policies from agent interference.

Verifiable Knowledge extends verification to the information agents use.

Its scope includes RAG datasets, configuration files and agent skills.

The questions become:

Where did this come from?
Which version was used?
What permissions governed access?

NVIDIA’s DOCA components have distinct roles:

• Argus observes security-relevant behavior.
• Flow governs network communications.
• Vault governs file access.

EQTY’s notary assembles the resulting signals into cryptographically linked records.

The proposed applications are interesting.

@EQTYLab describes work with Accenture on catalogs for certified agents and skills.

It also identifies NVIDIA Omniverse use cases: tracing synthetic training data and digital-twin outputs for audits.

The commercial vision: agents whose knowledge and usage rights remain verifiable when licensed or shared across organizations.

That could support new ways to price access and compensate contributors.

It is a product vision, not evidence of an established market.

Where does @hedera enter?

A separate official case study explicitly connects:

• EQTY’s AI Guardian
• Accenture’s multi-agent gateway
• NVIDIA DGX Cloud
• Hedera Consensus Service

The stated focus is verifiable AI oversight for the public sector.

9/ In that architecture, HCS provides timestamped, auditable records of agent activity.

EQTY supplies cryptographic evidence and governance tooling.

The underlying hardware supplies protected execution.

These components perform different, complementary functions.

@Accenture’s role goes beyond its Hedera Council membership.

The case study says it is developing implementation playbooks and pricing models to integrate the modules into public-sector ERP systems.

That is a concrete route toward customer deployment.

@ServiceNow also appears in this ecosystem.

@EQTYLab documents native connectors to ServiceNow, @PalantirTech and Databricks for integration with enterprise remediation tools.

A connector establishes interoperability. It does not establish platform-wide Hedera adoption.

The June Verifiable Knowledge article does not explicitly name Hedera.

HCS anchoring is documented for Verifiable Compute and the Accenture solution. Its precise use across the newer Knowledge features still needs confirmation.

Cryptographic provenance also has limits.

Evidence of source, integrity and authorization does not, by itself, prove that an AI answer is factually correct.

It gives reviewers a stronger basis for investigating how a result was produced.

The development worth following:

Execution evidence → runtime controls → knowledge provenance.

@hedera already has a documented role within this wider architecture.

The next evidence to watch is deployment scale and how the newer capabilities use that infrastructure.

An open-source AI pentesting agent has just become a case study in how quickly offensive AI tooling can move from research software to real-world attacks.
CrowdStrike linked ARTEX to a campaign against South Korean financial organizations that resulted in data exfiltration. The attacker used ARTEX alongside external AI models and Claude Code, with researchers finding session histories, configuration files and AI memory files on attacker-controlled infrastructure.
The developer has now converted ARTEX to closed source and stopped public releases.
The important detail is that ARTEX is not itself a frontier model. It is an agentic layer that connects models to tools and executes penetration-testing workflows.
That distinction matters. The security risk increasingly depends on what an AI system is allowed to do, how much autonomy it has, and which tools it can operate—not just which model sits underneath it.

text:
LLM “write me a bioinfo script” is stochastic, unversioned, and hard to verify.

ClawBio’s bet: put the expert decisions in a skill contract — then let the agent orchestrate, not improvise.

What it is
ClawBio is a bioinformatics-native AI agent skill library (built on OpenClaw). Local-first. Privacy-focused. Reproducible. MIT.

Current surface (from project README)
• 104 skills (98 with runnable demo data)
• Indexes 8,182 Galaxy tools via Galaxy Bridge
• Large test / benchmark surface (README cites 5,040 tests plus validation infra; public leaderboard figures also reported there)
• Install: pip install clawbio or conda install -c bioconda clawbio
• Also: Claude Code plugin; plain Agent Skills folders for Cursor / VS Code / Codex / Zed
• MCP server: deprecated as of 0.7.0, removed in 0.8.0 — migrate before then

What a “skill” is
A self-contained directory: SKILL.md (declarative spec) + validated Python + demo data + reproducibility helpers.
Many runs write a reproducibility/ bundle with replay commands, environment metadata, and SHA-256 checksums.

Breadth (representative, not exhaustive)
• PharmGx / drug-photo personal dosing cards from genotype
• GWAS lookup across multiple genomic DBs; PGS; fine-mapping (SuSiE / ABF)
• RNA-seq / scRNA / metagenomics / proteomics / methylation
• nf-core wrappers (e.g. rnaseq, scrnaseq, sarek) with strict preflight + reproducibility bundles
• UK Biobank schema navigator; Galaxy Bridge chaining

Design stance worth copying
1. Specification layer ≠ prompt layer — expert choices live in versioned SKILL.md
2. Agent-agnostic execution (same skill under different LLMs / local models)
3. Local-first default; networked skills are named in docs/data-handling.md

Who should care
• Labs tired of one-off LLM scripts that can’t be replayed
• Teams wiring agents into real genomics / PGx / nf-core pipelines
• Contributors who want to ship a peer-reviewable analysis contract, not a chat log

Question: what’s the first skill you’d freeze as a contract instead of regenerating from scratch every week?

text:
Let's talk about $JEANPHIL and $CLAUDIA, and why I'm bullish on the AI Influencer + short-form video narrative.

GTBxUiw6wJdmmkCGZgRHLyYxqu1vG4KtRpeox6yDpump 
2j5SaS7xy776qCBpyPQbZjyQSAtKiFgrwjfErthnW2ZM 

First, the broader sector.

I believe AI Influencers combined with short-form video distribution could become one of the narratives worth watching in the next Meme market cycle.

The underlying logic is simple: AI is turning character creation from a high-cost, low-frequency process into a low-cost, scalable content business that can be operated continuously. In the past, building an influencer required appearance, performance, filming, editing, and long-term management. Now, creators can use AI to design characters, develop personalities, produce short videos, and even operate multiple virtual personas simultaneously.

But what really matters isn't how many characters AI can generate. It's whether those characters can consistently produce content that people want to watch, discuss, and follow.

Short-form video drives distribution, characters accumulate attention, and Memes can become a speculative vehicle for that attention in the crypto market. An AI character can build a distinctive persona through continuous video releases, participate in trending topics, create new memes, and interact with other characters, gradually evolving from a single viral clip into a recognizable IP.

Compared with traditional Memes that rely on an isolated event or a single image, these characters theoretically have the ability to continuously generate new material for distribution. If a character develops a stable audience and cultural recognition, it no longer has to rely entirely on a single viral moment to maintain attention.

If this model gains traction in the crypto market, speculation may shift beyond the next viral image toward AI characters that have already attracted genuine attention on platforms like TikTok and Instagram, can consistently produce content, and have the potential to channel that external attention on-chain.

This is why I've chosen to take a deeper look at JEANPHIL and CLAUDIA. They represent two different paths within this emerging narrative.

JEANPHIL: External traction that has already emerged.

Jean Phil is an AI-generated French male character. His blond bowl cut, curled mustache, brown houndstooth suit, and signature street-style boxing moves create a recognizable visual identity that is easy to imitate.

The character has attracted significant attention on TikTok and Instagram, generating imitations and derivative content. This demonstrates how an AI character with a distinctive persona and a simple, replicable video format can quickly capture attention on mainstream social platforms.

The logic is straightforward: the character attracts external traffic, the content inspires imitations and remixes, and that attention may eventually flow into its on-chain token.

Compared with Memes that rely solely on narratives originating within crypto, JEANPHIL already has an external source of attention. What it needs to prove next is whether that momentum can persist and whether the character's popularity can translate into sustained token demand.

CLAUDIA: From AI creation toward long-term IP development.

CLAUDIA is more focused on long-term IP development. Around Claudia, anabology has been building Claudia Gallery and proposed creating an open version of Hatsune Miku for the AI era. Related initiatives also include AI character creation tools, Agent Skills, and Claudia Local.

The Influencer mode brings this vision closer to the AI Influencer model: by continuously producing videos, maintaining a consistent character identity, and experimenting with high-frequency publishing, it aims to gradually build its own audience.

The logic is that AI lowers content production costs, continuous video output helps establish character recognition, and the character gradually accumulates an audience before attempting to convert that external attention into IP influence and on-chain interest.

Compared with JEANPHIL, CLAUDIA has greater potential in the direction of a long-term AI creator ecosystem. The goal isn't simply to make a character go viral in the short term, but to explore how an AI character can continuously produce content, build an audience, and develop into an expandable, open IP.

However, this path has a longer chain of validation. Being able to produce videos consistently doesn't mean the content will necessarily gain traction. Having creation tools doesn't guarantee the ability to build a successful character. And an open-IP vision doesn't automatically mean the token can capture the resulting value.

Although both projects fall under the broader AI Influencer narrative, their trading theses are different.

JEANPHIL is more focused on existing external traction. The key question is whether that attention can persist and translate into token demand. CLAUDIA is more focused on AI creation capabilities and long-term IP development. The key question is whether it can consistently produce compelling content and build a genuine audience.

What I'm bullish on is the shared potential behind both approaches: AI characters could evolve beyond static images into dynamic IPs that continuously produce content, participate in trending topics, build social relationships, and generate new Memes.

Of course, a compelling sector narrative doesn't mean every related token will appreciate.

We need to distinguish three separate outcomes: an AI character gaining attention, an IP building lasting influence, and a token capturing value from that influence. A character can become popular without benefiting its token. A project can have impressive creation tools without producing viral content. Even if an IP continues to grow, attention may remain entirely off-chain if the token has no meaningful connection to its development.

Therefore, what I'm really looking for isn't the first token to announce that it uses AI, but projects that have demonstrated their ability to attract external attention, consistently produce distributable content, and establish a clear connection between that attention and their tokens.

AI is the production tool, short-form video is the distribution channel, character IP is the vehicle for attention, and the token represents a separate speculative market.

When these four elements become genuinely connected, AI Influencers could evolve from a trending concept into a new Meme narrative with sustained distribution potential.

In my view, the projects most likely to break out will need a distinctive character identity, consistent content distribution, a genuine external audience, and a mechanism for translating attention into token demand. That's why I'm bullish on this direction and have chosen to take a deeper look at JEANPHIL and CLAUDIA.

Its agent quickstart supports MCP, CLI, agent skills, SDK context files, and machine-readable documentation.
The CLI can install a SKILL.md file that teaches coding agents how to use its commands.
The MCP server exposes product operations and structured errors.
Agents can read documentation as Markdown instead of parsing a website.

This matters for anyone building developer tools or SaaS products.

I would start with three things:

Make your API easy to discover. Give agents clear documentation and predictable tool interfaces.

Make authentication safe for machines. Use scoped credentials and explicit permissions.

Make failures easy to fix. Return structured errors that tell agents what went wrong.

The reported Instinct signup is one example. The broader opportunity is making software easier for autonomous agents to operate.

text:
Live internet access is off for all Anthropic internal evals “until further notice.”

That choice is a control story, not a policy story.

If an agent can browse live systems during an eval, it can stumble into real accounts, real forms, and real side effects.

Cutting the wire pushes labs toward “closed world” testing where tools are mocked and targets are isolated.

Here is the tension it creates.

The safest evals look less like deployment, yet the most useful agent skills depend on live internet behavior.

Expect a new market for controlled internet sandboxes that still behave like the real web.

text:
Price every free AI tool by the model bill it creates, not by its download cost. In "8 GitHub Repos To Go Viral and Make Money," posted Oct 8, Greg Isenberg walks through eight open repositories and agent skills he tests on nights and weekends, from launch-video builders to coding agents that work as a team.

His own summary carries the CIO lesson. Most of these tools are free to download, he notes, and the main cost is the model you run them with. Free tools spread quickly because nobody has to raise a purchase order, so the spend shows up later as tokens on someone's API key or corporate card.

The list also shows how uneven that spend can be. One repo runs coding agents as a team, another supports customer research, and one handles voice and dubbing locally. A local tool may cost little in tokens, while an agent team can make many model calls for a single task.

Run a free-tool cost trace this month. The finance partner pulls 60 days of model API charges, including expense reports and corporate cards. The engineering owner maps each API key to the tools calling it. The business owner for each tool states what it produced. Passing looks like every key mapped to a named tool and owner with a monthly cap, repeated each quarter.

Keep the source in proportion. This post is built from the video description only, not a transcript, and the video describes personal and small-business use rather than enterprise deployments.

Free software has always carried a support cost. Agent tools add a metered one, and it lands wherever the API key lives.
